278.title: WCAG 3 Review: Section 3.1 Text Alternatives - collection of comments
278.body:
It was good to be able to review the various types of examples of criteria and how they could potentially be presented in WCAG 3. Hopefully these comments are helpful. This issue contains thoughts and impressions on the Text Alternatives Guideline, How-to, Outcomes and Methods, and scoring as a whole. 

-  The Guideline short text and critical errors seem to imply that all non-text content must have an alternative or it's a failure. However, there are cases where the non-text content is decorative, so a text alternative is not needed. To the uninitiated, they read this and say – every image needs a text alternative – go write it (an incorrect interpretation). It is only by reading details in how-to examples that you learn the details that decorative images really just need to be marked properly (don’t need text developed) and alt=”” is OK. We all know this criteria is one of the most often misunderstood. Even with today's WCAG, this SC is implemented in authoring tools where there is no way to identify any images as decorative. It's important to be clear about the options more up front.  
- Some readers are more visual rather than text (reading) centric. It might be helpful to show some pictorial examples of what is non-text content and then show some good/bad examples of alternatives in their context of use. Or point to some really good articles specifically covering this. 
- Wondering if there should  be a “learn” tab (or instead include on the Design tab) that points out the visual good vs. bad examples for alternative text for the different types of non-text content. Our designers are always asking for visual examples.
- **Plan tab** The plan tab does not cover what I thought it would. Was think ing the Planning Responsibilities tab should explain that the content development team should identify who is responsible for providing the alternative text (depending on your team it may be designer, content writer, etc.), who should review it, decide if you plan to do user testing for it, when in the dev cycle you plan to test and how. You would also need to know if the tool is capable of counting the images tested along with a count of how many images pass or fail the automated test.  Since it will take some time for tools to migrate over to the new conformance model, identifying tools that support the new model may be difficult. The team instead may plan to focus on critical user paths or specific views first.
- **Confusing** This may already be planned for a future iteration of the SC... Most of the information for this guideline focuses on images (including the editor’s note), yet examples and other places in the How-to, etc. talk about additional non-text examples not covered in the ratings or other parts of the supporting material. For example, audio/video files, meaningful audio beeps/buzzes, animations, interactive visual elements like maps and data visualizations are required to have some sort of text label, and in some cases a longer description. The methods and rating/scoring also needs to take the additional types of non-text content into account - those things beyond just images.
- **Functional categories:** 
    - auditory functional categories need to be added (e.g., alternatives for beeps/buzzes given in example for a test that gives auditory indication of right/wrong answers, or the example of an audio file where one needs to provide a text name or short description of the file's content.) 
    - Since many of these functional categories are quite new to WCAG, some text explaining how alternative text is useful for all of these cognitive categories would be helpful - either in the main WCAG 3 document or in a supporting document (Outcome or How-to). For example, I’m not sure how alternative text helps in the functional category of Cognitive – Mental Health. Is this mainly with regard to understanding what interactive images are used for (e.g. icons) that can cause stress to the user? And, while this may be the case, the programmatic provision of alternative text is primarily for assistive technology. Perhaps the outcomes should be teased apart.  There are users that need to identify the usage/meaning of an interactive image in visible text. Other users need it programmatically so AT can relay it to them aurally. 
- Methods: 
    - I'm sure other methods will be added in another iteration, as additional methods are needed. e.g. for media (audio-only, video-only or multimedia),  interactive images (e.g. image maps, complex visualizations, etc.) or sounds used to indicate status (e.g. chime for success, buzzer for failure). 
    - The differences between Functional, decorative, informative, and image of text are not described in the methods. An initial clear definition (or pointer to one) would help. 
    - For scoring, not all automated test tools today count how many images there are or present the alternative text (with the context of use of the image) to make manual inspection for accuracy quicker. Additionally, manual inspection for accuracy may not be possible in very large websites, where sampling must be done. I am unsure as to how such a combination of testing could be reflected in the scoring.
    - It may be difficult for a tester of a complex application or website to quickly know what images they encounter when testing a “path” and which of those are “important”. For example, visually identifying interactive images (links, buttons, icons) and then obtaining the alt text. As a hypothetical example: There’s a number of icons in the top menu of an email application. The important tasks are identified that the user can send, receive, reply, delete, file and forward email. Those icons in the top menu have alt text, but the top level menu also has text attributes icons that do not have alt text. Are those considered “important” to the identified tasks?

279.title: Email: Comment: WCAG 3.0 accessibility guidelines: Accessing a "virtual" meeting using a teleconferencing application such as Zoom - receipt of streamed text content
279.body:
[Comment from Email](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-agwg-comments/2021Mar/0003.html): 

From: Rod Macdonald (rjmacdonald@hawaiiantel.net)

Re: W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0 - W3C First Public Working Draft 21 January 2021

Issue: Accessing a "virtual" meeting using a teleconferencing application such as Zoom - receipt of streamed text content

Background: For purposes of this discussion, individuals who are Deaf-Blind can be grouped into four sub-groups:

(1) The Deaf-Blind individual retains sufficient residual hearing, with amplification and/or other enhancements, to access web content in the of a hearing person.

(2) The Deaf-Blind individual retains sufficient residual vision, with screen magnification and/or other enhancements, to access web content in the manner of a sighted person.

(3) The Deaf-Blind individual cannot access web content via speech or hearing, but can do so using braille.

(4) The Deaf-Blind individual cannot access web content using vision, hearing or braille, and thus cannot access web content at all. (There may be extremely rare cases when the use of unusual technology may circumvent this.)

This discussion refers exclusively to Deaf-Blind individuals in the third group - braille users.

Problem: Spoken language is typically at about 200 words per minute. Adding additional information, such as identifying the speaker and adding punctuation, increases the volume of text being transmitted. The text is never enhanced for braille display.

The average adult braille reader reads at about 15 words per minute. This speed assumes error-free content, somewhat shortened into "contracted" (or "Grade 2) literary braille correctly formatted on paper.

The speed at which streamed text is rendered makes it impossible for 99% of the braille-reading population to read it. The process is made even more impossible by the fact that the braille reader is typically using a braille display that can only hold 40 characters at a time; after the 40-character limit has been reached the display jumps to a new line to continue with incoming text. No existing braille device I am aware of will allow the user to control this streaming process. In reading a document one can "pan" text forward, one 20-character display at a time; but when the input is a continuous stream the braille device will always follow the dynamic cursor - one cannot go back and read prior text while the input stream is active.

For all practical purposes a braille reader can NOT access streamed text during a Zoom meeting. There is no known solution to this accessibility issue.

The only known workaround would be for the meeting to employ a designated CAN (Computer Assisted Notetaker) interpreter to provide real-time communication for the Deaf-Blind consumer. However, a CAN interpreter typically types at about 50 words per minute and must therefore condense the communication, especially when speaker-identification is required, and the physical separation of the meeting and Deaf-Blind consumer makes for additional logistical issues - is the interpreter placed at the meeting site or at the consumer's end? How can the consumer communicate with the interpreter if they are separated? Can the funding source pay for an interpreter located off-site? In any case this solution does not address the problem with the teleconferencing application itself.

(Additional note: Youtube transcripts usually do not identify the speaker.)

280.title: Email: Intopia Feedback - WCAG 3.0 FPWD (5 - Processes)
280.body:
[Comment from Email](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-agwg-comments/2021Feb/0015.html): 

FPWD: Is this approach of using complete processes as the smallest unit of conformance workable for different types of organizations? These include organizations with very large, dynamic, or complex content, medium-sized organizations relying on external accessibility resources, and very small organizations with limited resources?

We believe that the approach can be workable across different types of organisations, as it allows them to focus on making core tasks accessible rather than individual pages, something that should be achievable regardless of organisation size.

Some additional clarity on the definition of a process is required. Processes can be complex (including across multiple pages of a website or views of an application).

Example: For a consumer merchant website that has an ‘Add to Cart’ and ‘Checkout’ step, would this be considered a single process or a number of processes? Depending on interpretation, only part of these steps could be accessible, but the organisation may still be eligible for Bronze status.

281.title: Email: Intopia Feedback - WCAG 3.0 FPWD (4 - Testing)
281.body:
[Comment from Email](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-agwg-comments/2021Feb/0015.html): 

FPWD: We would like constructive feedback on the testing approach, and examples of why you would or would not implement it in your organization.

Significant work would be required to adopt the testing approach within our organisation, but we will consider adoption as the guidelines continue to develop.

Initial areas that would impact on adopting the testing approach include:

  *   Clarity on recording test results – if results need to be recorded per atomic test result for every element, this will increase the amount of work needed to prepare documentation. The greatest impact will be for clients that have retesting that needs to be completed (as multiple sets of documentation may be required dependent on testing methodology)
  *   The suitability of atomic tests will need to be reviewed given that no assistive technology is required as a part of the tests
  *   For any tests that are technology specific, clarity on how often these will be reviewed (and superseded) is needed
  *   List(s) of tests should be collated as the guidelines are finalised – the current content structure makes it difficult for testers to work through a seamless flow of tests

282.title: Email: ITI Comments on First Public Working Draft of W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0 (19 - Representative Sampling)
282.body:
[Comment from Email](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-agwg-comments/2021Feb/0012.html): 
from [PDF](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-agwg-comments/2021Feb/att-0012/ITI_Comments_on_WCAG_3.0_First_Public_Working_Draft_20210224_1_.pdf)

FPWD: Representative sampling is an important strategy to large and complex sites. We welcome suggestions and feedback about the best way to incorporate representative sampling into WCAG 3.0.

Representative sampling will be a highly customized process for different content providers. Sampling techniques have different issues for different types of sites. For example, a sampling process that requires manual testing on 5% of views would be a major challenge for a site with 50,000 views (2,500 manual view tests), let alone one with millions. A requirement that the content provider selects the top ten workflows to test is much more achievable. However, workflow definition may vary greatly between providers so guidance is needed on what level of detail should be included.

287.title: CFAA Response to WCAG 3.0 Draft Release - 2.2.3 Clear Meaning, Foundational Requirement: Unambiguous Text
287.body:
We are concerned that the current classification of unambiguous text as a foundational requirement. Unambiguous text should not be foundational for the following reasons:

•	The concept of "unambiguous" is subjective and varies depending on interpretation.
•	Not all authors are going to be aware of all possible interpretations of a word or phrase.
•	Ambiguity is sometimes crucial to the content of a website, as it allows for the communication of subtle or nuanced ideas. Much informal language is inherently non-literal, even that which would normally not be classified as poetry or artistic work.
•	In some cases, ambiguity itself is essential to the meaning of a sentence, particularly humour (e.g., “Time flies like an arrow, fruit flies like a banana”), and no unambiguous alternative can convey the same idea.

This requirement could inadvertently result in websites becoming overly simplified or corporate in style solely to meet accessibility standards, potentially undermining the richness of diverse web content.
We recommend one of the following changes:
1.	Remove the requirement from the foundational guidelines, making it applicable only in specific contexts (e.g., government websites).
2.	Expand the exceptions to exempt non-corporate websites (e.g., hobbyist sites etc.) from this requirement.

297.title: Non-normative, passing mention of APCA
297.body:
On [https://www.w3.org/WAI/GL/WCAG3/2022/how-tos/visual-contrast-of-text/](https://www.w3.org/WAI/GL/WCAG3/2022/how-tos/visual-contrast-of-text/), on the "Get Started" tab, it currently says:

> The complex, interrelated nature of font and graphic elements to provide visual readability is aided by the use of the APCA algorithm (Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) which allows authors to input color pairs to find a predicted contrast value. That contrast value then defines the minimum useable font weight and size. 

The phrase "is aided" gives the impression of an optional item; perhaps one choice among many for predicting a contrast value.

If there are other options available, which WCAG considers equivalent, please list them.

If APCA is the sole option, please strengthen the wording to indicate that this is the correct and sole way to calculate a predicted contrast value.

299.title: Consider switching to bikeshed for a11y reasons
299.body:
respec, unfortunately has some accessibility issues. Particularly the jump to table of content arrows are links without an accessible name. This problem could be resolved by switching to Bikeshed.

Another problem is actually in using GitHub itself. GitHub does not line wrap HTML files in a pull request in the "unified" view. Arguably this is the right choice for programming languages, but for content, this seems like it would count as a violation of 1.4.10 Reflow. You have to put the content in the "split" view if you want to avoid two-dimensional scrolling. The problem there however is that rendering two files side by side on a significantly zoomed in screen doesn't fit properly either, which is also a violation of 1.4.10 Reflow.


The solve is to use markdown, which GitHub knows can be wrapped safely, and so in unified view, it does line wrap. Because Bikeshed uses markdown instead of HTML, using bikeshed for WCAG 3.0 would solve both problems. Drawback is obviously that Bikeshed has a build step, but this is fairly easy to implement, and is just a one-time task.

302.title: Additional requirement - clarifying responsibilities
302.body:
There is an implicit requirement that I think needs to be made more specific in [Silver requirements](https://w3c.github.io/silver/requirements/): 
The guidelines (in the sense of the whole spec / set of documents) need to make clear what the authors responsibility is.

It wasn't captured in the [WCAG 2.0 requirements](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag2-req/), but it is actually a topic that takes a lot of the discussion time and is one of the key rationales for various decisions. It will be more important to be explicit for WCAG 3 as it is not just for authors.

In a WCAG 3 context it could be generalized to being clear about author responsibility, AT responsibilities, tool responsibilities etc.

I don't have a strong opinion on where it is captured, perhaps as a Design Principle?
"Support various stakeholders in understanding what their responsibility is within the web technology ecosystem. For example, people writing web content can understand what their responsibilities are, and what aspects are the responsibility of the browser, assistive technology etc."

If it were captured as a requirement, it could be more of this form:
"Clarifying responsibilities
The supporting documentation makes it clear where responsibility lies for meeting each guideline. For example, whether it is something a designer or developer needs to do, or whether it can be met by relying on assistive technology, or a combination of both."

304.title: About Bronze - Silver - Gold and scope of views etc.
304.body:
Views and processes: 
It says a view is akin to a Web page. Sowhile evaluating a process the entire Web page(s) is judged, including common header/footer section, right?
But then there is a feedback question about whether an image in the footer without an alt is critical to the process.
So here is a thought: Grading system: Bronze-Silver-Gold 
Bronze: should cover specific views and processes for accomplishing task flows / accessing information.
parts of Web page, like header nav that enable one to find the particular task or section of interest should also be within the scope of this review.
Help documentation linked from the view / process should be within scope
Out of scope: Footer sections / banner / complementary sections as long as they pass non-interference requirements.

Silver: Bronze plus
Cover all declared scope i.e. including footer / banner etc. sections excluded from bronze

Gold: Silver plus
i. Include a mandate to perform usability testing.
ii. Passing selective Level AAA SCs 

Note: While above appears to be in the context of Web content, it can be applied to software / apps too.
Thanks,
Sailesh

307.title: Peer review of color contrast research
307.body:
The work, research, and changes to the color contrast formula is an amazing step in the right direction from what I can tell.

However, I'm not a color scientist and I honestly don't understand the science behind it. I can't find anything regarding whether or not the research has been peer reviewed by other color scientists. This raises further questions and concerns for me because this sort of change could have vast ramifications into the future.

Questions that I'd like answered:

* Has the research and outcomes been peer reviewed? If yes, by who and what are their credentials? If no, when will it be peer reviewed?
* Was the research tested with actual humans? If so, what was the makeup of the sample, sample size, and research methodology? If no, will this happen?
* Is the research reproducible? 

Again, I'm pleased to see progress here, but I'd feel much more comfortable if I could answer those questions.

314.title: About definition in Glossary: Functional need in Explainer for WCAG 3.0
314.body:
Refer to Glossary section in https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0-explainer/

Functional need-
A statement that describes a specific gap in one’s ability, or a specific mismatch between ability and the designed environment or context.
Comment: i. Expressing it in a positive  fashion without "gap", "mismatch" might be more useful. 
ii. Is functional need really the gap or mismatch? The need is the whole of the ability. The gap is what AT provides accommodation for. 
Alternative definition for consideration:
Functional need means skills or abilities required in order to reach specified outcomes while using digital content in the environment or context it is designed for.

Process-
A sequence of steps that need to be completed to accomplish an activity / task from end-to-end.
Comment:
Consider replacing "steps" with "user actions". The focus is on the interaction. The step may also involve a background process that is not a user action which is not working for some reason.
Ability to focus on an inaccessible "user action" will strengthen advocacy efforts as opposed to a "step" in the flow.

325.title: Clarifying and Enhancing Requirements for Sign Language and Subtitles in WCAG 3.0
325.body:
**Title:** Clarifying and Enhancing Requirements for Sign Language and Subtitles in WCAG 3.0

**Summary of Proposal:**

We propose that WCAG 3.0 more clearly define and strengthen the roles of sign language and subtitles as part of its accessibility framework. The current draft lacks specific provisions for sign language and does not distinguish between types of sign language delivery. Subtitles are addressed, but more emphasis is needed on their quality and multilingual support. Our proposals are as follows:

---

### 🔹 Background and Rationale

Users who are Deaf and use sign language as their first or primary language often encounter accessibility barriers when content is provided only in written form. Captions are essential, but they are not always sufficient. Automatically generated subtitles may be inaccurate or fail to convey tone and nuance.

WCAG 2.0 included sign language as a AAA criterion, which led to limited implementation. In practice, many public-facing web videos lack sign language support entirely. WCAG 3.0 presents an opportunity to change this by elevating both sign language and high-quality subtitles as core accessibility features.

Additionally, current guidelines do not distinguish between:

- **Sign language interpretation**: real-time signing used in live contexts.
- **Sign language translation**: carefully prepared signing created in advance, with attention to clarity, accuracy, and viewer accessibility.

We strongly recommend that WCAG 3.0 encourage **sign language translation** for pre-recorded videos intended for repeated viewing by a wide audience, as it offers greater precision and quality.

---

### 🔹 Proposed Enhancements

1. **Explicit inclusion as Outcomes**  
   - Clearly define "Provision of videos with sign language translation" and "Provision of subtitles synchronized with audio content" as distinct Outcomes in WCAG 3.0.

2. **Integration into Supplemental Requirements**  
   - Position sign language (translation and interpretation) and subtitles as essential elements that supplement basic accessibility for Deaf and hard-of-hearing users.

3. **Specific reflection in Conformance Levels**  
   - **Bronze**: Basic subtitling (e.g., auto-generated or simple captions).  
   - **Silver**: Accurate, descriptive subtitles and sign language (context-appropriate: interpretation or translation).  
   - **Gold**: Comprehensive support, including culturally appropriate sign language and multilingual subtitle options.

4. **Recognition of Language Preferences**  
   - Align with “Preferred Language” principles by supporting signed and written language alternatives based on users’ native or preferred languages (e.g., JSL, ASL, English, etc.).

5. **Guidance on Quality Standards**  
   - Include best practices or minimum quality recommendations for subtitles and sign language content (e.g., accuracy, speaker identification, emotional tone, cultural context).

---

We believe these additions will strengthen WCAG 3.0 and help ensure that accessibility guidelines meet the needs of sign language users worldwide. We would be happy to assist further in drafting or reviewing guideline language related to these topics.

Thank you for your consideration.

comments.body: @InfoGapBuster please can you clarify? Are you stating that at the Gold level, website text should be translated to or presented in sign languages? And that the rationale is that sign language is the first, preferred or only language for some Deaf sign language users?

> [@InfoGapBuster](https://github.com/InfoGapBuster) please can you clarify? Are you stating that at the Gold level, website text should be translated to or presented in sign languages? And that the rationale is that sign language is the first, preferred or only language for some Deaf sign language users?

@md84419 

Thank you for your question, and for the opportunity to clarify our proposal.

**1. On the scope of Gold-level requirements**
We are not suggesting that *all website text* must be translated into sign languages at the Gold level. Rather, our proposal is that:

* For **multimedia content (e.g., video, audio)** that is intended for repeated viewing or broad distribution, **sign language translation** (not only captions) should be strongly recommended and recognized as a Gold-level outcome.
* This ensures that Deaf sign language users—who cannot achieve full comprehension through written captions alone—are provided equitable access.

**2. The rationale: sign language as a first, preferred, or only accessible language**
Yes, the rationale is indeed that for many Deaf people, sign language is their first or preferred language. For some, it is the only fully accessible language. This is supported by well-documented evidence:

* In the United States, **250,000–500,000 individuals** use ASL as their primary language, according to Gallaudet University and related studies ([Gallaudet](https://www.gallaudet.edu/documents/Research-Support-and-International-Affairs/ASL_Users.pdf)). Broader surveys indicate millions of adults use some form of sign language ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36423340/)).
* Globally, the **World Federation of the Deaf** estimates about **70 million Deaf individuals**, many of whom rely on national sign languages as their main language ([Nimdzi](https://www.nimdzi.com/sign-language-market-gaps-trends-opportunities-for-growth/)).
* In Japan, approximately **60,000 individuals** use Japanese Sign Language (JSL) as their first or main language ([Researcher Life](https://discovery.researcher.life/download/article/c38f07af89d330f1b130b27cea148085/full-text)).
* Critically, **90–97% of Deaf children are born to hearing parents**, often without early access to sign language, which creates risks of **language deprivation** and long-term cognitive impacts ([BMC Public Health](https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12889-025-23456-y), [Hall et al. 2019](https://cssh.northeastern.edu/cali/wp-content/uploads/sites/57/2024/09/Hall-et-al-2019-deaf-children-need-language-not-just-speech.pdf)).

These figures demonstrate that sign language provision is not an optional enhancement but a fundamental requirement for equitable access.

---

**In summary:**

* We are calling for **multimedia content** (not general website text) to include sign language translation at the Gold level.
* The rationale is that **millions of people worldwide rely on sign language as their first, preferred, or only accessible language**, and that without it, accessibility goals cannot be met.

Also  (I believe) that Gold can be achieved without doing everything listed at the gold level.   But we have not finalized what any of the levels will be so - we really can't say anything definitive about Gold or silver or bronze.

@InfoGapBuster I agree with everything you've written, but I would go further.

My view is that the Gold level should be treated as a Gold standard - an aspirational benchmark that organisations strive to achieve.

- **We call for the following guideline (supplimental requirement): sign language users should have access to a sign language alternative for website text.**
- **The rationale is (a) millions of people worldwide rely on sign language as their first, preferred, or only accessible language, and that without it, accessibility goals cannot be met; (b) Discrimination based on language is prohibited under various treaties and frameworks; ensuring that individuals receive information in their preferred language is considered a reasonable accommodation in some jurisdictions.**

The above statement is made based on the following rationale:
•	Discrimination based on language is prohibited under various international, regional, and national legal frameworks (e.g. national laws enactments of treaties and charters such as Universal Declaration of Human Rights, International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, and American Convention on Human Rights). Ensuring that individuals receive information in their preferred language can be considered a reasonable accommodation to prevent discrimination, especially if language barriers are a factor of ethnicity, nationality, or other protected characteristics.
•	In the US, Americans with Disabilities Act requires public entities (state and local government) to provide auxilary aids and services when needed for effective communicaiton with people who are deaf or hard of hearing.
•	In the UK, the BSL (Scotland Act) 2015, the BSL Act 2022, the Equality Act 2010, providing sign language interpreting & translation is often a “reasonable adjustment” in public services, courts, health, education etc.
•	In Ireland, the Irish Sign Language Act 2017 requires public bodies to provide ISL in certain cases.
•	In South Korea, the Korean Sign Language Act 2016 requires national & local governments to provide Korean Sign Language translations in certain circumstances.
•	In Philippines, Filipino Sign Language is mandated in official communication involving Deaf persons and in deaf education.
•	In New Zealand, New Zealand Sign Language Act 2006 requires translation into NZ Sign Language in certain official and public circumstances.
•	ISO/IEC FDIS 12792:2024 (Transparency Taxonomy of AI Systems) emphasizes the importance of clear and accessible information for stakeholders, which includes considerations for language and comprehensibility. Note that at the time of writing, this specification is a final draft, conditional on final publication.
•	CNIL Recommendations on AI and GDPR Compliance recommends providing information in a manner that is easily understandable to individuals, potentially involving translations or adaptations to preferred languages
•	ISO 24495-1:2023 and ISO/IEC 29184:2020 emphasizes the importance of accessibility and comprehension in the individuals' preferred language; requires communications (e.g., consent, redress) be clear and culturally appropriate.
•	Additional specific examples:
       •	EU GDPR Article 12(1): Requires information to be provided in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language.
       •	EU GDPR Recital 39: Emphasizes that any information addressed to the public or the data subject should be concise, easily accessible, and easy to understand.
       •	EU AI Act Articles 14 and 50: Requires information to be provided in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language.
       •	EU AI Act Recitals 71 and 72: Emphasizes that any information addressed to the public or the data subject should be concise, easily accessible, and easy to understand.

@md84419 

Based on Michael Davey’s comment, I would like to further refine my earlier proposal, *“3. Specific reflection in Conformance Levels,”* into more detailed categories.

As a Deaf person, I have often seen that when sign language is not defined as a required criterion, many organizations and companies choose not to include it in their web content and instead rely solely on captions. This is why I strongly propose that WCAG 3.0 explicitly include sign language as a requirement, to provide stronger motivation for its adoption.

Currently, resources for sign language interpretation and translation—qualified agencies and professionals—are limited. Precisely for this reason, WCAG should encourage more proactive implementation. This would generate demand and help expand the pool of available resources. Moreover, as more sign language interpretation and translation is produced, valuable data will be accumulated, which could eventually serve as training material for future AI-based translation technologies.

In this way, by positioning sign language clearly within WCAG 3.0, we can not only achieve greater accessibility today but also create momentum for innovation and broader inclusion in the future.

Based on this, I would like to propose the following framework within the **WCAG 3.0 conformance levels (Bronze / Silver / Gold):**

**Bronze (minimum accessibility)**

* Multimedia content: Provide auto-generated or basic captions.
* Text content: Sign language alternatives are not required.

**Silver (intermediate accessibility)**

* Multimedia content: Provide accurate captions and, where appropriate, sign language support (real-time interpretation or pre-recorded translation).
* Text content: Provide sign language alternatives as a reasonable accommodation when needed (not required, but recommended).

**Gold (highest accessibility / aspirational benchmark with cultural considerations)**

* Multimedia content: Provide high-quality sign language interpretation and translation with cultural and linguistic appropriateness, along with multilingual captions and support for expressive diversity.
* Text content: Provide sign language alternatives for key information (e.g., policy documents, educational materials, terms of service), taking into account the user’s preferred language (e.g., Japanese Sign Language, International Sign).

I note that this issue is currently tagged as '[Path: Image and Media Alternatives & Control](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues?q=state%3Aopen%20label%3A%22Path%3A%20Image%20and%20Media%20Alternatives%20%26%20Control%22)'. However, what is being discussed here is actually text alternatives. In addressing these requirements, the document probably needs a new section in 2.2 Text & Wording (not in 2.1 Image and Media Alternatives).

333.title: Consider using the GitHub Releases Feature on a periodic basis for WCAG3; Also referencing comment contributors where possible/desired
333.body:
Github Releases provide a mechanism to collect a list of contributions , even if its just a Git Log redaction, of people who contributed from GitHub Issues. These can include contributions from people who are not full participants in the creation of the document but who make some kind of useful contribution on a GitHub Issue.

## Example: Sustainability Guidelines Community Group Draft Release:

https://github.com/w3c/sustyweb/releases/tag/v1.0-D2

Ideally this is a way that a log of people who contribute could be kept for positive purposes, such as showing growth or background of contribution on GitHub before potentially becoming an IE or part of a Member Organization. 

My intent is that I had a positive experience with the Draft Sustainability Guidelines with the way that comments I made were credited in release statements. It could become unwieldy to use this feature all the time, but on a periodic basis it could be a good addition something like it.

337.title: ANDI's Output different from the screen reader's: One answer missing from an FAQ
337.body:
Refer to https://www.ssa.gov/accessibility/andi/help/faq.html
Q. Why is ANDI's Output different from the screen reader's?
Comment:
One reason that is mentioned in the tutorial is omitted from the answers listed against this question: 
If the accessible name for button contains the word  "button", a screen reader appears to speak that word twice. In fact the screen reader is doing its job as expected: voice the role. The accessibility name in fact is the culprit which should exclude the role from the accessible name.

340.title: 1.4 Distinguishable - Missing Change of font family
340.body:
PROBLEMS
A) [Success Criterion 1.4.4 Resize Text ](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#resize-text)(alias Change font size)
does not have an equivalent for Change font family.
This is particularly usefull for dyslexic audience.
This service is already available in most browsers and ebook reading systems (by changing default font, and overriding authors'/editors' font.

B) The WCAG 2.2 is supposed to fully cover the European Accessibility Act (EAA). But this is false on this point.
Annex I, section II, paragraph b, sub-paragraph v
"Presenting in FONTS of adequate size and suitable SHAPE, taking into account foreseeable conditions of use and using sufficient contrast, as well as adjustable spacing between letters, lines and paragraphs."
This has been forgotten in the [EPUB Accessibility - EU Accessibility Act Mapping](https://www.w3.org/TR/epub-a11y-eaa-mapping/#annex-I-section-III-b-v).
Nota : the oversight has been reported in ticket https://github.com/w3c/epub-specs/issues/2752

SOLUTION

Add a new Success criterion 1.4.14 Change font family.
Sufficient Techniques : Using a technology that has commonly-available user-agents that allow the adding of OpenDyslexic, and its activation as default font family.

369.title: Decoration is still information, of course ... Guideline 2.1.1 Image alternatives
369.body:
I am perplexed, and have been for a long time, how "decorative" imagery in WCAG is defined and discounted and dismissed as non-informational. 

I was having a discussion last week with a web designer who was claiming that any stock photo, like a diverse group of people in a grassy field, reading books, in front of a university building, was "decorative" and therefore not required by law to be described. I have heard other people say portrait photos, of say, organizational leaders, are "decorative," plus many other similar claims, and of course, when a decorative element is used, like a fleur-de-lis, or whatever, a visual designer still chose to include that image in the interface for some reason, right? Is there a connection to French culture? Is there some reference to a lily or iris? Why was it placed there? Since visual designers ALWAYS have the option to include or not include imagery, and when they do choose to include it, it always has some rhetorical purpose, I think this "decorative" loophole in WCAG needs to be eliminated. 

No. 1, what is the purpose of this "decorative" exemption? If that answer is not audience-oriented, which I'm assuming it's not, then is WCAG for the ease and convenience of the designers, or for the inclusion of the audience members? 

No. 2., if people who are blind are excluded from learning about all of these "decorative" elements on websites and mobile apps, how will people who cannot see or cannot see well be included fully in societal discussions? 

No. 3, what is the downside of eliminating this loophole? More Audio Description for websites, more of a focus on inclusivity for blind people, more data and content for listeners and readers? I just don't understand in any way why this exemption should exist. My assumption is that it provides a loophole for computer scientists, web designers, and content creators to avoid tough decisions about their workflow and responsibilities to diverse audiences. What else could it be? 

No. 4, maybe a long time ago, a bit of extra screenreader text could have microscopically slowed down a webpage page loading, but those days are long gone. So is this a technical issue, and if so, is this a contemporary (or antiquated) technical issue? 

No. 5, already inferred, but if "decorative" is going to be kept as a loophole to avoid full media accessibility, then WCAG is obligated to clearly define "decorative" in a legal sense, and also justify why decorative imagery is not information that also should be shared with all audience members.

Hope that helps!

Commenting on the following:

2.1 Image and media alternativesDeveloping
Guideline 2.1.1 Image alternatives
Users have equivalent alternatives for images.

Which foundational requirements apply?
Foundational requirement: Decorative imageDeveloping
[Decorative](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-decorative) [images](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-image) are [programmatically](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-programmatically-determinable) hidden.

comments.body:
This was much better scoped in WCAG 2 where it was "pure decoration". Most "pure decoration" images are now able to be implemented with CSS. Defining decorative as "Would removing the image impact how people understand the page?" is way too low of a bar. With this definition, any portrait photo in a company index is decorative. Any content image in a news article is decorative, because the page is still understandable and it doesn't affect how.

Neither impact, nor understand are defined here.

This topic arises almost every week on one accessibility forum or another, and there is no "right" answer. Furthermore, opinion has changed over the last 20 years or so. Back then, there was pretty much universal acceptance that text alternatives for images should just be the information that is necessary for understanding the content. Almost no one would have said that text alternatives are required for decorative images.

However, in recent years, some people have started to say that they like decorative images to be described because they convey the feel of the website even if they do not provide information. The problem is that this is a serious impediment to screen reader users who do not want to hear all that fluff, and they are annoyed that it slows them down. Anecdotally, I would say that opinion is split about 50:50, and I would say there should be a substantial majority one way or the other before changing anything.

We now have ridiculous situations where content creators are over-compensating by writing lengthy literal descriptions of decorative images. It's not uncommon for these to comprise several sentences totalling as much as 50 words. It can be necessary for a screen reader user to listen to a large proportion of this before deciding it's fluff they don't need to listen to.

I recently suggested that a new CSS "prefers-reduced-fluff" property should be introduced so users can choose whether to hear the descriptions of decorative images. I was only partially joking but I don't think there is any other way to satisfy both camps.

FWIW, I don't accept the premise that undescribed decorative images discriminate against blind people in some way. You may as well argue that painting our walls any colour other than white, or hanging wallpaper discriminates against people who can't see it. Would you have us all wear the same colour clothes?

Great points, Eric; I agree with these calls for better definitions. ...

   it takes, and as I wrote earlier, the easy solution to someone who doesn't
   want it, or has had enough, one button push to move on to the next piece of
   content.
   - "I don't think there is any other way to satisfy both camps." ...
   There is, actually: Provide the robust content, per WCAG guidelines, and
   create usable screenreader systems, coding schemas, and writing
   templates/training that allow people to make navigable content and to
   easily navigate to what they want to listen to, and for how long. *Why
   should people who want less information be privileged over people who want
   more, when the less crowd and more crowd can be both satisfied with the

Almost no one would have said that text alternatives are required for decorative images.

WCAG said literally that there is only an exception for images that are “pure decoration” since 2008. Just being mildly decorative never qualified for the exception. WCAG comes from when you had to use images to render shadows for containers. When you used image replacement techniques for headings. You cannot argue that the image of a person in an index of personell is “pure decoration” or that news images are.

> However, in recent years, some people have started to say that they like decorative images to be described because they convey the feel of the website even if they do not provide information.

> The problem is that this is a serious impediment to screen reader users who do not want to hear all that fluff, and they are annoyed that it slows them down. Anecdotally, I would say that opinion is split about 50:50, and I would say there should be a substantial majority one way or the other before changing anything.

Yes, some people do too much, and in some situations it’s too much. This can happen.

It's not uncommon for these to comprise several sentences totalling as much as 50 words. It can be necessary for a screen reader user to listen to a large proportion of this before deciding it's fluff they don't need to listen to.

Again, this is not a requirement, and people might overcorrect. I have not seen this, I still see the majority of images undescribed. The WCAG 3 wording forbids alternative text for every image that does not contribute to the understanding of the page at all. Even if it would be interesting or good context.

The rest of your comment is irrelevant to this issue.

I think the WCAG aim is "equivalent" information, not too much, not too
little; in the Goldilocks zone. At this point, I think it is very difficult
to argue that any audience member is getting "too much" information,
holistically, by trying to use the web with a screenreader, at least in
comparison to the individuals using the same web pages through sight and a
visual interface with the same informational needs; in other words, in an
equivalent state of need and use. So I think this argument is a red
herring. It's sort of like saying, there are way too many books in the
library, way too many shows on television, way too many movies in the
theater; novels are too long; and so on. The simple answer: When you, as
the consumer of the information, have enough to satisfy you, do something
else.

If you flip this idea on its head, the argument becomes ridiculous to
suggest that sighted people have too many photos, too many videos, too many
maps, too much visual media everywhere all of the time, so the answer is to
somehow and in some way arbitrarily decide for everyone what the *right*
amount of information is. Don't you really think the audience should
decide, not the WCAG board?

370.title: Equivalence in "image alternatives" 2.1 Image and media alternatives Developing Guideline 2.1.1 Image alternatives
370.body:
Equivalence (or "Equivalent") information on image alternatives has been a greatly abused standard under WCAG 2.0. This problem has its legacy in "alt text" originally being a computer science adaptation (not a disability studies-oriented suggestion) to early-days loading problems with images, providing a text label to alert users that, yes, a photo was supposed to be in that outlined box. 

But in today's world, what happens in practice most often is that "alt text" becomes a legal compliance standard for "equivalent," and alt text often reads like a cryptic file name. For example, an alt text / equivalent "standard" of "dog32234.jpg" means an image on a website is legally complaint in all ways, but, of course, it fails miserably any common-sense idea about equivalent information transfer. We don't know if this is a Great Dane or Chihuahua; or it could be Dog, The Bounty Hunter; or it could be a slang label for a person who is a friend or a dastardly creep; what is the "dog" doing in the park? What does the park look like? None of those questions have certain or even probable answers, and they all would include a great deal of nuance, if described properly, as well as equivalent informational content. When I shared the alt text of "dog32234.jpg," did you picture a French Bulldog, named Pinky, on a sandy beach in Hawaii, with a beachball in her mouth, running alongside the waves? Or did you picture a Rottweiler, named Buddy, sprawled out on a grassy field, with the sun on his smiling face, while he's beginning to roll on his back? Or something else entirely? That's what I mean. The image is distinct in some way. It was chosen for some rhetorical purpose by the page designer. It is filled with information; what kind of beachball? A blue and white beachball, or a rainbow colored beachball, or a black beachball; those all change the information and the subtextual and unspoken communication happening between viewer of the image and the creator of the image / designer of the page.

Why does all of that matter? If it doesn't matter, then I suggest we turn off all images on the Internet for a day, and provide people only with the alt text that exists right now, and determine if that has any material effect on the use and understanding of the web. If you think it would, then I think you would agree with me that equivalent needs to be much, much better defined, and also extended in guidance to standards for describing people, maps, tables, charts, data visualizations, etc., beyond just the title of the image, and a one-sentence overview. Think about how much of the current Internet is inaccessible, in terms of just new photographs, maps, and data visualizations, and how that inaccessibility is EXPONENTIALLY increasing every single day because of a lack of standards and legal requirements about media accessibility. Just think of Instagram, as an example, where more than 1 BILLION mostly inaccessible photos are being uploaded a day. The current "requirement" for using Instagram makes adding even cryptic alt text a hidden process; Instagram is pushing people to use GenAI; the GenAI is providing very limited descriptions, including of people, like Might be a man, wearing glasses. That is not equivalent to what a sighted person can see, of course. ... So Instagram, Facebook, etc., are perpetuating and growing media inaccessibility based on their designs and lack of accessibility support. That's purposeful, because they don't have to, and NOBODY, including WCAG guidelines, are even suggesting that they need to do this in any meaningful way. 

Please change that trajectory by defining "equivalent" in a meaningful way, in relation to information exchange (academic literature does it, so you can borrow from those scholars).

The fact that authors use inappropriate text alternatives does not mean there is a loophole. A lot of testers don't test the success criterion correctly, and automated tools cannot yet verify whether a text alternative is appropriate. Many testers say that websites are WCAG conformant when they are not. None of this means there is a loophole either. It's just people not doing their job properly.

If the text alternative for an image is inappropriate, the website is non-conformant, although that does not necessarily mean it is inaccessible. The problem is mostly due to a lack of education and partly due to authoring platforms that don't help authors apply the appropriate text alternatives. WCAG 3 can't and won't fix this.

There is a relatively new phenomenon that is making this even worse. In the old days, you wrote the text alternative when you added an image to a website. Now, many organisations store their images in a digital asset management system and the text alternatives are stored with them. This means the text alternative is created without any knowledge of the context in which the image will be used. For any given image, the text alternative may be appropriate in some places it's used and not appropriate in others. The absence of context means that the text alternatives are invariably literal descriptions of the image contents.

You raise good points about the technical act of decontextualizing images,
in large databases, and then the ensuring need to recontextualize them for
a new use, for AD to be effective (and sometimes even appropriate). That is
a complicated issue and deserves much more discussion, not really central
to this particular issue of how to guide the creation of "image"
description in general, though. Just to start that discussion, I think the
AD should be crafted for each use, and then logged, so a forensic
recontextualization process could occur. Right now, in most cases, that is
impossible. But it also would take a major shift in archiving practices and
a variety of interdisciplinary steps to address this concern. Again, I
think we're drifting far away from the point of the discussion down that
road.

I also don't really understand your point about WCAG compliance not being
carried out properly, so therefore WCAG can't do anything about it? That
seems like a defeatist attitude, and like WCAG might as well just close
down the shop, if that's the case. I know you didn't mean it that way,
though, so for a productive solution, how about WCAG3 tightens up its
definitions, adds more scaffolding, creates more metrics and benchmarks and
closes this gap between intent and practice? I think that's what we all
want, right?

>

WCAG can only define what conformance is, it cannot enforce conformance. That's what laws and policies are for. And if your alternative text does not meet the success criterion, and "dog123.jpg" generally doesn't, then you don't conform to WCAG.

So how does WCAG respond to claims in its name of conformance, like "This
website is WCAG compliant," when it's not, per the examples provided? Can
it create a cease and desist letter for using that label, which everyday
consumers can send when they find violations (if so, is 1 violation enough,
2, 5, 10, 100)? Just wondering where the buck stops on that one? Because I
highly doubt there will ever be a government-funded WCAG police force
roaming the internet for it, shutting down non-compliant websites. If WCAG
is legally "required" but not legally enforced, what real value does it
have in practice? ... Also, I think that if WCAG fails to properly frame
the bar for compliance, with lots of room for interpretation, loopholes,
and fuzzy definitions, then most corporations (and people) will continue to
reach for the lowest and most generous benchmarks of compliance possible. I
was at one of the world's biggest tech companies last week, and was told
about meetings there, where the overriding question regularly is "how does
this company initiative address legal compliance?" Not, how does this
company initiative position us as thought leaders in accessibility, or
innovators, but more like, where is the lowest bar, let's hit that, and
only respond when the bar is raised and not meeting it will be a
public embarassment. ... But, of course, too rigid of guidelines would be
counterproductive, too, because so few people would meet them (i.e. 95+
percent of websites already are failing for people who are blind). So is
this really an exercise in "moving the ball forward," or in significantly
raising standards to the culturally appropriate level for our time, or in
pollyannaish hopefulness, or something else?

This is legally enforced in different ways, for example as a customer you have rights in case a website is not accessible. This is mostly civil rights, so you can sue a website for not being accessible and WCAG is then used as the standard to measure against.

In the EU the European Accessibility Act does require companies legally to meet WCAG 2.1 as part of the EN 301 549. The countries are required to create agencies that ensure that everyone in the market that falls under the EAA meets its requirements. There are fines for non-compliance. (This has started only this year, there will be a lot happening in the next 12 to 18 months. Also this is simplified, of course.)

W3C does not enforce standards like WCAG, it's the place where stakeholders come together and agree what the standards should be. Keeping to the standard is technically optional, but companies have an interest in operability. W3C has neither the budget nor the intent to review billions of websites.

Hope that helps.

Yes, thank you. I think the EAA is very promising, and I'm wondering how
the DOJ's final ruling will be enforced next year, creating our own version
of a similar idea. ...

371.title: "image" as the label in "image alternatives" 2.1 Image and media alternatives Developing Guideline 2.1.1 Image alternatives
371.body:
While technically accurate, to a degree, the "image" label in WCAG is severely outdated and should be updated. 

No. 1, when most people think about "image," they do not think about maps, tables, charts, data visualizations, etc., at least in any significant depth, which creates major accessibility issues for audience members who can't see a map on a website and get as the "image description" something like "Yellowstone National Park map.jpg," which, of course, is totally unusable even for cognitive mapping exercises, like where is Old Faithful in relation to Yellowstone Falls?

I suggest aligning with the use of "Audio Description" by [The American Council of the Blind](https://adp.acb.org/), [The American Foundation of the Blind](https://www.afb.org/aw/22/6/17586), the [Royal National Institute of the Blind](https://www.rnib.org.uk/living-with-sight-loss/assistive-aids-and-technology/tv-audio-and-gaming/audio-description-ad/), the [World Blind Union](https://www.pathstoliteracy.org/resource/results-first-worldwide-survey-audio-description-activity/), and dozens of other associations of blind people around the world, who use that term more often than others (like image description, verbal description, etc.), plus associations of public attractions, such as museums (i.e., [The American Alliance of Museums](https://www.aam-us.org/2019/08/28/partnering-with-the-blind-to-make-exhibits-more-accessible/)), libraries ([Washington State University Libraries](https://crln.acrl.org/index.php/crlnews/rt/printerFriendly/26803/34733)), national parks ([U.S. National Park Service](https://www.nps.gov/subjects/hfc/upload/DOI_CreatveCommAD22MAR2018.pdf)), etc.  ... I have documented about 20 different terms for this same basic process of audiovisual translation/remediation, and many organizations, including of blind people, think first of video/TV as the application for AD. Yet the vast majority of people working in this field academically (in the humanities) use AD more generally (computer scientists almost entirely use "image" description as the term, more on that below). Practitioners might just refer to it as "description," but there is a long history of its development as a very specific label in the United States (per this link, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0145482X221116903), which originated in the United States and then spread to the rest of the world. 

2. In the humanities, in academia, scholars generally split their interests into two camps: A. Dynamic Audio Description, for videos, TV, sporting events, theater, dance, etc., and B. Static Audio Description for photographs, illustrations, maps, tables, charts, etc. I'm in Camp B. ... It's one of those situations where no matter what term gets chosen, other people are going to be using different labels. So we pick the most prominent one among the biggest audience of listeners, aligning with people who are blind or with low-vision (focusing on the primary audience for the description, rather than the primary producers of the descriptions). Also, if you want to dig deeper into this rabbit hole, I recommend checking out the [ARSAD conference](https://webs.uab.cat/arsad/), which is the only major AD conference in the world for scholars. 

3. In legal terminology, the issue gets more vague, with references to "descriptive aids" and "alternative texts." But, in short, making media accessible to the general public — regardless of a person’s sensory abilities — is a legal mandate that has been in place and reinforced in the U.S. for decades, starting with [Section 504 and Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973](https://webaim.org/articles/laws/usa/rehab), and expanded by a variety of other key pieces of legislation or rulings, including the [Americans with Disabilities Act in 1990](https://www.ada.gov/), the [2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design](https://www.ada.gov/law-and-regs/design-standards/2010-stds/), and most recently, the final [Department of Justice ruling](https://www.ada.gov/resources/2024-03-08-web-rule/) on regulations of Title II of the ADA. There is a consistency of intent among the laws but not labels. WCAG should help to set this standard, not to confuse it even more by loosely using a term that is too narrow. 

4. I could go point by point why I think AD is the best term for this subject matter (AD, by the way, is both a product and a process, making it even more confusing!). But I'd say the two main competitors for the label are Audio Description and Image Description (which the computer science / tech folks use). In short, though, Image Description, for me, and probably for all of the organizations that have opted instead for AD, is too limiting of a term, because most people would not call a map, a table, or a chart an image, even if it is presented as an "image," and beyond that, we often describe other static media, such as waysides signs (in national parks, for the content on the signs as well as the physical environment around them), plus landscapes/views, on their own, exhibits, objects/artifacts, such as statues, [university campuses and buildings (inside and out)](https://unidescription.org/account/project/export/324), classroom materials, and so on. Image Description just doesn't work very well in those cases.

Hope that helps!

Commenting on:


2.1 Image and media alternativesDeveloping
Guideline 2.1.1 Image alternatives

Foundational requirement: Equivalent text alternativeDeveloping
Equivalent

text alternatives
are available for [images](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-image) that convey [content](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-content).

374.title: Grammar issue on 2.3.4? "users have interactive components"
374.body:
The text of Guideline 2.3.4 Expected behavior is:
"Users have [interactive components](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-interactive-element) that behave as expected."

Its not really the Users that have the components; its the application or website that has the component. In this case it would be more appropriate to say something like "users can navigate using interactive components that behave as expected."

381.title: Interactive Content? Escaping the linear Page/Form/linear media paradigm.
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
Path: User control and prevent harm
381.body:
I would greatly appreciate some clear recognition in WCAG 3 that not all in-browser content is oriented towards linear page/document/form abstractions. We produce medical simulation software (for training nurses and lifesavers) which runs in the browser, and I must say it has been an uphill struggle to find clear guidance which were not all about pages and forms. 

In particular, the browsable/operable distinction (which is central to many AT implementations) is poorly represented in WCAG for those who need to build anything with an interaction model based on something more rich than just form-filling and submission. The time-based media guidelines in earlier versions of WCAG seemed only vaguely applicable to content such as games and simulations. Time-based media is neither Prerecorded nor Live when scripted animations have their own logic, or include random elements, often with a huge variety of unpredictable output. Where do these kinds of multimedia fit in? How do we approach the construction of audio descriptions for something which is different for every user, every single time?

Or, say, if you have a cutaway view of some complex machine or organ, which allows you to 'open' layers and reveal parts within, is it more appropriate to say that the user 'browses' or 'operates' this content? You're not 'operating' the heart when you inspect a diagram of the valves and atria, surely?

Or, say, you have a lifesaving algorithm, explaining which steps should be taken depending on the symptoms you observe. How can you talk about a 'meaningful sequence', when there are multiple possible sequences through the algorithm, and the only truly meaningful sequence is the one which saves the life of the patient, yet WCAG says "only one meaningful sequence is sufficient" in this case. This particular piece of guidance is useless, but we can earn compliance by compromising the quality of our content to a potentially lethal degree.

I do understand the historical emphasis in guiding people in accessible *page* construction, and media players since so much of the web is about that, but I hope that other kinds of content, especially more fluid application-like interactions will get explicit attention in the new WCAG. 

I've been advised that there are ongoing efforts elsewhere to produce 'accessible game design' guidelines, which would be very useful for training simulations too, but where is the w3c in that effort? And what use are those separate efforts, if our games and simulations are nonetheless legally obliged to be WCAG compliant?

382.title: Changing disability model from medical to social
382.body:
The current document talks a lot about "people with disabilities" but doesn't mention at what times those people are disabled. This feels like an awkward adherence to the medical model of disability, where someone's condition makes them disabled. For WCAG 3.0 it would be better to include something about the aim of the document being that applications and websites are built so as not to disable people. 

Some examples:
1) a user with sensory disorders is disabled using a website when the site uses automatically playing audio and video; they may not be disabled when the site doesn't do that
2) an autistic user is disabled when the site uses jargon and idiom that the user isn't used to. If the site uses plain language, the user isn't disabled
3) a user with limited dexterity is disabled when a site or application requires a greater amount of dexterity

In these instances, the user is disabled by the website or application, not their condition. 

When talking to businesses about disabilities and web accessibility, the greatest success I've had is when I talk to them about changing their mindset from "disabled people" to "people we disable". They're more likely to accept that their actions are what disables people and take action to prevent that, rather than trying to build something "to help disabled people." Not disabling people seems an easier concept to grasp.

A small acknowledgement in the introduction that the aim is to prevent people being disabled by apps and websites would go a long way towards shifting the conversation, making it easier for people who design and build websites to understand the impact their actions take (it's their actions that disable people).

386.title: Notes that are significant  need to be distinguished as normative?
386.body:
WCAG 2.X section 5.1 states that notes are not normative. Is this how notes are to be treated in WCAG 3.0 too?
Consider In WCAG 3 (Sept 2025 draft): 
Note 1 for abbreviation: "This includes initialisms, acronyms, and numeronyms".
Likewise, for audio description:
Note For audiovisual media: "audio description provides information about actions, characters, scene changes, on-screen text, and other visual content". (This note actually clarifies what "important visual detail" in the main definition means without leaving it up for interpretation.
while:
Note 2: "Some companies have adopted what used to be an initialism as their company name. In these cases, the new name of the company is the letters (for example, Ecma) and the word is no longer considered an abbreviation".

Would it be possible to distinguish notes that are significant that they should be normative  and those that are not?
Is it possible to bifurcate these as, say, "Caution" or "Tips" and "Notes" and state that caution / tips are part of normative content? Then the first note  for abbreviation and the one for audio description above should perhaps be caution / tips and the one that relates to Ecma may remain a note. I have no problems if a different term is used to distinguish them instead of caution or tips as suggested if you think such a distinction is needed. I would not makes "notes" as the normative one as it will be a break from WCAG 2.X and lead to confusion.
Thanks

387.title: Measurable test coverage: Silver requirement?
387.body:
A challange in WCAG 1 and 2 is that it's impossible to say anything about conformance unless a web page is fully tested. Because you don't always have a complete picture, it is difficult to say anything about the accessibility. It'd be very helpful if in addition to allowing pages to conform if not 100% of the content passes the requirements, to also allow conformance claims of pages that aren't 100% tested.

This is going to be relevant when testing websites too. How much of the site should be tested before someone can claim conformance? Currently I think this is only ever done by counting numbers of pages. But I don't think that has to be the only way to do it.

This could in theory work if applicability of a requirement could be made programatically determinable. For instance, if a requirement is applicable to all img elements, and a page has 100 of them, with 90 img elements tested, you have 90% test coverage for that requirements. WCAG 2 doesn't have this concent of applicability, making a measurement like this impossible.

If we allow incidental issues in conformance of Silver, it makes sense to also allow test coverage to be lower than 100%. By writing Silver in such a way that it can be used to measure test coverage, it becomes possible to maintain conformance over time. Rather than have the conformance claim get outdated the moment a page changes, conformance claim can stay relevant as long as the test target didn't change too much. Even better, you can programatically determine the moment the conformance claim becomes outdated, as that will be the moment the test coverage drops below a certain level.

388.title: WCAG 3 for personal and small business websites
388.body:
This issue is per request of @jspellman, as discussed on today's Silver call. The numbers in this post aren't real costs of any particular organisation, they're just examples.


Testing a site for WCAG is labor intensive. Depending on a variety of factors, it often takes at least a full day of work, often quite a bit more. For an organization of a budget of 100k doing an annual accessibility audit isn't a big deal. But if you have 8k to build a site, it is hard to justify spending 2k of it on an accessibility audit. That's not even fixing any accessibility problems, it's just to test for them.

The need for accessibility is universal. So WCAG 3 should be too. In my opinion the lowest conformance level of WCAG 3 should be one that is achievable by low-budget and no-budget websites. Ideally it is one that can be tested with minimal effort, without the involvement of an expert.

Having a lower entry level to WCAG 3, makes WCAG more inclusive. It may work better in countries where there is no legal presidency too, and it gives a starting point for organizations new to accessibility.

393.title: Potential ARIA role for summary
393.body:
In a pre-draft we have suggested creating an HTML tag / ARIA role for “summary.” This idea needs to be discussed with APA first. 

The requirement (drafty-draft) is:

<hr>

**When applicable:** A page/view whose main content is an article, or set of paragraphs on a topic, that is at least 300 words (TBC). 

**Requirement:** A summary of the article or related set of paragraphs is available and:
- identifiable visually and programmatically,
- uncommon words are explained, and
- sentences are concise.

**Except when:** An article continues on multiple pages/views, only the first page/view requires a summary.

<hr>

Te programmatically identifiable bit doesn't have a perfect solution yet. 
We are suggesting this because an aria-label can only be applied to interactive elements that receive focus, and a block of text doesn't receive focus. Content creators could use role="region" and an aria-label, but semantically the summary is not a separate section.

This issue is a to-do item for us, to get in touch with the ARIA group.

395.title: accessibility supported: definition switches emphasis from AT to user agents
395.body:
Definition in working draft: supported by in at least 2 major free browsers on every operating system and/or available in assistive technologies used by 80% cumulatively of the AT users on each operating system for each type of AT used
Comment:

398.title: Foundational Requirements: meaning and presentation
