399.title: Proposed pointer definition
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
399.body:
**Pointer**
An input mechanism that enables a user to target and interact with specific coordinates within rendered content. The form of the pointer input can vary depending on the hardware and software.

**Example**
The pointer can be represented by, but are not limited to:
The cursor controlled by a mouse or trackpad.
The point of contact on a touchscreen (e.g., a finger).
The tip of a stylus on a graphics tablet or screen.
The coordinates targeted by an eye-gaze or head-tracking system.

**Note**
The position of a pointer is used to determine pointer-specific events, such as hover, and to initiate activation of an element, such as through a click or tap.

Pointer-based interaction is distinct from the programmatic focus. While a pointer click can move the focus to an element, the focus state is an independent concept that indicates which element will receive subsequent input from devices like a keyboard. Users navigating via keyboard or certain assistive technologies interact directly with the focus state without using a pointer.

User agents determine the pointer's coordinates based on signals from hardware (e.g., a mouse, touchscreen, or camera) and the operating system.

400.title: Recommend provisions for AI transparency & control, required tool/plugin disclosure, and login-gated content notice
400.body:
**AI transparency & control**

_Requirement_: If AI is used to generate or alter content that affects understanding, decisions, or assessments, users are informed and provided human-readable explanations and accessible controls to review, correct, or opt out.

_Why in WCAG 3_: WCAG 3 is expanding toward outcome- and task-based methods; AI-driven UIs are now common and materially affect accessibility outcomes.

**Required tool/plugin disclosure**

_Requirement_: If content requires a specific tool, plugin, or feature flag, the requirement is disclosed up front with accessible install/enable steps and an accessible fallback or equivalent experience.

_Why in WCAG 3_: WCAG 2.2 already ties conformance to accessibility-supported tech and non-interference; WCAG 3 keeps aligning minimums while modernizing conformance.

**Login-gated content notice**

_Requirement_: If critical content/actions are available only to logged-in users, disclose this before sign-in and ensure authentication is accessible (no cognitive-load traps) and offers an equivalent guest preview when feasible.

_Why in WCAG 3_: “Complete processes” and authentication burdens are long-standing barriers; WCAG 3’s task-based testing supports measuring real user flows, including authentication.

403.title: How does the guideline ensure text is sufficiently readable for people with CVD (colourblindness)
403.body:
In the current draft guideline, passing the 'visual contrast of text' guideline appears to be based solely on the score from the APCA tool. However, a quick investigation suggested it was possible to pass the APCA tool for text that became almost invisible with CVD

For example, if I enter #f00 foreground and #000 background for red text on a black background, APCA says I can pass at score 4 with 400-weight text at size 48px.  Yet if I screenshot this colour combination and feed it into the myndex CVD simulator, it is clear the red text becomes almost invisible, as per the screenshot below.
![Untitled-2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/79691399/109296496-49603980-7828-11eb-88d8-2e4feaacebb6.png)

I wondered if it would be possible to combine these 2 tools, so that the APCA tool runs the foreground and background colour combination through the CVD simulator, and reports the minimum of the Luminance contrasts from all the different types of colourblindness?

404.title: Suggesting testing tools / templates
404.body:
**Relevant section:** Testing
**Comment:** Will these include “tools” to guide atomic and holistic assessment? Specifically, tools that can easily be used or merged with existing accessibility testing tools? For example, templates, rubrics, or outlines that a reader can download, modify, and deploy easily. These tools could dynamically update and grow with future WCAG 3.0 edits. I suggest this to help address the problems of readability and barrier to entry of use identified in the [Requirements draft document](https://www.w3.org/TR/2021/WD-wcag-3.0-requirements-20210121/). I also suggest this based on professional experience conducting accessibility testing, and professional experience creating human factors (HF) and user experience (UX) assessment rubrics based on HF and UX principles, descriptions of methods, etc.
Note that this could be covered by WCAG 3.0 techniques or methods structures that I’m not aware of.

Commented by Ronna ten Brink, Senior Human Factors Engineer at the MITRE Corporation.

405.title: How-Tos should be an Overview

406.title: Change of User Need Definition - should also apply to the physical world and human interaction
406.body:
The definition for User need is:

> The end goal a user has when starting a process through digital means.

This is purely focussed on 'digital' and excludes the physical world or human interaction.

Working on the Maturity Model Note there's a wish to use the term 'User Need ' for contexts within the physical world or human interaction like how to interact with each other from an accessibility perspective, language to use, or reasonable accommodation.

Re-using the term and its related definition is not possible at the moment.

I suggest to change the definition to include the different perspectives for user need to make it more generic **OR** scope the definition by adding one or more words, like 'digital user need' or alike.

407.title: 2.2.1 Text Appearance: reformulate minimum size requirements?
407.body:
I see that you set the minimum requirement for standard text size to ~10pt.
This is lower than the current de facto standard practice of 12pt, which have been around for quite some time.
I would at the same time point out that since that recommendation arose, the CSS pixel density of screens have significantly increased, so that the physical size of a 12pt letter is noticable smaller now than back then.

I would therefore suggest to reformulate a bit:

- Minimum default size >= 12pt
- Absolute minimum size >= 10pt (can for instance be used on certain elements in footer or shorter texts like image subtexts)
- Recommended default size >= 14pt

Best regards 
Torbjørn Helland Solhaug

comments.body:
You are mixing up Minimum with Body   text size

This says the the MINIMUM text should be that size.  and that the body text should be larger.     

We don't use the word default since it is not defined - and you can't have a requirement that is not clearly defined.  

Maybe change default to "text on 50% or more of the page"  ? 

hmmmm

But for accessibility if the min font size is sufficient to be read -- then requiring something larger seems to be a recommendation not a requirement.   Since we already say that the minimum is good enough... 
PS that is the minimum when at least 200% magnification is available.  Double that if not

Some authors don't set a size. As this results in a `16px` base font size in most browsers and is more accessible than the sizes recommended in our draft requirement, I think we should account for that in our requirement. As in, this requirement should not force people to have to set a font size at all.

Also, could I understand “default” is not defined, but can't we say “at least the size the content would have without setting a size”, or something like “except when the content's font size is or is larger than the user agent's base font size”?

Relevant to this topic: a new `meta` tag is being introduced that lets websites opt-in to respecting the OS (accessibility) settings for font size. 413.title: Alternative link style method for high link-density content (addition to Guideline 1.4 – Adjustable text style)
413.body:
## Background

The standard link style is a [solid underline](https://example.com/).  
However, WCAG 2 [G183](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/general/G183.html) states:  
> “If there are not a large number of links in the block of text, underlines are recommended for links in blocks of text.”

This implies that when there *is* a large number of links — such as on wiki pages or glossaries — a different, less visually distracting approach may be acceptable.  

On the other hand, [G182](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/general/G182.html) provides various examples of non-underlined link styles such as blue bold text or red italic text, but these may not be reliably recognized as links by users.  
Because most users’ experience still associates links with some form of underline, purely color- or font-based cues can reduce discoverability.

Therefore, I propose introducing an alternative, accessible link style — for example, a **dotted underline** — that remains recognizable as a link while reducing visual clutter in high link-density content.  

## Proposal

This is an additional proposal to [Guideline 1.4 – Adjustable text style](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#adjustable-text-style).

While the current draft focuses on font size, line height, and spacing,  
this Method extends the concept to link text decoration, showing how authors can adjust visual presentation (e.g., using dotted underlines or subtle visual cues) to maintain link perceivability while improving overall readability.

Example: Use `text-decoration-style: dotted` instead of a solid underline to reduce clutter.  
[dotted-underline-link-example.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23142829/dotted-underline-link-example.html)
[![Image from Gyazo](https://i.gyazo.com/958094964ec4de60af1e5912babe3f41.png)](https://gyazo.com/958094964ec4de60af1e5912babe3f41)

## References

- WCAG 3 [Guideline 1.4](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#adjustable-text-style)
- WCAG 2.2 Techniques [G182](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/general/G182.html) / [G183](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/general/G183.html)

419.title: Identify functional needs as part of normative WCAG 3.0
419.body:
I believe a pivotal change and fundamental ingredient of WCAG 3.0 against WCAG 2.X is the reference to "functional needs". This is highlighted in the first para About WCAG 3.0 section 1.2.
It states:
"WCAG 3.0 supports a wide set of user needs, uses new approaches to testing, and allows frequent maintenance of guidelines and related content to keep pace with accelerating technology changes. WCAG 3 supports this evolution by focusing on the functional needs of users.
 These needs are then supported by guidelines that are written as outcome statements, requirements, assertions, and technology-specific methods to meet those needs".

Therefore, the conformance process should allow one to determine how the needs are met. It should be tied to the functional needs as suggested in
https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/w3c-wai-gl/2025OctDec/0059.html

Please consider incorporating the functional needs as part of the normative content of WCAG 3.0 in a manner similar to Functional Performance Statements (Clause 4.2) in EN 301 549.
This does not limit future versions (like WCAG 3.1 say) from adding /tweaking functional needs if circumstances warrant.
Thanks very much
Sailesh

420.title: 'Media alternative in all spoken languages' needs adjustment
420.body:
The working draft lists the following:
> Foundational requirement: Media alternatives in all spoken languages Developing
[Media alternatives](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-media-alternatives) are provided in all spoken languages used in [audio](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-audio) [content](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-content).

I do not believe this is properly scoped.

First, in many movies, there may be incidental occurrences of people speaking foreign languages that are not intended to be understood by the movie's target audience. If the main character cannot understand a foreign language, it is a fairly established convention that the audience for the movie is not expected to either (i.e., in an English-speaking movie, the main character cannot understand what the people are saying when visiting a foreign-language country). The established convention for captioning is not to translate what the protagonist cannot understand, but instead put in something like "[Speaking Japanese]" The current wording would seem to require that any incidental foreign language used in a film would force the full translation of all alternatives into those languages. I am assuming that is not the intent.

Second, I do not believe the language _spoken_ in the movie should be the determinant on the accessible requirement. There is language in a video that is not spoken (such as onscreen text).

Third, many movies that are released internationally use subtitles, not dubbing. In such a case, none of the language spoken in the movie matches the intended audience. I think it should be the existence of a version of a movie intended for a language-specific audience. If there is a French-speaking movie, its alternatives should be available in French, but if there exists an English-language subtitled version, then all the text alternatives should be available in English for that version.

For commercial film releases, the requirement simply needs to have the alternative match the language-indicated version of the release.
For amateur videos, there is no arbiter to help determine the language, so there is going to have to be reliance on the video's content. I would suggest:

> **Media alternatives in matching language
[Media alternatives](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-media-alternatives) are provided that match the human language used in [audio](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-audio) and visual [content](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-content), including in subtitles, except when the human language is not intended to be meaningful to the audience.**

Subtitles would need to be defined, and clearly differentiated from captions (which they are not, currently). There may be an easier way of phrasing that doesn't involved subtitles.

We have previously used the term "ambiguous" in SCs like Link Purpose. The exception I'm proposing involves the same basic concept.

421.title: Status messages
labels: Path: User control and prevent harm
421.body:
WCAG2.2 clause 4.1.3 says:
(Level AA)
_In content implemented using markup languages, [status messages](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-status-messages) can be [programmatically determined](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-programmatically-determinable) through [role](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-role) or properties such that they can be presented to the user by [assistive technologies](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-assistive-technologies) without receiving focus._

There are two guidance notes to accompany section 4.1.3:

- https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html
- https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#status-messages

Recently, GitHub have updated their guidance to note that the use of toasts and snackbars are considered an anti-pattern. They aren't the first - many other technology companies already have similar guidelines about the use of _transient floating notifications_ or _floating ephemeral messages_.

I'd therefore like to propose a tightening of the equivalent WCAG3 section:

>   ## **Requirement:**
>   Ensure status messages are perceivable.
>   1. Users must be able to perceive and review status messages for long enough to understand them and take action.
>   2. Such messages must be [programmatically determined](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-programmatically-determinable) by and presented to [assistive technologies](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-assistive-technology), without receiving focus.
>   3. Such messages must be perceivable and actionable by users (including Sign Language users (issue #325)), through assistive technologies.
>   
>   ## **Applies when:**
>   Presenting status messages.
>   
>   ## **Except when:**
>   * the change is already fully visible and self-evident within the interface without additional messaging; and
>   * the information is accessible by another, persistent, mechanism.
>   
>   ## Notes
>   Note1: Examples of anti-patterns: Use of:
>   * toasts
>   * snackbars
>   * other transient floating notifications or floating ephemeral messages
>   
>   Note2: Inline, ideally persistent, status messages are preferred.
>   Note3: Examples of _programmatically determined_ include through [role](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG3/#dfn-role) or properties. See notes 5 & 6 for further information.
>   Note4: This requirement is consistent with, for instance, Gov.UK Design System, US Digital Service guidelines, and guidelines from multiple technology vendors.
>   Note5: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html
>   Note6: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/#status-messages

429.title: Clarify contrast requirements for passive content grouping (Cognitive Barriers)
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
429.body:
We've been having a discussion in the Drupal community about how to simplify the cognitive barriers for a complex user interface (our authoring tool). Specifically, how do we address passive structures (containers, regions) better?

If a user cannot discern where one "idea" ends and the next begins, the interface becomes a "wall of text" or a "soup of controls."

This article from Fable came along and re-kindled the discussion: https://makeitfable.com/community-content/common-cognitive-barriers-in-digital-experiences/

The Gap in 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast) provides some guidance, but it could be clearer regarding non-semantic barriers between different chunks of text.

We are struggling with how to best navigate the various blocks of content. How do we improve predictability and give people cues on what they can ignore? How do we reduce the noise associated with the wall of text that some sites become?

Ideally, we'd have guidance on how to incorporate color contrast for these page elements. It could be a line, or a different font, but we need to encourage the visual representation of navigational elements as distinct from others. Having a 1px border between the sidebar and the main content can be very helpful, as can having a block of content where the light/dark is reversed from that of the main content. 

The Dark Mode Complication This is complicated by the implementation of Dark Mode, as there are more elements to consider. Subtle changes often do not have much contrast (not even 3:1) and so are easy to miss.

Proposed Guideline / Discussion - A new guideline stating that any visually grouped "chunk" of content (e.g., a fieldset, a sidebar block, a card in Layout Builder) must have a boundary that meets a 3:1 contrast ratio against the adjacent background or equivalent way to distinguish grouped content. 

We are looking for guidance on what other blocks of content should be made more distinct so that people with visual or cognitive disabilities can better navigate them.

430.title: Gap in WCAG: Toast Notifications That Dismiss on Scroll or Focus Change
labels: Path: User control and prevent harm
430.body:
WCAG 2.x does not adequately address accessibility failures caused by toast notifications that dismiss when users scroll or move focus. This pattern creates a significant barrier for users with low vision, screen reader users, and keyboard users, yet is not clearly covered by existing Success Criteria. As a result, this harmful pattern persists in production systems despite causing real usability and accessibility failures.

This issue documents the gap and proposes consideration for WCAG 3 outcomes that better reflect user experience realities.

**Description of the Accessibility Problem**

Some toast notifications provide important and unique system feedback. In many implementations, these toasts dismiss automatically when the user scrolls the page or when keyboard focus changes.  (I'm not talking about toasts that disappear after a specific time, like 5 seconds, because that will be reviewed under 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable)

This behavior creates an accessibility barrier because users must often scroll or move focus in order to read or understand the toast.

**Affected users include:**

- Low-vision users, who scroll to magnify different portions of the screen
- Screen reader users, who move focus to navigate content or review context
- Keyboard-only users, who naturally change focus during interaction

When an important toast disappears during these essential actions, the user may never receive the feedback the toast was meant to convey.

**Why WCAG 2.x Does Not Adequately Cover This**
Relevant Success Criterion: WCAG 2.2.1 – Timing Adjustable (Level A)

While this criterion addresses content that disappears after a time limit, it does not clearly apply when dismissal is triggered by:

- scrolling
- focus movement
- tab navigation

In these cases:

- There may be no explicit time limit
- The dismissal is tied to required navigation actions
- The user has no reasonable way to pause, extend, or recover the content

As a result, these implementations often pass WCAG conformance reviews while still producing inaccessible user experiences.

**Why This Is a Meaningful Accessibility Gap**

This pattern:

- Removes critical feedback before users can perceive or understand it
- Penalizes users for necessary accessibility behaviors (scrolling, focus movement)
- Is especially harmful for magnification and screen reader workflows
- Undermines user confidence and task completion

While not a WCAG 2.x failure, it violates the intent of accessible design and results in real-world exclusion.

**Recommendation for WCAG 3 Consideration**

WCAG 3 offers an opportunity to address this gap by:

- Explicitly considering focus- and scroll-triggered dismissal as equivalent to timing-based loss
- Evaluating user ability to perceive, understand, and recover system feedback
- Treating valuable system feedback as essential content, not purely transient UI

A potential WCAG 3 outcome could focus on ensuring that critical user feedback remains available until the user has a reasonable opportunity to perceive and understand it, regardless of navigation method.

      * the speaker in the captions.
      * the language of the speaker in the captions.
      * significant sound effects and non-spoken audio in the captions.
  * (ALL) Play the media with captions on and determine
      * if the captions are consistently styled throughout the media.
      * if the speaker is consistently identified in the captions when there is more than one speaker present.
      * if the language of the speaker is consistently identified in the captions when there is more than one language present.
      * if all significant sound effects and non-spoken audio are consistently identified in the captions when they occur.

465.title: Likely a player issue - Visual indicators 360 (Foundational)
465.body:
**Visual indicators 360 (Foundational)**

> In 360-degree digital environments, the direction of a sound or speech is indicated when audio is heard from outside the current view.

* Depending on how we think this would be implemented, this is likely a player issue, and if so, should we remove this requirement?

466.title: "purely decorative" vs "decorative" - Decorative images (Foundational)
466.body:
**Decorative images (Foundational)**
> Decorative images are programmatically hidden.

* Need to discuss how to distinguish "purely decorative" from "decorative"so that different testes would agree. 
  * "Purely decorative" images don't need text alternatives at all, but text alternatives for "decorative" images can be useful for some users if provided so that users can picture the image.
  * **Examples of "purely decorative images"**: icon used alongside text, thumbnail image within a link, etc.
  * **Examples of "decorative images"**: image photo, illustration, etc.

**FYI:**
* **Method**: Ensure that a purely decorative image has no accessible name.
* **Best practice**: Provide a text alternative for a decorative image unless it is purely decorative.
* **User needs for the best practice above**:
  * As a user who lost my sight later in life, I would like to get the description of the image even if it is decorative.

comments.body: I would not distinguish between "decorative" and "purely decorative". If the image is valuable content, i.e. it adds meaning to the page, it is not "decorative" at all. Images, photos, and illustrations can either be decorative or non-decorative, depending on what they are and the surrounding content and context where they are placed. Many will convey meaning and deserve to have an alternative description. Defining them as "decorative" (in need of a text alternative) is highly likely to confuse.

I agree with Grace. I wouldn't class a photo or an illustration as decorative. Even if it doesn't add information, it is still relevant to the content (or should be). When deciding whether an image is decorative, I ask myself whether I could change the image for something completely different without it affecting the content or meaning. So, for example, a swirly line at the bottom of the page could be changed for a wiggly rainbow line and it would make no difference to the information or content. By contrast, a photo of my dog on a page about assistance dogs could not be changed for a picture of a unicorn without it becoming confusing and weird. 

I'm not keen on having "decorative" and "purely decorative" as this could create confusion. I think decorative is sufficient but it should be well defined.

467.title: `img` element meet this requirement? - Detectable images (Foundational)
467.body:
**Detectable images (Foundational)**
> Non-decorative images are detectable.

* Can "non-decorative images" be defined as "Images that convey meaning"?
* For HTML, does using an `img` element meet this requirement?

**FYI**
* **User need**:
  * As a user, I need to know if the content is an image.

comments.body: In my opinion use of the img element does not necessarily mean the image is not purely decorative.

468.title: Move to method? - Editable alternatives
468.body:
**Editable alternatives**

> Automatically generated text descriptions are editable by the content creator.

* Recommend moving to method and updating the management sheet to removed?
  * Move to method for "Equivalent text alternatives"?

469.title: Define “image types” and "purely decorative" - Image type
469.body: **Image type (Supplemental)** > The image types (photo, illustration, chart, etc.) are indicated. Background * For web pages, screen readers will tell a user that it is an image or a graphic when they encounter `` or any other elements with `role="img"` in the HTML code. But a user has no idea on what type of image it is. User need(s) * As a user without vision, I need to know the image type. * Screen readers just tell me that it is an image or a graphic. I have no idea on the type; a photograph, an illustration or anything else. * An image on a shopping site is identified as a photograph so that I can ask somebody to see and describe the photograph for me if I want. * An image on a website is identified as a headshot and the text alternative describes “headshot of Mr. Suzuki” so that I can imagine the web page has a headshot of Mr. Suzuki on it. * As a user with low vision who can see a screen but also uses a screen reader, I want to perceive the image type when I have a difficulty seeing the image. Need to define “image types” * Specific type(s) of an image to be identified in the text alternative where appropriate. It allows users to perceive what kind of image it is even if a user can’t see the image or has difficulty seeing the image. Need to define "purely decorative" * Examples include an icon used alongside text, a thumbnail image within a link. * [Image type (Exploratory to Developing) - A document the subgroup has been working on](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1tEVoCFxYQ3G355VWpV30jry_QzicscqjPvoo7SvpWJc/edit?usp=sharing)

470.title: Separate this into two? - Meaningful visual information (Foundational)
labels: P - Visual information identified in transcripts
P - Visual information identified in audio desc
470.body:
**Meaningful visual information (Foundational)**

> Visual information needed to understand the media is described in the transcript and audio description.

* Should we separate this into two requirements, transcript and audio description?

471.title: Supplemental rather than assertion? - Sign language live (Assertion)
471.body:
**Sign language live (Assertion)**

> We provide sign language interpretation for all live audio content.

* Should this be a supplemental requirement rather than an assertion?

472.title: Need concrete examples - Speakers identified (Core)
labels: P - Speakers identified in audio descriptions
472.body:
**Speakers identified (Foundational)**

> Speakers are identified understandably within all media alternatives.
> 
> Note
> Full name then use part of name
> Hidden identity as part of narrative structure
> Recognizable position within the context of use

* Need clarification with concrete examples for each note.

473.title: What if it was 10 years ago? - Testing with users (Assertion)
labels: P - Usability testing for unnecessary steps
473.body:
**Testing media alternatives with users (Assertion)**

> Tests were conducted with users who need media alternatives, and the issues were fixed based on the findings.

- What if it was 10 years ago when the tests were conducted?

474.title: Differ from "Equivalent text alternatives"? - Non-text content
labels: P - Non-text content not relied on
474.body:
Non-text content (foundational)

> All :term[non-text content] that is not decorative includes a programmatically determinable equivalent text alternatives.

* What is the difference between this and "Equivalent text alternatives"? Need clarification.

475.title: What counts as "most text" in Readable Text Style (minimum)?
475.body: To make this part of the requirement testable, need to define "most text" in "Most text is not bold, italicized, and/or underlined."

476.title: Clear blocks of content - Address ambiguities + clarify visual, programmatic, and spacing requirements
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
476.body:
- Re-evaluate whether the visual and programmatic aspects of meaningful content blocks should be treated as separate requirements, since one may be satisfied while the other is not
- Clarify what is meant by “sufficient surrounding space”
- Define exceptions (or at least consider) where spacing may not be required due to specific layout choices
- Review Gregg's points:
    > This is requiring that information be programmatically determinable that is not visually determinable. If you mean, "when information appears as a block of information which has semantic meaning as a block than this needs to also be programmatically determinable. Or some such. As written, it doesn't quite make sense and is requiring things be programmatically determined that are not necessarily visually determinable. Also, this talks about sufficient surrounding space but the word sufficient is not testable. It is subjective.

    and 

    > Often have no more space between them than the lines in the paragraph. Yet they are meaningful blocks. Is this going to require that every document has additional space between paragraphs or any block of text? How much space? What is sufficient? One pixel, two pixels, three pixels,?

477.title: Section labels - Define "meaningful blocks of content" and provide clear exceptions
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
477.body:
- Clearly define what is meant by "meaningful blocks of content", addressing @GreggVan's concern
    > Does this mean that if I post a letter on the Internet that I need to label the introduction and label the different sections of the letter? If this is talking about sections, it needs to say sections or something. "Meaningful blocks of content" is used here to both mean section and headings and even blocks with in a section or within a heading such as a paragraph. We can't use the same term to mean three different things.
- Clearly define any exceptions to the requirement. The current exception 
    > a label is not needed to understand the purpose of the content within the context of use

    may be invoked too broadly; provide clearer guidance on when this exception does and does not apply.

478.title: Heading structure - Clarifying terminology and exceptions
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
478.body:
- Replace the terms "higher" and "lower" when referring to heading levels to avoid ambiguity.
- Clearly define "meaningful block of content" and specify exceptions, recognizing that many content types (such as paragraphs, letters, or emails) may not require headings. Ensure that any exception is explicit and cannot be used as a loophole.

Note: These issues may be resolved through a clear and consistent definition of "meaningful blocks of content".

479.title: Clear blocks of content (enhanced) - Clarify "meaningful blocks" and visual spacing requirements + exceptions
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
479.body:
- Clarify what is meant by “sufficient surrounding space”
- Define exceptions (or at least consider) where spacing may not be required due to specific layout choices
- Review Gregg's points:
    >This requires that styling be used. If I have meaningful blocks "again I don't know if that means sections or paragraphs or bullets or sentences a period of sentence to me as a meaningful block of content? And we use the same term for sections and headings and paragraphs and? If I have a document and I put a space between my paragraph that would mean it was visually separated, but I'm not using any styling to do that. Do I fail this requirement?

480.title: Ordered content - Expand and provide additional clarification within the understanding materials
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
480.body: Additional information is needed in the understanding document to clarify cases where the visual layout presents ordered content (e.g., background images) that is not programmatically available.

481.title: Clear structure review process - Clarify language + re-evaluate applicability
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
481.body:
- Clarify the language so that requirements don't hinge on conditionals, avoid overly specific terms like "icons" and ensure the assertion reflects guidance rather than absolute conformance.
- Address that requiring all foundational requirements to be met makes the assertion fragile, since any single already existing violation in any of the requirements of the same guideline would technically fail it

482.title: Controllable infinite scrolling [EXPLORATORY] - Switch off infinite scrolling
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
482.body:
- Review @GreggVan's point:
    > This one makes no sense at all. You can't switch off something that has infinite scrolling. If you turn off infinite scrolling on something that has infinite scrolling, you basically are saying don't show me any more of the information that you're going to show everybody else. It's very easy to stop infinite scrolling. Don't scroll down. There is no way to turn off infinite scrolling without deleting all the rest of the information that would show up if you kept scrolling. So this one should be just removed cause it doesn't make any sense.
One could replace this with a provision that says incremental presentation on scroll should be able to be turned off when it is possible for all of the rest of the information to be presented at once rather than incrementally as you scroll. (This is different than infinite scrolling where they're essentially is no reasonable end to the content.)

483.title: Consistent navigation terminology - Simplify understanding + definition of consistent
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
483.body:
- Make the requirement easier to understand
- Consider defining "consistent" to prevent confusion or misinterpretation, particularly where "consistent" may be mistaken for "identical"

484.title: Customization questions about Readable text style (enhanced)
484.body: Is the purpose of this supplemental requirement to encourage developers to set their default text presentation to meet the values specified in the foundational requirement for adjustable text style? If so, how can we make clearer the connection between these two requirements? And does this mean we are not encouraging customization of text presentation beyond the values specified in adjustable text style? Commenters raised similar [customization questions about readable blocks of text (enhanced)](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues/485).

485.title: Customization questions about Readable blocks of text (enhanced)
485.body: Is the purpose of this supplemental requirement to encourage developers to set their default text presentation to meet the values specified in the foundational requirement for adjustable blocks of text? If so, how can we make clearer the connection between these two requirements? And does this mean we are not encouraging customization of text presentation beyond the values specified in adjustable blocks of text? Commenters raised similar [customization questions about readable text style (enhanced)](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues/484) .

486.title: What about language of the page and language of parts (in Human Language requirement)?
486.body: The current draft does not differentiate between the dominant language of the page/view versus the language of parts.  Do we need to add this differentiation?

487.title: Customization questions about unambiguous numerical formatting
487.body: What about users who'd prefer a customizable format? Instead of making this a foundational requirement, should it be a supplemental requirement that makes alternatives available so assistive technology can develop customizable user preferences?

489.title: Add dark mode
489.body: During the 2025 Editors Week, we agreed that we should add a dark mode requirement, but ran out of time to create the content. This issue is to flag that we should add dark mode.

490.title: Clarify if the diacritics requirement only applies to Hebrew and Arabic
490.body:
We need to explain more clearly where this needs to be done and where it doesn't need to be done.
- Does this requirement apply only to Hebrew and Arabic? 
- If the requirement isn't calling for all diacritics to be included, how can testers tell which diacritics are needed to determine the correct pronunciation?

We also need to add a definition of diacritic.

491.title: Change numerical alternatives to an assertion?
491.body: We need more clarity on what counts as complex numerical information. We also need more clarity on what counts as a sufficient alternative or explanation. Consider making this an assertion rather than a supplemental requirement.

492.title: Clear language definition
492.body: Need to dig up or draft definition of clear language.

493.title: Guidelines are not guidelines
493.body:
I know this is pedantic, but WCAG 3.0's guidelines aren't written as guidelines. A guideline is something to follow or do. But the "guidelines" in WCAG 3.0's latest draft are phrased as requirements or as expectations.

> "Users have equivalent alternatives for images."

Should be something like: 

> "Ensure users have equivalent alternatives for images."

494.title: What does "detectable" mean in "Non-decorative images are detectable"
494.body:
https://deploy-preview-414--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#detectable-image

> **Detectable image** Non-decorative images are detectable

Please explain / define "detectable". This is painfully vague. To who should an image be detectable? What counts as "detectable"? Like, should screen users need to know that an image of text is an image? Does this (also?) need to be programmatic, if so, what part? The role, the accessible name, both? Those seem covered by other requirements, so presumably not. But if not, what then?

**Recommendation**: Drop this requirement, it makes very little sense.

495.title: Decorative image requirement has self-contradicting definition
495.body:
> Decorative images are programmatically hidden.

> > programmatically determinable
> > meaning of the content and all its important attributes can be determined by software functionality that is accessibility supported

> content
> information and sensory experience to be communicated to the user by an interface, including code or markup that defines the content’s structure, presentation, and interactions


These definitions are contradictory. According to the definition of "content", decorative images are not content. If decorative images aren't content, it can't be content that has programmatically determined properties. If it can't have programmatically determined properties, it can't be programmatically hidden. Making this definition impossible.

**Recommendation**: Use WCAG 2.0's definition for programmatically determined. It was better. It also doesn't have this arbitrary "important" word in it.

496.title: Remove the term "outcome" from WCAG 3.0
496.body:
The latest editors draft still has a whole bunch of uses of the world "outcome", even though the group seems to have moved away from that term in favor of "requirement" (a good choice IMO). Having both terms into the draft can be confusing.

It should be.a simple search/replace to get rid of these. Here are some example:

> To meet the varying needs of this audience, several layers of guidance will be provided including guidelines written as **outcome** statements, requirements that can be tested, assertions, a rich collection of methods, resource links, and code samples.

> guidelineDeveloping
> high-level, plain-language **outcome** statements used to organize requirements

> Guidelines provide a high-level, plain-language **outcome** statements for managers, policy makers, individuals who are new to accessibility, and other individuals who need to understand the concepts but not dive into the technical details. They provide an easy-to-understand way of organizing and presenting the requirements so that non-experts can learn about and understand the concepts.

497.title: Typo in the editors note on 2. Guidelines
497.body:
https://deploy-preview-414--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#guidelines:~:text=Unless%20otherwise%20noted%2C%20all%20items%20in%20the%20list%20as%20exploratory%20at%20this%20point

> Unless otherwise noted, all items in the list as exploratory at this point

I think what is meant here is:

Unless otherwise noted, all items in the list are exploratory at this point

However since I'm looking at a draft that should only have **developing** content in it, this statement as a whole seems like it should be pulled from the spec.

498.title: programmatically associated is not explained in "text alternative" definition
498.body:
https://deploy-preview-414--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#dfn-text-alternative

> > text alternative
> > text that is [programmatically associated] with non-text content or referred to from text that is programmatically associated with non-text content

In WCAG 2.0 this term is explained with the following sentence, but for some reason that sentence was dropped from WCAG 3.0. I don't think it's right to just link to the programmatically determined definition and hope people will understand what that means because they read it in WCAG 2. WCAG 3.0 needs to be self-explanatory.

> Programmatically associated text is text whose location can be [programmatically determined] from the non-text content.



I don't think WCAG 3.0 should have this be part of the definition, for two reaons:

1. Firstly I question whether this actually matters. The way this has worked in practice is that if an image has information, and that information is also available in a nearby text, that image is just considered decorative. I'm not aware of anyone who for example of an icon with a text next to it, who'd fail that if the image didn't have aria-labelledby pointing at the text. I don't think anything really changes if we remove this part of the definition.

2. If we do want to keep this, I don't think this belongs in a definition. This is really just a hidden requirement. Text alternatives need to be programmatically associated with non-text content. That can be its own requirement, or it can be part of the current one, but I think by putting it in the definition WCAG 2.0 has kind of hidden that this actually is required.

499.title: What does a text alternative need to be equivalent to?
499.body:
https://deploy-preview-414--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#equivalent-text-alternative

> Equivalent [text alternatives] are available for [images] that convey [content]

This requirement is pretty vague about what the text alternative needs to be equivalent to. Knowing what I know about WCAG 2 I can assume the intent is the purpose of the image, but reading this just as a stand-alone statement, I would take this to mean the content of the image rather than the purpose of the image. So "House icon" would be correct, but "home" would not be because that isn't the content the image shows.

500.title: "2.1.1 Which foundational requirements apply" seems incorrect
500.body:
https://deploy-preview-414--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#image-alternatives

> (2.1.1) Which foundational requirements apply?
> 1. Would removing the image impact how people understand the page?
> No, Decorative image is programmatically hidden. Stop.

Just because you can remove an image without changing the meaning of the page doesn't mean the image is decorative:

> decorative
> serving only an aesthetic purpose, providing no information, and having no functionality

Lots of images can be removed from the page without problems and not meet that definition. Images that provide redundant information for example. Explaining the requirement this way is fairly misleading about what images need to be programmatically hidden.

501.title: What counts as "high-contrast" in Adjustable text color?
501.body: The tests involve using a "high-contrast light-on-dark theme" and a "high-contrast dark-on-light theme." What counts as "high-contrast"?

502.title: Interoperable vs non-interoperable formats in Exported/saved/prints supports text-appearance customizations
502.body: A note in the current draft lists examples of interoperable vs non-interoperable formats. Need to make clear why this information is relevant.

503.title: [Error notification] Rename to “Application errors available”?
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
503.body:
In our meeting of 5 January we discussed how exactly Error Notification relates to Input Errors and where the overlap is.

It seemed to us that potentially it would make sense to make “Error notification” about just “Application Errors”, and make it mirror “Input Errors” such that both requirements exist independently.

This would adding the requirement that the description is clear to “Input Errors”.

504.title: [Error notification] “Automatic” and “clearly” are vague, consider removing or removing
504.body:
In: 

> Errors that can be automatically detected are identified and the problem is clearly described to the user.

* “automatically” adds confusion. SK said he interpreted it as “detected by the browser using `required`”; it's unclear whether server side and/or client side detection are included.
* “clearly” is undefined and untestable, requiring that the problem be _described_ should already applies that it is done in a clear manner, or it arguably doesn't meet the bar of being described.

Questions: 
- is 'automatic' actually needed here? can we (a) remove it, or (b) make more explicit what we mean by 'automatic', (c) say what does the detection ('page/view' or product)?
- what does 'clearly' mean? when is the description good enough and if it's vague wouldn't it allow for almost every description to conform?
- what about errors the author cannot do anything about? like the server that needed to check their identity is on fire… that's not a problem the user can do anything about
- what about errors the site/app cannot get into detail about for security reasons?

505.title: Should bidirectional navigation be symmetrical?
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
505.body: The subgroup is considering making this require that the navigation be symmetrical (i.e., if you navigate forward and then backward you always end up back in the same place). We are interested in comments on this.

506.title: Retro-Compatibility
506.body: The W3C has stated that WCAG 3.0 will not be backwards compatible with the 2.x series. Organizations that spent years reaching WCAG 2.2 AA may find that their existing "compliant" code doesn't meet the new "Foundational" requirements of 3.0. This creates a risk of "Compliance Debt," where teams must re-audit and re-remediate previously "fixed" content.

507.title: Testability of Clear Language requirements
507.body: WCAG 3.0 includes much more guidance on cognitive accessibility (e.g., "No unnecessary words," "No nested clauses"). These are harder to test objectively than technical criteria like "Alt text exists.". There is a risk of Inter-rater Reliability—two different accessibility testers might disagree on whether a sentence is "unnecessarily complex," leading to inconsistent audit results.

508.title: Could emphasis on “usability” and “outcomes” pave the way for overlay companies?
508.body: With the new emphasis on "usability" and "outcomes," some vendors may claim their AI overlays satisfy WCAG 3.0 better than they did 2.x. Industry experts warn that overlays still cannot fix the "Critical Errors" defined in WCAG 3.0 (like logical focus order or complex interaction failures).

509.title: Conformance (scope and sampling)
509.body: The draft does not currently explain how to test a small sample of pages to represent a massive website. We cannot adopt this standard until a statistically valid sampling method is defined.

510.title: Image Alternatives (Foundational Requirements)
510.body: The text explaining how foundational requirements relate to the outcome rating is currently difficult to follow. Please simplify the language to clearly show how passing the basics affects the final score.

512.title: [Speakers identified] lack of clarity for user who can’t or choose not to be identified
labels: P - Speakers identified in audio descriptions
512.body:
"Speakers identified" There lacks clarity here for the scenario where a user can't or chooses not to be identified. For example, for a live meeting or meeting recording - when multiple people are in a room, independent users are not identified - they are grouped as part of a room. I would like this section to specifically indicate that it's limited to speakers who are systematically identifiable.

Another scenario is when a video has only one speaker who introduces themselves in the beginning. It would feel repetitive to announce the speaker every time. I think this needs more work or be supplemental for now.

513.title: [Adjustable text size] should require all mechanisms rather than “at least one”
513.body: The test for 2.2.1 (Text and wording, Guideline Text appearance), "Foundational requirement: Adjustable text size" says "2. Check that at least one mechanism can achieve a 200% text-size increase." I think this should be "Check that all mechanisms can achieve 200% text-size increase", which would align with other recent changes (e.g., Guideline 2.12.7 User agent support, User settings).

514.title: [Captions synchronized] consider removing or improving latency definition
514.body: "Captions are synchronized" This is too broad of a statement. There is latency & added latency can also occur to improve accuracy. I would suggest this is either edited to better define what latency is (ex. <5 seconds) or redacted.

515.title: Explainer: clarification needed in 8. User-generated content
515.body: "The web content publisher should identify all locations of user-generated content (such as commentary on hosted content, product descriptions for consumer to consumer for sale listings, and restaurant reviews) and perform standard accessibility evaluation analysis *for each*." - in this sentence, it's unclear if "for each" means each type of content, or each entry (ie, every single comment posted to date). Each entry is not feasible, so I think W3C should clarify what they mean.

516.title: Explainer: 8.1 Steps to Conform — acknowledgement needed for user-generated content via native mobile
516.body: Overall, the user-generated guidelines are written for web content. A lot of user generated content is done on mobile, and using native mobile apps. This should at least be acknowledged in the writeup.

517.title: Explainer: 2.2 Out of Scope — explicit coverage for native mobile
517.body: "Non-web technologies" are listed as out of scope. Does that mean native mobile is out of scope? There are some references to mobile testing so maybe it would be more explicit that native mobile apps are out.

518.title: [Image alternatives] “decorative“ and “purely decorative” distinction not useful
518.body: The distinction between "decorative" and "purely decorative" images is not well-defined, and I don't believe is useful as a distinguisher without a clear and mostly objective means of differentiation.

comments.body: Duplicates #466.

519.title: [Transcripts Available] background video unclear
519.body: It is unclear from the text what a "background video" is.

520.title: [Sounds Identified]: contradicts “transcripts available”?
520.body: This criterion contradicts "transcripts available", which states that transcripts are not needed when there is no spoken content. This criterion requires that sounds needed to identify the media are identified in transcripts, which may not include spoken content.

521.title: [Hue not relied on] definition for “artistic or expressive”?
521.body: A definition is needed for "artistic or expressive". Those terms are too broad.

522.title: [Numerical alternatives available] scope too broad?
522.body: The scope of this criterion is extremely broad, and places unnecessary burden on content creators in a way that may not actually enhance understanding. From the example - I don't think a single value (60,000) is "complex numerical information", and a "small city" may vary wildly from location to location.

523.title: [Data entry validated] what about fields that depend on content of other fields?
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
523.body: It is unclear how this criterion applies to situations where things like form fields depend on the content of other form fields to not be in error.

524.title: [Clear language] focus on complexity instead of word count?
524.body: Requiring summaries is excellent, but relying only on a word count might not always be the best approach. I believe this guideline should focus on the complexity of the topic, ensuring summaries are provided when they are needed for understanding.

525.title: [Captions available (prerecorded)] define “important sounds”?
525.body: The term "important sounds" is subjective and often leads to missing context. The guidelines should clearly define what counts as an "important sound" so users don't miss anything.

526.title: [2.2.3 Clear language] Consolidate editor's notes?
526.body:
Can we consolidate the following so that editor's notes are not stacked on top of each other?

527.body:
Spell out acronyms on first reference in keeping with this guidance?

AG, COGA, etc

536.title: Text Appearance - Text style readable (minimum)
536.body: If "the default minimum contrast level should be roughly equivalent to the WCAG2 4.5:1 level for small/body text", why are we changing it? This would break tooling, design systems, testing protocols, entire UIs, etc. Any change to the long accepted contrast values, especially something as disruptive as switching to APCA, needs to be backed up by robust research showing serious benefits which outweigh the disruption.

comments.body:
Great question, and worth exploring the fuller picture. The current WCAG 2 contrast ratio has actually been a source of ongoing concern among vision researchers and accessibility practitioners since its adoption. It produces well-documented false passes and false fails — color pairs that technically comply but are hard to read, and readable combinations that are rejected. Some of the worst examples include rejecting many colors against white that offer good readability for those with CVD, while passing those same colors against black, which makes them unreadable.

The WCAG 2 formula doesn't account for polarity, or how font size, weight, and stroke thickness interact to affect readability, and it wasn't designed with today's display technologies in mind — mobile, OLED, dark mode, and HDR screens all behave differently than the display assumptions of the late 1980s/1990s used as the basis.

On the tooling — that's an understandable concern, but the reality is essentially replacing a few lines of code. Tooling has always updated alongside specification revisions across web standards. It's also worth noting that the candidate contrast method you mentioned is under evaluation, and has already seen enthusiastic voluntary adoption by designers and developers, with working tools, plugins, and design system integrations already in use as part of the public beta and ongoing research.

If the goal is improving actual accessibility, then there is no justification for carrying forward the existing method, which was adopted without empirical validation of its readability predictions, and has been widely criticized since. WCAG 3 is an opportunity to fix the errors of the past and improve actual accessibility.

But I do have to ask one thing, you said:
> ...*especially something as disruptive as switching to APCA*...

My question is, why do you view that as disruptive? And I'll note that the working group has not committed to any specific replacement — you're the one who named APCA here.

545.title: Consider using “user agents” in definition of support instead of “browsers”
545.body:
In our subgroups discussion of #504, concerns were raised that the definition of “programmatically determined” relies on web content, in this way: 

“programmatically determined” talks about software that is “accessibility supported”, “accessibility supported” mentions “browsers”, and “browsers” imply web content. 

Proposed change: use “user agents” instead of “browsers” in the “accessibility supported” definition. The definition of “user agents” mentions content and software, rather than web content, which would resolve the issue.

So the new definition would be: 

> *accessibility supported* 
> 
> supported by at least 2 major free ~browsers~ user agents on every operating system and/or available in assistive technologies used by 80% cumulatively of the AT users on each operating system for each type of AT used

546.title: Ambiguity of the term "character" and its impact on internationalization and testability
546.body:
The term “character” as used in accessibility-related specifications (and [Draft Definitions](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WhaesDbhuB8SmOeX05-qfo0nSvdXHugpCJUw8rA9nfI/edit?pli=1&tab=t.0#heading=h.hw5a0snww1ed) of the Text and Wording subgroup) raises a fundamental concern. In the context of Unicode, character is a highly nuanced and context-dependent concept, and it cannot be assumed to correspond to a unit that users perceive, read, or manipulate as a single entity. Treating character as a self-evident unit introduces ambiguity at the normative level and undermines the technical soundness of the specification.

Unicode itself explicitly distinguishes between encoded units and user-perceived text. A single unit that users experience as “one character” may consist of multiple code points, as in the case of combining character sequences, surrogate pairs, variation selectors, or emoji sequences. This distinction is formally documented in Unicode Standard Annex #29: Unicode Text Segmentation
https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/

which defines both legacy grapheme clusters and extended grapheme clusters precisely because earlier assumptions about characters proved inadequate. The existence of these two models already demonstrates that “character” is not a stable or self-explanatory concept even within Unicode.

However, even extended grapheme clusters are explicitly defined as a segmentation heuristic, not as a definitive model of user perception or comprehension. They provide a lower bound for avoiding incorrect splitting of encoded text, but they do not capture higher-level, language-dependent textual units that are directly relevant to accessibility.

This limitation is particularly evident in documents using CJK scripts and ruby annotations. In such contexts, a base ideograph and its associated ruby annotation may together form a single meaningful unit for reading, navigation, comprehension, or text-to-speech output. Treating these components as independent “characters” can fragment information that users naturally and legitimately process as a whole. Unicode grapheme clusters do not and are not intended to model such relationships.

As a result, accessibility requirements that rely—explicitly or implicitly—on the notion of “character” face a twofold problem. First, they fail to specify whether character refers to a code point, a legacy grapheme cluster, an extended grapheme cluster, or something else entirely. Second, even if grapheme clusters were assumed, they remain insufficient for capturing accessibility-relevant units in many non-Western writing systems.

It may be argued that, by “character,” the specification intends to mean a user-perceived character. This clarification does not resolve the issue. User-perceived character is not a defined term in WCAG, Unicode, or any referenced normative specification. Without an operational definition, the phrase merely replaces one undefined term with another. The critical question therefore remains unanswered: what is a user-perceived character, and how is it determined in a testable and interoperable manner?

Accessibility specifications must be implementable, testable, and interoperable across languages, scripts, platforms, and assistive technologies. Reliance on an undefined notion of “character”—whether qualified as “user-perceived” or not—fails to meet these requirements. This is not a matter of editorial clarity but a substantive defect in the conceptual foundation of the specification.

Unless the term character is rigorously defined or its use reconsidered, accessibility requirements risk being formally correct while practically indeterminate, particularly for users of non-Western scripts. This objection concerns the validity of the specification as a global accessibility standard, not the choice of any particular technical remedy.

547.title: Ambiguity of the term "word" and its impact on internationalization and testability
547.body:
The use of the term “word” in accessibility specifications (and [Draft Definitions](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WhaesDbhuB8SmOeX05-qfo0nSvdXHugpCJUw8rA9nfI/edit?pli=1&tab=t.0#heading=h.hw5a0snww1ed) of the Text and Wording subgroup) raises concerns that are even more fundamental than those associated with “character” (see #546). Unlike character-related units, which at least have a formalized representation within Unicode, the concept of a word is explicitly acknowledged to be language-dependent, purpose-dependent, and technology-dependent.

Unicode addresses word boundaries in Unicode Standard Annex #29: Unicode Text Segmentation (https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr29/), which makes clear that word segmentation is not a single, universal operation. Instead, it varies significantly depending on the writing system, the linguistic structure of the language, and the intended use case. UAX #29 explicitly states that word boundaries depend on purpose. For example, word segmentation suitable for cursor movement may differ from segmentation intended for line breaking, text selection, search, indexing, or text-to-speech.

Crucially, this variability is not merely a matter of natural language diversity. It is a consequence of differing technical goals. Word segmentation for assistive technologies may prioritize predictability, learnability, or cognitive load reduction, while other applications may prioritize linguistic precision or algorithmic efficiency. Unicode explicitly acknowledges this tension and does not claim to resolve it.

The limitations of the concept become especially evident in languages that do not use explicit word delimiters, such as Japanese and Chinese. In such languages, what constitutes a “word” depends heavily on morphological analysis, context, and purpose. There is no single segmentation that can be assumed to be correct across all accessibility-related operations. In Japanese, units corresponding to phrases (such as bunsetsu) are often more relevant to reading, comprehension, and speech output than units corresponding to words. This further demonstrates that “word” cannot be assumed to be a universal or accessibility-relevant unit across languages.

Appealing to an intuitive or “user-understood” notion of word does not resolve this defect. Unicode’s own documentation demonstrates that “word” is not a stable perceptual unit even for native speakers, let alone across languages and scripts. The relevant question is therefore not what a word “normally means,” but how the specification expects a word to be identified, processed, and tested in a reproducible manner.

In this context, the unqualified use of the term “word” in accessibility requirements is inherently problematic. Without specifying which segmentation model, which purpose, or which operational definition is intended, the specification leaves implementations with no objective basis for determining compliance. Accordingly, the use of “word” as a normative unit in accessibility specifications represents a substantive conceptual flaw. It undermines testability, interoperability, and the claim of language-neutral applicability.

548.title: [Blocks of text readable (minimum)] make text characteristics optional?
548.body:
In [1.4.12 Text spacing](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#text-spacing) we require content not to break if a user stylesheet sets certain values, effectively allowing for different values, as long as content doesn't break.

Can we consider to:

- make the text characteristics in “Blocks of text readable” similarly optional? 
- mark this requirement Supplemental
- remove the requirement altogether

To force specific values seems overly restrictive to me, while with a “as long as setting the values doesn't break the content”, like in 1.4.12, still allows anyone who would want those specific values to trivially do so via a user stylesheet / software that enforces a user stylesheet.

I think the existence of reader modes in most user agents removes a lot of the need for this requirement, so I would personally be open to removing it altogether.

550.title: Is the Summaries requirement overly prescriptive of what summaries should look like?
550.body:
In January 2026 WCAG 3 survey, @sydneycolemanfromgoogle commented:

"Summaries" This is an overly prescriptive definition of what summaries should look like. Summaries for meetings may appear very different & may allow users to customize the formatting they want. Please redact this section.

551.title: Should "Summaries available" change from core to supplemental?
551.body:
In the January 2026 WCAG 3 survey, @sydneycolemanfromgoogle commented:

- Summaries Available: It will be tricky to define a min amount of words/characters that would need summarization, and testing steps would be hard to define in a reliable way. I feel like there are so many tools for summarization nowadays, that this should be supplemental, allowing users to use summarization tools they prefer.

Sydney's comment raises an interesting question:
Should WCAG 3 consider having a pair of requirements about summaries?
- **(Core requirement) Text content summarizable** would ensure text content is available to/detectable by user agents/summarization tools.
- **(Supplemental requirement) Text content summaries provided** would require content authors to provide a summary.  

As we consider these possible changes, we need to look at other sections of WCAG 3 to see if adding a new requirement would create unnecessary overlap, such as with "Text detectable" in the Text-to-speech section.

552.title: Is "No nested clauses" too hard to implement?
552.body:
In the January 2026 WCAG 3 survey, @sydneycolemanforgoogle commented:

"No nested clauses - This is going to be incredibly challenging for parties to meet when they do not have dedicated writing resources or support, and does not seem like it adds significantly to understanding."

FYI, after the WCAG 3 survey closed, we changed "No nested clauses" from core to supplemental. We should reach out and see if this change helps resolve some of Sydney's concerns about this requirement.

It's also worth noting that free AI tools can already flag complex sentence structures. As WCAG 3 takes shape, it could encourage these tools to explicitly call out nested clauses and suggest ways to remove them.

comments.body:
TL;DR: It isn't too hard. Removing nested clauses is often good. This Requirement is too simplistic.

More detailed explanation:

It takes work to meet this requirement. It is very hard to meet wIthout anyone who works on language. But there are few sites that have nobody working on content.

Does removing nested clauses improve understanding?

There are probably exceptions, but the answer is by and large "yes". Much more so for deeply nested clauses.

~~There is also a question of depth, bearing in mind that single nested clauses are, while not differentiated according to the complexity of nesting in the current requirement text, almost certainly less impactful on the comprehensibility of the relevant conceptual exposition...~~

I don't think It is a problem that doing this requires work. I do think it is a problem that this is too simple to be very useful. I also think this does have value.

Writing clearly is hard. Mostly because different people have different ideas of what is clear. That means it is also very hard to test.

And different languages have different rules and customs, so testing for one language is often not very useful in a different language.

553.title: Should Text and Wording add Japanese as a guardrail language?
553.body:
In the January 2026 WCAG 3 survey, Jan McSorley commented on behalf of W3C's Global Inclusion community group:

- 2.2.3 - Clear Language - this is written in a way that appears to suggest that content creators should avoid using Kanji characters (Chinese Characters) and use Kana (Japanese Characters) instead. The global-inclusion group is very concerned about this note because no language is similar to the Japanese language - Japanese uses different scripts - both Kanji and Kana. The approach to Japanese is very different. Depending on the literacy levels, you may not use Kanji. UN 6 languages have nothing similar to Japanese. The way this is organized is biased. The Japanese language needs to be elevated in our guidance so that we can avoid this kind of bias. It is not one of the "guardrail languages" for the internationalization work, but this is an example of why it should be. We need a definition of clear language because it's confusing to know what to do without knowing what it means.

554.title: Clarifying "Descriptive errors" for backend and non-user-driven failures
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
554.body:
Outcome/Requirement: [2.5.1 Correct errors] -> Descriptive errors

### Problem Statement:
The current wording of the "Descriptive errors" requirement ("Error messages clearly describe the problem") assumes that the "problem" is always identifiable and relevant to the user (e.g., an incorrectly formatted field). However, in modern web applications, errors often stem from unknown backend failures or system timeouts. In these cases, describing the technical "problem" (e.g., "500 Internal Server Error" or "Database connection failed") is unhelpful to the user, potentially confusing for those with cognitive disabilities, and may pose a security risk.

### Proposed Change:
I propose adjusting the requirement to ensure that when a specific cause cannot be described, the message must prioritize actionability (what the user can do to resolve the situation).

**Suggested Revised Text:**
"Error messages clearly describe the problem or provide clear instructions for user recovery when the specific cause is unknown."

### Rationale:
1. Actionability over Description: For many users, especially those with cognitive or learning disabilities, knowing how to fix the situation is more important than knowing why the server failed.
2. Task Completion: A requirement that focuses solely on "describing the problem" may lead developers to provide technical jargon that doesn't help the user complete their task.
3. Security: Providing a "descriptive" error for a system failure can inadvertently leak infrastructure details. A functional instruction (e.g., "Try again in a few minutes") satisfies the user's need without compromising the system.

**Examples of the proposed change in practice:**
Current (Description only): "An unknown error occurred in the data processing layer."
Proposed (Action-oriented): "We couldn't save your information right now. Wait a moment and try again, or contact support if the issue continues."

This question was raised at the February 3rd AG meeting. As part of this discussion:

564.title: Pointer Controllable vs Pointer Cancellation
564.body:
Pointer Controllable is not the same as Pointer Cancelation.
1. The requirement is only about “clicking” -- activation under the pointer.
2. The requirement is **not** about controlling the pointer, which implies something about how the pointer moves.

569.title: Nested clauses: impact on readability is language-dependent
569.body:
The concern about “nested clauses” seems to reflect an English-specific intuition rather than a universal principle.

For example, in English, a sentence like:

> The rat that the cat that the dog chased killed ate the cheese.

is clearly difficult to process.

However, the equivalent structure in Japanese:

> 犬が追いかけた猫が殺したネズミが食べたチーズ

is not particularly difficult for native speakers. Similar patterns are also natural in Korean and other head-final languages.

This suggests that nested clauses are not inherently harmful to readability. In some languages, they are routine and easy to process. The real source of difficulty may differ across languages (for example, word order ambiguity or unclear referents), rather than simply the presence of clause embedding.

Therefore, treating “nested clauses” as a general readability problem may risk overgeneralizing from English-specific experience.
