590.title: Rendering‑aware contrast model proposal for WCAG 3
590.body:
Body:

I would like to propose a rendering‑aware contrast model for WCAG 3, based on empirical measurements of how anti‑aliasing and rasterization systematically reduce perceived contrast across platforms.

As an accessibility evaluator, I frequently en[encounter](https://github.com/nakano0949-web/wcag-aa-contrast/blob/main/proposal.md)counter cases where text passes WCAG 2.x contrast requirements based on CSS color values, yet appears significantly lower in contrast when rendered. This discrepancy becomes especially severe for small text, thin weights, and certain font cuts.

Below is a summary of the conceptual model, empirical findings, and a feasible extraction algorithm.

---

1. Rendering structure: Core / AA / BG‑Ring

Figure 1:  
[1.svg](https://github.com/nakano0949-web/wcag-aa-contrast/blob/main/1.svg)

Explanation:  
Rendered text consists of three predictable regions:

- Core — pure glyph color, no anti‑aliasing  
- AA band — blended pixels between text and background  
- BG‑Ring — background sampling region  

This structure exists across all platforms and rendering engines.

---

2. Font size and AA dominance

Figure 2:  
[2.svg](https://github.com/nakano0949-web/wcag-aa-contrast/blob/main/2.svg)

Explanation:  
As text becomes smaller, the Core region becomes extremely thin and the AA band dominates.  
This causes significant perceptual contrast loss even when CSS contrast is sufficient.

---

3. Core Ratio Model

Figure 3:  
[3.svg](https://github.com/nakano0949-web/wcag-aa-contrast/blob/main/3.svg)

Explanation:  
The perceptual contrast loss can be approximated by:

- Core Ratio = (C / W)²  
- AA Impact = 1 − Core Ratio  

This provides a mathematical basis for predicting contrast loss.

---

4. Measured AA impact vs font size

Figure 4:  
[4.svg](https://github.com/nakano0949-web/wcag-aa-contrast/blob/main/4.svg)

Explanation:  
Empirical measurements show a rapid increase in AA impact below 14px.  
At 12px and below, Core thickness becomes extremely small, and AA dominates.

---

5. CSS contrast vs rendered contrast

Figure 5:  
[5.svg](https://github.com/nakano0949-web/wcag-aa-contrast/blob/main/5.svg)

Explanation:  
The gap between CSS contrast and actual rendered contrast increases sharply for small text.  
This demonstrates that CSS color values alone cannot reliably predict readability.

---

6. Extraction algorithm (feasibility)

Figure 6:  
[6.svg](https://github.com/nakano0949-web/wcag-aa-contrast/blob/main/6.svg)

Explanation:  
A rendering‑aware contrast evaluation is technically feasible.  
The algorithm:

1. Detects text region  
2. Applies distance transform  
3. Estimates font size  
4. Computes Core thickness  
5. Segments Core / AA / BG‑Ring  

This shows that rendering‑aware evaluation can be automated.

---

Interim approach: font size and weight heuristics

Existing contrast tools could incorporate font size and font weight as a preliminary screening method.  
However, due to platform variability and font cut differences, this cannot fully address the problem.  
A rendering‑aware model is ultimately necessary for reliable perceptual contrast evaluation.

---

Conclusion

WCAG 3 provides an opportunity to address a long‑standing gap between nominal (CSS) contrast and actual perceptual contrast.  
The empirical data, conceptual model, and extraction algorithm presented here may help inform future rendering‑aware contrast guidance.

I would be happy to provide additional data, code, or implementation details.

comments.body: x-ref https://github.com/w3c/wcag/issues/4954 for some earlier discussion

Thanks for the cross-reference.

Issue #4954 was my earlier proposal focusing on the impact of anti-aliasing on measured contrast.  
The current issue (#590) is a follow-up that provides a more detailed rendering model, including:

- the Core / AA / BG-Ring structure,
- empirical measurements across platforms,
- and a feasible extraction algorithm for WCAG 3.

This new issue is intended to complement #4954 by offering a more formalized and implementation-ready model.

The draft APC-RC considers anti-aliasing, and also provides for methods to match font weights and x-heights of unknown fonts to a reference font. [The font matching method.](https://readtech.org/ARC/tests/visual-readability-contrast/?tn=methods#size-weight)

Thank you for sharing the update regarding the APC‑RC draft and its new font‑matching and x‑height normalization approach. I understand that the draft aims to model visual readability by incorporating anti‑aliasing and font normalization.

One concern I still have is that the current APC‑RC documentation does not appear to address readability issues for users with color vision deficiencies or low vision. These user groups often experience reduced or altered contrast perception that cannot be fully captured by physical contrast models alone.

Could you clarify whether APC‑RC includes considerations or planned extensions for color‑vision‑deficient users and low‑vision users, or whether additional guidance will be provided for these cases?

Hi @nakano0949-web 

> ...*for users with color vision deficiencies or low vision. These user groups often experience reduced or altered contrast perception that cannot be fully captured by physical contrast models alone*.
> *Could you clarify whether APC‑RC includes ...planned extensions*...

### Yes, absolutely.

One extension we are very excited to release this year is the protan compensator extension. This pre-shapes the luminances for colors that have high red primary content, which is the color that can cause luminance contrast deficits for protans, when it's the lightest color.

APCA already greatly improves CVD accomodation over WCAG2 for protans in particular, but the protan compensator will extend improved visual accessibility into even very wide gamut displays.

Interestingly, the vast majority of CVD types have better lightness contrast sensitivity and better overall visual function, than standard vision in most respects—this is well established in the existing research. And for advanced hue-based accomodation, we are continuing work on SACAM, an a11y-adjustable color model, which enables dynamic personalization.

### Docs

I'll be the first to admit some of our documentation can be hard to parse at times, and the current backlog towards the next release is causing delays—but we added Pro-MAX seats of Claude AI to help us develop more accessible and easier to follow documentation. Also, we have a lot of draft and experimental documentation at our [forum here on GitHub](https://github.com/Myndex/SAPC-APCA/discussions).

While some of this is mentioned in the docs, APC-RC contrast is already geared towards low vision. The selected contrasts for Silver and Gold levels are intended to improve readability for a Pelli Robson contrast score down to 1 (profound contrast deficit¹.

Please feel free to to reach out with questions. 


Thank you for reading,



Andrew Somers
*Director of Research*       
*Inclusive Reading Technlogies*



> [!NOTE]      
> ¹ *A PR score is a profound impairment. A PR score of 2 is "perfect", and it's a -log measure, where lower scores represent greater contrast deficit.*

591.title: WCAG 3.0 Requirements: clarification for native mobile apps
591.body:
There appears to be an inconsistency between the Requirements doc and Explainer doc.
Generally the term "mobile apps" includes "native mobile apps". 
Native mobile apps is digital content but is not web technology.
So maybe the use of the term "mobile apps" in the statement that also includes "software"  needs to be clear. 

Under 1.2 WCAG Scope in the Requirements doc, it says:

"software and web applications, including mobile apps; and
operating systems and other platforms who may want advice for features to better support people with disabilities".
And, The Explainer doc states:
"Several items are out of scope for WCAG 3:
Non-web technologies...."

So I believe this inconsistency needs to be addressed or am I not interpreting the above content as intended?
Thanks

592.title: Requirements doc should explicitly state: WCAG will include normative guidance for authors, but not user-agents or authoring tools
592.body:
Section 1.2 WCAG Scope states:
"The current project design does not intend to write separate specifications or normative requirements for the technology stack beyond digital content".
The above statement  follows a list that includes:
"authoring tools, such as content management systems;
user agents, such as browsers and media players;
assistive technologies, such as screen readers, screen magnifiers, and assistants for memory, organization, or simplification;"

Admittedly later on, 4.8 Scope does refer only to "informative guidance":
"The scope of the associated informative materials will include guidance for a diverse group of stakeholders including content creators, browsers, authoring tools, assistive technologies, and more".

In the interests of plain, unambiguous and understandable  text, maybe   it will be helpful to explicitly include the statement from explanation you provided in issue #224 (https://github.com/w3c/silver/issues/224).
The statement I refer to is:
"AG can produce normative guidance for authors, but not user-agents or authoring tools". 
or
"WCAG 3 is not intended to normatively cover "features an authoring tool / browser /OS should offer to facilitate / enhance accessibility" 

This clarification IMO should be right after the statement in the Requirements doc Section 1.2 WCAG Scope:
"The current project design does not intend to write separate specifications or normative requirements for the technology stack beyond digital content".
Thanks,
Sailesh

593.title: Explainer minor editorial on 2.2 Out of scope
593.body:
From:  2.2 [Out of scope](https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/DNOTE-wcag-3.0-explainer-20260226/#out-of-scope):

> Several items are out of scope for WCAG 3:
> - Non-web technologies.
> - Normative requirements for platforms, operating systems, software in the web technology stack, etc.

This is minor editorial and certainly can wait.
1. “several” is more than two.
2. “etc.” is doing a lot of work, and is not exactly plain language.

599.title: Recommend removing “Keyboard navigable if responsive”
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
599.body:
The [Keyboard navigable if responsive](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#keyboard-navigable-if-responsive) provision seems unnecessary. Can it be removed?

If a page/view is not keyboard navigable, then it will surely fail [Keyboard accessible](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#keyboard-accessible) whether or not it “[_uses responsive design_](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#keyboard-navigable-if-responsive:~:text=uses%20responsive%20design)”.

600.title: Reorganization of WCAG 3: Core + Satellites
600.body:
I propose a modular WCAG 3 specification structure that systematically addresses language and cultural dependencies, leverages the *Lreq success experience from the I18N Working Group, and enables rapid development of a Latin-Language (Western languages) Satellite specification.

Under the **Core + Satellites** model:

- Core comprises the existing WCAG 3 material excluding language-dependent sections (e.g., Text and Wording), capturing universally applicable accessibility requirements.
- Satellites are language- or culture-specific extensions building on *Lreq-style language requirement experience; a Latin-Language Satellite for Western languages can be developed first for practical and rapid adoption.

This structure supports inclusive internationalization — each Satellite can progress independently while Core remains stable. Following the example of modular specifications like CSS and their periodic Snapshots, annual combined Snapshots of Core and Satellites could provide up-to-date integrated references for implementers before final Recommendation status.

603.title: Equivalent for 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts?
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
603.body:
The current [WCAG 3 working draft](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/) doesn’t seem to have an equivalent for the [Character Key Shortcuts](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/character-key-shortcuts.html) success criterion added back in WCAG 2.1. Should it?

Although the original SC is mainly positioned around voice control, it does describe [barriers for other people](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/character-key-shortcuts.html#:~:text=Keyboard%2Donly%20users,across%20different%20applications.) as well.

I put together [a quick experiment](https://cdpn.io/pen/debug/jEMPwvL/06f138a6e48b1f8bd3fc93b6fc341160) to see how today’s voice control solutions behave in this regard.

Could there be a way to address this issue while not putting a burden on authors to create custom UI for disabling or re-mapping shortcuts? Some example conditions that crossed my mind:

- Character key shortcuts must not be executed while the user is inputting text
- Character key shortcuts must not be provided for ‘consequential’ or irreversible operations

605.title: 2.1.1 - Core requirement: Images detectable: "Detectable" is ambiguous and requires a definition.
605.body:
The term “detectable” is currently ambiguous and requires a clear, normative definition.

**Proposed definition:**
"A detectable element is one that can be identified programmatically in code and is presented to users in a way they can perceive."  

This definition would support the intended test scenarios; the current information necessary to understand “detectable” appears only in a non-normative Test section. For clarity and enforceability, this concept should be defined normatively.

From the Test section, it appears the intent is for an element to be programmatically determinable when code is available and perceptible to assistive technologies (e.g., screen readers) when code is not directly available. While this intent can be inferred from the non-normative test, it is not explicitly stated in a normative way that supports consistent interpretation.

606.title: 2.1.1 - Core requirement: Images detectable - Test needs update
606.body:
Combining two test modalities "code inspections" and "screen reader inspections" into a single test case opens it up to incorrect interpretation. 

If these are equivalent tests under different conditions based on using alternate modalities to test the same scenario, they should be split into two tests with alternate conditions with number ordering at the same level:

Sample suggestion:

For each non-decorative image that can be detected with a code inspector:
1. Check the code to see if it has been marked up in a way that makes it detectable.

Alternatively, for each non-decorative image that cannot be programmatically determined through code inspection:
1. For technologies where the code cannot be checked, use a screen reader to test that the image is detectable.

comments.body: Before jumping right to a screen reader test - if there is not code access we could check the accessibility API first.

607.title: 2.1.1 - Decorative images hidden - Test procedure update.
607.body:
In the test section, there is help text that is redundant of the second test procedure. There is no need to state "(HTML) Using an empty alt attribute for an image element" in the first procedure since it is a test condition in the second procedure, "Check that an alt attribute is present and empty."

> This section is non-normative.
> 
> (General) No accessible name
> 
> Procedure
> 
> 1. Check for any images that add no information to the content.
> 2. Check that the image has no accessible name.
> Expected results
> 
> #2 is true.
> **(HTML) Using an empty alt attribute for an image element**
> 
> Procedure
> #
> For any image that adds no information to the content:
> 
> 1. Check that title, aria-label, aria-labelledby etc. is either absent or empty.
> 2. **Check that an alt attribute is present and empty.**
> Expected results
> 
> #1 is true.
> #2 is true.

608.title: Keyboard navigable if responsive. - breakpoints are problematic.
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
608.body:
This is a pandora's box when we say that "breakpoint defined by the author" as this is ambiguous and easy to bypass the normative requirement. I think we need to answer the questions of what is meant by "defined by the author" and what the scope/definition of a breakpoint is. Breakpoints are wildly different in scope and approach.

What does "Defined by the author mean"?  
- Could this be an accessibility document on the site that states which breakpoints are supported? If I were a nefarious company/individual that wanted to bypass this requirement, I would just say that the site works at 320px width. Then I only have to meet the 320px requirement and all other sizes would be out of scope for the test.
- If we mean "as defined in css or programmatically", then the problem here is that only strategies like media queries would be supported and using something like css flex would be out of scope or difficult to define when the page could be dynamic at every pixel width. 

How do we define what a breakpoint is?
- we never define what a breakpoint is.  I fear that this will be so broad that it always passes; or never passes. 
- - is a breakpoint the moment that a containing element switches to a different css definition based on media queries?
- - is a breakpoint a supported width in the view while the entire page is dynamic.
- - For dynamic pages that have no true breakpoint, using flex, percentages, or undefined widths, how is a breakpoint determined? Off of the min-width, combined with all other min-widths? What about the upper limit, or all moments in-between as the page is changing while resizing.

610.title: "Media Alternative" use of "Usually text" is not in alignment with defined RFC2119
610.body:
### Original:
"alternative formats, usually text, for audio, video, and audio-video content including [captions](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-captions), [audio descriptions](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-audio-description), and [descriptive transcripts](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-descriptive-transcript)"

The "including" portion of this includes audio alternatives in the "usually text" list (audio descriptions). This is confusing and encourages/allows incorrect solutions when a media alternative is required. Additionally, the "usally" breaks from the RFC2119 defined standards that should be used.

### Proposed:
Recommended to update the definition to be more clear about expected outputs. And to use RFC2119 standard "may" instead of "usually"

"alternative formats, may be presented as text or audio-descriptions dependent on the requirements of the content medium. Audio, video, and audio-video content alternate formats include [captions](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-captions), [audio descriptions](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-audio-description), and [descriptive transcripts](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-descriptive-transcript)"

### Reference link:
[RFC2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119)

611.title: 2.1.2 Media Alternatives - Test case (and definitions)
611.body:
The document does not define what formats are usable for each medium. The definition for [media alternatives](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-media-alternative) does not provide meaningful additional information about acceptable formats either.  The test should be broken out into separate tests for audio, video, and audio-video content. Each of these requires a different solution and as it is stated, it is not clear from WCAG 3.0 in its entirity when a particular solution is appropriate. 

Absurd, but passing example due to the ambiguity of the media alternatives definition:
1. video only content, a closed caption with no information could be included. This would meet the requirement as defined. 

Recommendation:

Expand the test procedure (or remove it since  to be more clear about what medium is being tested and expected media alternative outputs for each. The procedures are examples and would require refinement.


Procedure

For each instance of audio-only content:

1. Check that a correctly sequenced text alternative is available for that content.
2. Check that the content of the media alternative is equivalent to the meaningful information in the media content.
 
Expected results

#1 and #2 are true.

Procedure

For each instance of video-only content:

1. Check that a correctly sequenced text alternative is available for that content; or
2. Check that an audio description alternative is available.
3. Check that the content of the media alternative is equivalent to the meaningful information in the media content.Expected results

#1 and #2 are true.

Procedure

For each instance of audio-video content:

1. Check that correctly sequenced closed captions are available for that content; or
Check that a descriptive transcript is available for that content; or
Check that Audio-descriptions are included when required.
2. Check that the content of the media alternative is equivalent to the meaningful information in the media content.Expected results
#1 and #2 are true.

614.title: Clarify that decorative images must add no information or functionality
614.body:
The current wording refers to images that “add no information to the content.” This could be interpreted too narrowly and may risk misclassifying images that do not add informational content but still serve a functional role in the interface. I purpose this is changed to:

:term[Decorative] images are :term[programmatically] hidden.

:::tests (General) No accessible name

Procedure

Check for any images that add no information _or functionality to the content._
Check that the image has no accessible name.
Expected results

#2 is true.

616.title: Focus placed should be a core requirement
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
616.body: "Focus placed" and "Focus retained" seem to be very similar, and both are currently a supplemental requirement. I think it is worth discussing whether they should be a core requirement. I have spoken with screen reader users who have seen it as a barrier when they are in the middle of completing a form and using a date picker, for example, only to have their focus lost when the date picker is closed and sent back to the `<body>` element. Is part of the reason for it being a supplemental requirement that browsers try to return focus to a logical place on their own?

618.title: 2.1.4 Captions - Core Requirement Suggestion
618.body:
A high contrast background is significant for partially-sighted persons for readibility of captions. So, at least 4,5:1 contrast ratio should be provided for caption text and its background.
This should be included in addition to captions adjustable supplemental requirement because it is directly affecting usability of people with low vision.

619.title: 2.1.1 Image Alternatives - Assertion Recommendation
619.body:
Organizational Description Guidelines and CMS integration can be assertions for this ctieria.
Generally, the biggest challange for organizations is making alt text process sustainable. In our organization, we prepared a document summarizing how to describe images and shared it with our content agency. 
Every organization should work on its own unique rulesets due to sectoral differences. For example, an e-commerce company may need different detail level and a travel website may need different details for the images in their digital channels.

In the criteria the bare minimum of this "Organizational Description Guidelines" can be specified.

622.title: Add explicit requirement for Scrollable regions to be included in keyboard tab order
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
622.body:
### Problem / User Need
Keyboard-only users — including people with motor disabilities, and screen reader users — rely on the Tab key to navigate interactive and readable content. When a page contains a scrollable region (for example, a `<div>` with `overflow: scroll` or `overflow: auto`), that region may contain critical content that cannot be accessed without a mouse scroll.

Safari on macOS does not automatically include scrollable regions in the Tab order, unlike Chrome and Firefox. Firefox makes any block-level element with an appropriate CSS overflow property keyboard-focusable automatically; Chrome, Edge, and Safari historically have not done this on their own - tabindex="0" must be added explicitly. This creates an inconsistent and unreliable experience across browsers that the current WCAG 3.0 draft does not explicitly address.

**### Proposed New Requirement**
Section 2.3.3 (Navigating content) or 2.4.1 (Keyboard interface input)

**Scrollable regions keyboard reachable**
Any element that has scrollable content must be reachable using keyboard navigation, unless:
- The scrollable content is purely decorative, or
- The content inside the region already contains keyboard-focusable elements that allow the user to scroll it

### Personal Note
I believe this addition would do more than just close a technical gap. Explicit language in WCAG 3.0 would create pressure on browser vendors - including Apple/Safari - to adopt consistent behaviour, rather than leaving the burden entirely on content authors. Standards like WCAG have historically influenced browser and platform behaviour. This is an opportunity to use that influence to push for a more consistent accessibility experience across products and browsers, benefiting all keyboard users regardless of which browser they use. Please feel free to contest if you believe this already exist in some form or another.

626.title: README link to process presentation is not publicly accessible
626.body: The README currently includes a link to a presentation describing the group’s process for addressing issues and updates: `https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/14qG2f-ZkhFDqox_qmzqC5tCUt1xJaumkJS2l5GaD-3o/edit#slide=id.p` At the moment, the presentation appears to be private, which prevents visitors from accessing the resource directly from the repository. This affects the usefulness of the README for external contributors and reviewers, since the linked documentation cannot be viewed without additional permissions. **Suggested fix** * Update the Google Slides sharing settings so that visitors with the link can view the presentation * Alternatively, replace the current link with a publicly accessible version or another public documentation source Also, this is my first time making an issue in this repository, so please give me any feedback/call me out if I did something wrong. I really appreciate it - thank you.

629.title: Can user-preferences be relied on for "No flashing"?
labels: Path: User control and prevent harm
629.body:
The draft has a note under the "No flashing over threshold" requirement:

> Note: If there is an [accessibility supported](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-accessibility-supported) method of setting a user-preference to prevent flashing, the content can be considered to avoid flashing if that preference is respected.

Assuming it was accessibility supported (which I don't think is is the case now), is this something we should rely on? 

@julierawe commented:
> This method seems dangerous for the no-flashing provisions. Do we really want to allow high-frequency flashing as long as user preferences are respected? What if a user looks at another person's device without first adjusting the preferences?

Also, this applies for animation as well, for reduced-motion.

comments.body: on a wider note, should there be some mandated warning when content does include (potential) flashing? as in users need to be notified/told about it first, and give them sufficient time to abort/back out of content
There is a separate "flash and motion warning" requirement [in the doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ucdwQdwGCuTPzKXAfF8tTe5RRXsWVFE2bB--6zFRjiQ/edit?tab=t.6h0wzorw34br).

Are we thinking this is an authorship thing to provide warnings, or should it be the browsers after detecting the content types and the user's preferences? I'm not sure on the feasibility of browsers doing the work, but we know what happens when left to those who create sites. 

I'm fine either way, but I've been looking at things from a bottom up approach (starting with the underlying tech) rather than a top down (Scan/audit site -> remediate) method and this seems like a ripe one that straddles both.
Noting that the animation based requirements are impacted by this.

631.title: Can flashing requirements account for zoom?
labels: Path: User control and prevent harm
631.body:
Within the flashing requirement there is a size-test:

> Flashes that appear to the user are smaller than 0.006 steradians within any 10 field of view (25% of any 10 field of view).
> 
> This equates to 25% of any 470 CSSpx diameter circle, or 20% of any 470x470 CSSpx square, on the screen. 

The 25% bit is because you could have small flashing areas that are widely spaced, those would not be a trigger. However, if it is within your focused view (not wide field of view, but the bit in focus) then it can be a trigger.

@WilcoFiers commented that the rule:
> needs to include viewport area, and in doing so needs to account for magnification / zoom / resize.

Using CSS pixels means the size specified is the viewport area, which will vary depending on the intended viewing distance for the device.

Personally, I don't think we can account for zoom, magnification or other methods of resizing content. If you try to, then there is no point in having a size, all sizing assumptions are gone. The test would only be on contrast and frequency.

That means we are missing an intersectional need (low vision + epilepsy), but if size was not included, it would make this a much more difficult requirement to achieve.

comments.body:
Thanks for opening this issue @alastc

I think this is achievable. We can be pragmatic about it. There are limits on how much content can be magnified. When people can no longer fit whole worlds on the screen they tend to switch over to screen readers. That seems fairly reasonable to me. Something like a 24x24 area. I don't think that's a particularly difficult thing to achieve in website. Just avoid flashing content all together.

Where that gets difficult is around video and games, but I think for those its perfectly reasonable to have an exception. Unlike interfaces with text and icons and stuff, people don't magnify on videos or games. You may need larger captions, but video itself isn't magnified, so there the 470 area seems reasonable.

the requirement is for it to be accessible before you zoom it. It becomes impossible if you can zoom it and you do not have any idea how much it could be zoomed.

It would be more accessible if nothing ever flashed and you could zoom it forever and still not have it cause a problem. But this is not practical.

If WCAG3 want to shrink the area to smaller than 25% by whatever factor of Zoom, they want to choose they can't of course do this. I strongly advise against it, but it could be done. It is not what is in.WCAG2.

The only "flashing" things I can think of that make sense and that are common are the dots indicating some ongoing activity state like "currently speaking", and they are usually quite small and have low contrast (sometimes too low) so constitute no problem (does there need to be a 2.2.2 exception for them, I wonder). Apart from ads, I cannot think of any other design elements that would be inconvenienced by ruling out flashing altogether.

I agree with Wilco that there shouldn't be a problem reducing the size to a much smaller area like a 24 x 24 since this area might be enlarged by zooming, and exempting video and games (if advance warning is given). Makes perfect sense. 

@GreggVan wrote:
> If WCAG3 want to shrink the area to smaller than 25% by whatever factor of Zoom, they want to choose they can't of course do this. I strongly advise against it

Why advise against it? What's the problem?

> Why advise against it? What's the problem?

False-positives: Failing things which aren't a problem for people in practice. That might be an acceptable risk compared to triggering seizures, but that's the main thing that comes to mind for me.

> There are limits on how much content can be magnified. When people can no longer fit whole worlds on the screen they tend to switch over to screen readers. That seems fairly reasonable to me. Something like a 24x24 area. 

I'm trying to figure out how that would work. 20% of a 470CSSpx square is roughly a 210 x 210 square (using maths I rarely used for >30 years, so please do correct if I'm wrong!). Zoomed in to say 400%, so taking 25% of that area, I think you get a 105px square. 

The bit that's then tricky is how does that figure with the visual field? The reason it's set to a 470px square to start with is that is roughly your focusing area of the eye at normal distances. If you are zoomed in (either digital zoom or nose-to-screen), that could be your entire field of view, which means some of it doesn't count. I.e. the flashing is from outside your focusable-area. 

I could be wrong about that, but I don't know who would have done research on the low-vision/seizure cross-over?

Two thoughts:
1. Some users may choose to enable flashing content on purpose - for example, a person who is deaf may want content with an audio alert to also flash - although likely in a safe threshold.
2. Adding a warning to flashing content doesn't make it accessible - adding timestamps to a video when it flashes can be helpful but it still doesn't address the access to the missed information or accidental activation.  There would still need to be some sort of mode.  Hopefully, one day, this could be solved at the platform level which would prevent display of flashing within the dangerous threshold.

While this is focused on low vision and epilepsy intersection, this also plays in with vestibular disorders and motion sensitivity. So far my research shows that animation that is 25% of the viewport is rarely a trigger unless the animation is presented next to content or is "aggressive" in the motion used. 

And to @mraccess77 point, if I'm warned there is a problematic moment coming, I'm more likely to bounce than sit through it. 

From the animation sensitive side we need more research. @GreggVan I saw in the Google doc you are doing some research. Let me know if you want more thoughts on just animation and how this may apply.

I don’t believe it’s feasible for the flashing requirements to factor in Zoom.

> Adding a warning to flashing content doesn't make it accessible - adding timestamps to a video when it flashes can be helpful but it still doesn't address the access to the missed information or accidental activation.

I agree that a generic warning, say before the program starts, is not so useful and not enough for WCAG3.  OTOH, I have seen many educational videos where a warning is use responsibly, at the top of the program and shortly before it occurs (or maybe there are time stamps).  In these cases, the flashing content is essential to the content and there is audio description if a viewer turns away or dims the screen.  IMHO this sort of mindful approach should be sufficient for WCAG3.  I can provide an example if anyone likes.

I do not consider browser zoom to be assistive technology. 

It seems like the author could know the viewport size or scale/browser zoom and while this may not relate to physical area or a small window it would provide some detail when combined with screen size to help determine if zoom is being used at the time.

> > Why advise against it? What's the problem?
> 
> False-positives: Failing things which aren't a problem for people in practice. That might be an acceptable risk compared to triggering seizures, but that's the main thing that comes to mind for me.
> 
> > There are limits on how much content can be magnified. When people can no longer fit whole worlds on the screen they tend to switch over to screen readers. That seems fairly reasonable to me. Something like a 24x24 area.
> 
> I'm trying to figure out how that would work. 20% of a 470CSSpx square is roughly a 210 x 210 square (using maths I rarely used for >30 years, so please do correct if I'm wrong!). Zoomed in to say 400%, so taking 25% of that area, I think you get a 105px square.
> 
> The bit that's then tricky is how does that figure with the visual field? The reason it's set to a 470px square to start with is that is roughly your focusing area of the eye at normal distances. If you are zoomed in (either digital zoom or nose-to-screen), that could be your entire field of view, which means some of it doesn't count. I.e. the flashing is from outside your focusable-area.
> 
> I could be wrong about that, but I don't know who would have done research on the low-vision/seizure cross-over?

The 20% of the colored square are meant area-wise, so I also calculate a resulting square of 210x210.
On the other hand, the zooming rate is measured in one dimension only: zooming 200% yields double text height, zooming 400% yields quadruple text height. As a consequence, a square which is 210 high in 400% zoom is only 52,5 px high in the unzoomed page.
So, the overall result is a 52 pc square,

In general, in WCAG 2.x the philosophy is, that the success criteria must be fulfilled at the same time. 
So, also a user needing considerable zoom must be protected from seizure triggers.
Therefore yes, in my opinion the flashing and flickering requirement should account for zoom.
On a mobile device, 470px usually cover the whole width and more that half the height, when resizing 200 it covers the whole screen.
The reflow requirement talks about 320 CSS pc width and 256 CSS px height.
So, definitely I think the flashing and flickering size threshold should take into account these requirements.

By the way, for light sensitive eyes, even a single flash can be harmful.
And even small flash can distract.
Therefore, if you ask me, the smallest feasible threshold is my favorite.

My thoughts - as the primary author and moving force for getting Flashing into WCAG in the first place. 

Flashing is not required to be passed if you zoom.  That was not the intent of WCAG2 and it is clear from the definitions and notes that accompany it. 

People with low visions often lean forward to view screens more closely - and do use large screens at lower resolutions -  (Same effect as zoom for field of view).  So even if you did say it needed to be 16 times smaller area (400% zoom)  and more (for larger screens) you would still not protect all low vision users who also can have photosensitive seizures but you would make the provision more that 10 times harder to pass.   

Even with the provision - there are some that are too sensitive to not be affected.  And there always will be.   We cannot make provisions that will protect everyone.  So we find a reasonable point and draw the line there.

the real solution (and one we are working on) is providing users with display-time detection and prevention tools  (as AT - eg glasses) or built into displays.   That will requires no changes to video for everyone else catch all flashing, is adjustable to user sensitivity, works for any zoom or display size or viewing distance (AT) and works better all around for each user.

But until then - we should not adopt a rule or interpretation in WCAG that is so draconian that it won't be accepted by the standards and regulatory bodies we want to adopt WCAG.

I think we need two requirements. One for full screen content such as videos and games. People (generally) don't magnify these because having the full view is essential for the experience. That's the most common case for flashing content, and I think for those its reasonable not to account for magnification.

For things that aren't full screen; inline animated images, animated UI elements, etc. which people do magnify on we really should have some requirement. I appreciate your point that we need to draw the line somewhere. But this is one of the most harmful things a content author can do. Surely we need to do better than "you'll only get proper protection if you have 20/20 vision".

> I think we need two requirements. One for full screen content such as videos and games. People (generally) don't magnify these because having the full view is essential for the experience. That's the most common case for flashing content, and I think for those its reasonable not to account for magnification.
> 
I agree. Still, I suggest to think in full screen on large monitors with a possibly quite short viewing distance (shorter than someone with good vision would choose).

> For things that aren't full screen; inline animated images, animated UI elements, etc. which people do magnify on we really should have some requirement. I appreciate your point that we need to draw the line somewhere. But this is one of the most harmful things a content author can do. Surely we need to do better than "you'll only get proper protection if you have 20/20 vision".

> I think we need two requirements.  One for full screen content such as videos and games.

As with WCAG2.x, I think the requirement has to presume full-screen content.  If not, how exactly would the exception be phrased?  Presumably something like:

> Except when using the viewport full screen is essential.

Which strikes me as so broad as to be of little utility.  I would like to see what specifically is being proposed for the wording of the requirement.

632.title: Relation from Flashing/motion requriements to the warning requirement
labels: Path: User control and prevent harm
632.body:
A bit of a placeholder, but having updated the flashing requirements we need to make sure that it works with the "warning" requirement.

Bruce commented:
> I looked for and easily found the example of YouTuber warning about flashing and giving time stamps (typically, the flashing is integral to subject matter topic of the video). As far as I can tell, this protocol seems to be in wide practice (and becoming common) and to be sufficient for addressing the disability-related need. (See Trigger Warning / Flash and Motion warning in Graham tab.) Does such a protocol satisfy the Core: No Flashing requirement? I believe so, because of the note and that such a protocol “is an accessibility supported method of setting a user-preference to prevent flashing”. It takes a bit of rationalization for that conclusion.
> 
> I suggest that the Note (or the intent behind it) be explicitly part of the requirement or the “easily avoidable” idea be surfaced early and strongly in the Guidelines. Superficially, a best practice YouTuber warning fails “any flashes are below the general flash and red flash threshold” and that seems problematic to me. [WCAG 2.x has this same defect (and not just with SC 2.3.1), but I am optimistic for WCAG3 to be more elegant with addressing this issue.]

We'll probably need to add an exception or "applies when" if flashing/moving content can be shown when preceded by a warning.

635.title: "View" definition should handle time-based and disappearing content
635.body:
I wrote this in response to https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/pull/630/changes I figured I'd create a separate issue for it since this is a probably a larger conversation than what fits in that PR

> :term[content] that is :term[actively available] in a :term[viewport] including that which can be scrolled, zoomed or panned to, and any additional content that is conditionally shown while leaving the rest of the content in the viewport actively available 


I think this definition is reassonble for static interfaces but it breaks down when you start considering time. For starters it isn't clear how video and audio factor into this. You'll probably just want all video and audio to be included, regardless of whether that video is prerecorded or live, whether you can go back and reply the content, or if it's a one-time thing, that probably should be in scope. It needs to be clearer that it is.

Animations are also a problem here. A loading animation is shown only once before the content is displayed, It's not clear whether that should be considered a separate view, since the loader is no longer actively available after the content comes in. More elaborate loaders such as in games might show information while loading too, that either goes away automatically after content is loaded or after a button press. 

Other types of one-time animiations exist too. Animating content in as you scrolled it into view the first time for instance. Just as tricky may be transition animations. What view are those part of? It's also not clear what happens if content automatically transitions, for instance going from one episode in a TV series to another, or an automatic transition in a social media video platform.

This definition has a part about additional content, but it doesn't consider what happens with content that is removed. If content is removed from a view, are we now looking at a new view? This matters for animations and such like before, but for plenty of other things too. Tab panels, carrousels and self-closing accordions are widgets add content, but they simultaniously remove other content to make space for it. are these separate views? Navbars essentially do that too, you click a nav item and the current page content is replaced with new page content. But it feels unintuitive to say that a page with five carrousel slides are five views.

Frames are another example of a way in which content is replaced. Links and forms inside frames result in a change within the frame, but not in the outer page. Is this one page, or multiple views? There are other things that disappear too, think of form errors for instance, content that exists on a timer, live content that goes into an archive after a certian time. Content that disappears after an interaction, such as the billing fields when I checked the "shipping same as billing" box.

I think what's missing from the definition is some acknowledgement that not every removal or inactivation of content results in a new view. This is what the "change of context" version from before attempted to do, although that approach came with its own pain points.

My feeling is that this isn't a solvable problem. We aren't going to find a drop-in replacement for web page that does everything web page does, and solve a bunch of additional problems as well. I think a better way forward (I've suggested this before) is to look at each place where WCAG 2.2 used web page and come up with a separate definition that addresses just what needs to be addressed there. If after doing that we find that there are indeed things that can be combined, great. But with the definition as proposed I feel like we're creating more problems then we solved.

636.title: WCAG 3.0 Working Draft — Comment on Autonomous Agents as Primary and Proxy Users
636.body:
To the Accessibility Guidelines Working Group,

I am submitting this comment as a previously W3C Invited Expert with over twenty years of experience in accessible educational technology, DHS Trusted Tester certification, and founder of Agent 403.

**The Gap I am Addressing**
The March 2026 WCAG 3.0 working draft defines user agents as browsers and assistive technologies. It does not address autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of human users, a category of web user that is already operational and growing rapidly.
This is not a future concern. AI agents are currently being deployed to help elderly users manage medications, assist researchers in retrieving academic literature, and support disabled users in navigating web content. These agents need the same semantic clarity, observable state, and navigable structure that human assistive technology requires.

**The Specific Problem**
Current WCAG 3.0 language creates an unintentional gap: a website can be fully WCAG compliant yet completely inaccessible to an AI agent acting as an accessibility aid. Bot barriers such as CAPTCHAs, JavaScript-only rendering, and absence of structured data are not currently framed as accessibility failures, but they are, when the blocked agent is performing an accessibility function.

**A Proposed Extension**
I have developed the AGAG — Agent Accessibility Guidelines — a dual-legibility framework extending WCAG 3.0 to explicitly include autonomous agents as first-class users. AGAG v1.0 organizes guidance around six pillars that map directly to the POUR principles: Detectable, Observable, Navigable, Economic, Verifiable, and Consent & Control.

**Key contributions beyond existing WCAG guidance:**
First, delegated access paths must be explicit. A system must distinguish between harmful automation and authorized delegated assistance, and must expose a compliant path for trusted assistive agents. The web cannot treat all bots as abuse if some bots are literally performing accessibility support.
Second, authentication must not depend on visual puzzles when no accessible alternative exists for legitimate assistive agents.
Third, a practical implementation pattern — the Two-Domain Pattern — allows any website owner to create an agent-accessible content layer using free static hosting alongside their existing site, requiring no changes to their primary infrastructure.

**My Request**
I respectfully request that the AG Working Group consider:

Expanding the definition of "user agent" to explicitly include autonomous agents acting on behalf of human users
Addressing bot barriers as potential accessibility failures when they block legitimate assistive agents
Including guidance for authoring tools regarding agent-accessible output

The current, work in progress, AGAG v1.0 guidelines are available at:
https://agent.openaix.org/agent-content.md

I welcome discussion and am available to present these findings to the working group.

Respectfully submitted,
Thea Eaton
mailto: hellotheaeaton at gmail dot com

637.title: Guideline 2.5.2 Prevent errors — “data entry interfaces” needs clarity
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
637.body:
The phrase "data entry interfaces" implies that the guidance that follows only applies to things like Excel/Sheets. To make this broader and more inclusive of the e-commerce example included in this guideline, "data entry interfaces" should be reworded or at least defined more clearly. 

Examples where "data entry interfaces" is used in a way that could be misinterpreted: 
"Data entry interfaces allow for users to do at least one of the following before submission"
"Data entry interfaces notify users of submission status at the time of submission."

638.title: Guideline 2.5.2 Prevent errors — validation timing in “Data entry validated”
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
638.body:
Under the data entry validated section, it's unclear as currently worded if the guidance regarding the user entering data applies to form fields only or to all field types (including search fields):
 
Data entered is validated after the user enters data, either:
when the user leaves the field, or
when the form is submitted.

639.title: Guideline 2.5.2 Prevent errors — ambiguity in “Error prevention review” assertion
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
639.body:
Two bullets under "Assertion: Error prevention review" are currently ambiguous.

Existing text: 
This review includes checking to make sure that we:
- use an interface where only valid input can be selected,
- automatically correct input errors when possible and reliable, and

Rewrite for the "use an interface" bullet to provide examples of "valid input": 
 implement an interface that enforces valid data selection, such as a dropdown or date picker, to eliminate manual entry errors

Rewrite for the "automatically correct" bullet to make it clearer that reliability is important: 
- automatically correct input errors when a reliable fix exists

640.title: Image types identified
640.body:
I'm glad to see this included. In discussions with several blind colleagues, I think this is often missing from alt text. As sighted people, we automatically clock the image type as soon as we see it, and this gives us context for the image itself. A photo of an assistance dog, for example, is very different from an illustration of an assistance dog, even if the content is similar. We often have guidance documents containing screenshots, but if some other image type is suddenly inserted in that document, it can leave a blind person a bit confused unless the alt text begins with the new image type. 

I'm looking forward to seeing how this requirement develops.

641.title: Text style readable: underlining of text
641.body:
Currently Text style readable (minimum) allows some use of underlining text but the equivalent enhanced requirement doesn't. As a voice recognition software user, I have lost count of the number of times I have been trying to open a "link" on a page, only to find that it wasn't a link at all... just randomly underlined text. 

I wonder whether underlining comes from the days when we hand wrote everything. At school, we had to underline the title and underline any emphasised words. Digital text brought in bold and italic for this purpose and underlining quickly became associated with links. 

I would prefer the minimum requirement to prevent underlining except for links, as it can be a genuine barrier for people who cannot use a mouse or keyboard.

642.title: Replace absolute units (px) with relative units (rem) as the baseline for font-size in WCAG 3.0 Outcomes.
labels: Path: User control and prevent harm
642.body:
As suggested by @patrickhlauke in w3c/wcag#5051, I am submitting this proposal here.

Hello W3C Silver Task Force,
As a Design Technologist and Graphic Designer with 25+ years of experience implementing W3C standards (since 1999), I have observed the shift from fixed layouts to fluid, user-centric architectures. I would like to submit the following proposal regarding the current WCAG 3.0 drafts.

### Context
In the current drafts of WCAG 3.0, there is a recurring reference to **16px** as a standardized baseline for legibility and contrast (APCA). While 16px is a sound visual target, defining it as an absolute unit (px) in the specification is a **technical regression** that undermines User Agent (UA) accessibility.

### Technical Arguments
* **User Autonomy:** Using \px` overrides the user's browser settings. Many users with low vision configure a larger default root font size (e.g., 24px). A specification based on `rem` respects this hierarchy. * Scaling Inconsistency: In a modern multi-device landscape (Baseline 2026), the CSS pixel is a logical abstraction. Relying on fixed pixels complicates fluid typography. * Consistency with UAAG: Reverting to `px` in the new WCAG 3.0 Outcomes creates an internal inconsistency within W3C’s own philosophy.

### Proposed Solution
Replace references to **16px** with **1rem** (or its equivalent relative value) to ensure that accessibility is not just a visual target, but a technical commitment to user-controlled scaling.
---
Best regards,
**Ignacio Llorente Fdez de la Reguera**
Design Technologist & Graphic Designer
@graphic-designer

comments.body:
Hi Andrew,
Thank you for such a detailed and technical explanation. As a professional who closely follows the evolution of standards, I deeply admire the technological revolution represented by APCA and OKLCH; I consider them fundamental advances for color and contrast precision in the modern web.

While my technical background does not allow me to challenge the complex mathematical basis of the 'canonical pixel' you present, I understand and share the need for a canonical unit as a measurement pattern to ensure an international mathematical foundation. Your analogy of the measuring tape and the wood is very enlightening; however, from the perspective of real-world implementation, we observe that this architecture is currently limited by the use of units that do not allow that technological precision to translate into total resilience for the user.

Regarding your point on the use of optical zoom: the fact that browsers had to implement 'hacks' like the aforementioned zoom is not the ultimate solution, but rather the consequence of standards historically lacking a native adaptive architecture.

In the past, the pixel was our only tool due to a lack of alternatives; but in 2026, maintaining that rigidity means ignoring technical progress and the 'visual health autonomy' that rem guarantees today. This is not just a technical matter, but one of social justice and legal compliance (EU Directive 2019/882, by reference among international rights): technology must evolve to serve the user equitably, rather than forcing them to use patches to fix a design deficiency.

If the standard says 'px', the world uses 'px'.

To facilitate the technical verification of this lack of interoperability, I have created a test case (2026 Interoperability Laboratory) for a better physical understanding of content overflow. I am also attaching the HTML source file to ensure this technical evidence remains available for future community reference:
Link. https://interoperability-test-2026.netlify.app

[2026-interoperability-laboratory.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26645578/2026-interoperability-laboratory.html)

Your contributions to this constructive thread are very interesting. Thank you for your time. I look forward to your thoughts on this and invite further proposals on the established criteria.
Best regards,
Ignacio Llorente Fernández de la Reguera

Hi @Myndex, Thank you very much for the historical perspective on the px unit. It is a fascinating analysis of the original intent of the 1996 specifications. However, from a perspective of applied architecture and current visual health, I believe there is a conceptual nuance that the "visual angle" theory does not fully resolve in the modern web:
### **1. Browser Zoom vs. User Autonomy (Font Scaling)** Equating Browser Zoom with Text Scaling is, in my view, a fundamental error in accessibility. - The **Zoom** is an external assistive tool (a magnifying glass) that scales the entire canvas (text, images, etc.). It is a **reaction** of the software to an existing barrier. - **Font Scaling (User Agent Settings)** is a declaration of **biological need**. It is the **prevention** of that barrier from the native architecture itself. When a specification is defined in px, it creates a barrier that ignores the user’s base configuration. The rem is not an arbitrary unit; it is the bridge that allows the web to respect the user's "**biological key**" of each person without depending on external tools. The 1996 theory was valid for a static hardware ecosystem, but in 2026, structural resilience must be native to adapt to the enormous diversity of current screen densities.
### **2. The "Building Code" Paradox** In your analogy: if the code states that a door must be "**80cm**" wide, but that fixed rule in "cm" refuses to adapt when someone needs to enter with a wheelchair, the rule becomes a limit, not a solution. This is what is known in physical accessibility as a systemic design failure: prioritizing the measurement of the object over the need of the subject. The standard should be a functional framework, not a rigid rule that ignores the diversity of human vision. Defining the success threshold in px conditions the practice of developers, forcing them to choose between complying with the standard or respecting the users visual health autonomy.¹
### **3. Invitation to Field Analysis and Professional Ethics** Regarding my laboratory, I believe there has been a misunderstanding in the way it was tested. It was not designed to test **Zoom (Ctrl +)**, which, as I mentioned, scales everything indiscriminately. I invite you (example: https://interoperability-test-2026.netlify.app) —and everyone in the community— to test it again correctly: do not use the zoom; instead, change the "**Default Font Size**" in your browser settings (e.g., to "Very Large"). From a technical ethics standpoint, I do not consider your previous statement that both systems scale equally to be correct. The laboratory itself details in its text the procedure for its correct understanding: the pixel remains static before the user's preference, while the rem adapts. Ignoring this distinction, when it is explicitly detailed to facilitate verification, is not only a technical error but a barrier to the honesty that should govern an accessibility standard.² Ultimately, we must decide whether we want WCAG 3.0 to be a manual of mathematical elegance based on fixed units, or whether it should evolve to become a manual of digital human rights that guarantees native adaptation to the health needs of all people. I would love to hear your opinion on this and that of other experts (if possible), as well as all members of the community who wish to contribute: How do you visualize this balance between the precision of the standard and the biological autonomy of each user? Your contributions are fundamental to making this standard truly for everyone. Best regards, Ignacio Llorente Fernández de la Reguera --- ¹ **Directive (EU) 2019/882, Annex I** (Accessibility requirements): [europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/ES/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32019L0882#anx_I) Legal requirements for "_personalization of the interface and visual health autonomy._" ² **W3C UAAG 2.0, Success Criterion 1.4.1** (Text Configuration): https://www.w3.org/TR/UAAG20/#sc_141 W3C technical regulations on the "_global configuration of the font size by the user._"

I welcome the inclusion of Issue #642 in the WCAG 3.0 workstream. To ensure this new standard is future-proof and globally harmonized—particularly with the European Accessibility Act (EN 301 549)—it is essential to move away from absolute px and adopt rem as the baseline for font-size and layout scaling.

A rigid pixels-based standard often conflicts with user-defined browser settings, creating barriers for users with low vision who rely on root-level scaling. By integrating rem units directly into the WCAG 3.0 motor, we ensure that the APCA and other outcomes support true user autonomy and fluid reflow by default.

I look forward to collaborating on a technical solution that prioritizes these interoperability requirements, ensuring the standard remains robust and legally compliant across all jurisdictions.

Sincerely,
Ignacio Llorente Fernández de la Reguera

Hi @graphic-designer,

> In the current drafts of WCAG 3.0, there is a recurring reference to 16px as a standardized baseline for legibility and contrast (APCA). 

The px unit is not included due to APCA. It is mostly used with the sizing requirements (e.g. text and layout sizing/resizing). 

Using the CSS pixels (CSSpx or just px) allows us to use a size **relative to the assumed viewing distance of the user.** All the available sizes are relative to _something_.

This is something I've looked into for quite a while (e.g. [in defense of pixels](https://alastairc.uk/2012/11/in-defence-of-pixels/), [how to hold your iPad](https://alastairc.uk/2013/02/how-to-hold-your-ipad/), and [pixels vs Ems commentary](https://alastairc.uk/2018/08/pixels-vs-ems-commentary/).) 

So where you say:
> Using px overrides the user's browser settings. Many users with low vision configure a larger default root font size (e.g., 24px).

This really isn't the case anymore. Finding the text-size settings is much harder than the default zoom settings. When people adjust the zoom settings this applies across all units, and works better with media-queries used to adjust layouts as well as text-sizes. Re-sizing only text gives much less range of sizing for the user, as layouts tend to break over a certain size. (Developers can use EMs/REMs across everything, but then it reacts exactly the same way as using zoom, so as a user why not just use zoom?)

Also, WCAG 3 is intended to apply across platforms more easily, and many platforms do not have an equivalent to REM.  As far as I know, all platforms have some default "pixel" size which relates to the viewing distance of the user. (e.g. iOS has points, Android has scalable pixels).

On another topic, there were some contributions from @myndex above, but he removed them. I don't know why, but that explains why it seems like there are missing bits of conversation above.

Hi @alastc, thank you for the detailed explanation and for the links to your research. I truly appreciate the perspective on why px is being prioritized for cross-platform consistency.

However, my concern remains centered on user autonomy. While most users rely on Zoom, those who do configure a custom root font size (often for specific visual health needs) find that px explicitly overrides their preference, whereas rem/em respects it. If WCAG 3 aims to be outcome-based, the focus should be on whether the rendered Accessibility Tree (AOM) reflects the user’s explicit settings.

Regarding the missing parts of the conversation mentioned, I am providing a permanent link to the full original proposal to ensure the working group has the complete context and data for transparency:

Link to the Full Proposal - Google Drive. https://drive.google.com/file/d/1CQmb6aONeW659bWoSUsb_A4gc5mFHGa6/view?pli=1

I believe this is a vital strategic debate for WCAG 3: Should we prioritize layout stability or user-defined scalability?

@graphic-designer asked

> Should we prioritize layout stability or user-defined scalability?

This is IMHO a really important question, but I think the right answer is "Neither. We should prioritise making sure that people can actually read what gets published".

The following attempted explanation is divided into "the practical bit" and "the philosophy bit". I think both are important.

**The practical bit**

TL;DR:

It's important to provide both
- a baseline that gives some sense of an absolute size for text that is commonly readable, and
- clear guidance that resizing is common, so it really is necessary to deal with it effectively. 

Roughly, the smaller the "absolute text size", the more likely that real people will just hit zoom (or pass on to some alternative provider if there is one). But we need to offer some more nuance.

- We should support and promote the ability to generate a layout that adapts to zooming, both by expanding items within a layout and adapting the layout itself.
- We should support and promote the ability for users to set a basic minimum font-size.
- We should explain that user needs will frequently break anything but fairly simple layouts if those layouts are fixed, and sometimes will even break that, with users who effectively work linearly through text and for whom layouts that do help many people are just another barrier.

People who read text at a size of around 2.5cm (or 1" or 200pt) or more are real users too, and with few exceptions (like testing) they don't interact with the web like that because they are trying to be difficult. 

There are also users with a very narrow range of vision but the ability to read things that are quite small or very small (the meaning of those terms varies widely), and who prefer to limit the *maximum* size. Layouts can readily respond to this need too, and should.

Some longer explanation:

Content publishers generally care about their layout, or overall look. History demonstrates many will go to considerable effort to preserve that, sometimes while looking for a way to claim a level of accessibility conformance that is technically justifiable without providing the actual accessibility, sometimes at the expense of accessibility, and sometimes working hard to achieve both goals.

Often, those who are trying to achieve accessibility look for support from WCAG to explain what they have to do, and what they have to understand, because many people don't get to learn a lot about accessibility and the range of needs people have as they learn to publish content.

If we focus only on supporting user-scaling without caring about layout, we are likely to see more publishers ignore our guidance as unrealistic. If we focus on enabling publishers to achieve their initial goals and claim conformance, we are likely to see poorer accessibility for actual people. Neither of these is a good outcome.

So it is important to explain the high-level goals of our requirements. (This is why we got success criteria in WCAG 2, among other things). I think we need to be clear that there are situations where a user isn't going to get benefit from a publisher's layout, and others where they are. Layouts are meant to help people understand content, and it's a fair assumption that in the "normal" case, that happens.

I see at a lot of text that is about 10pt in its default presentation. That's often pretty difficult for me to read.

So I use zoom most days, varying from none up to maybe 200%, and I expect the layout not to break down. Generally it doesn't - although sometimes it adapts - usually in a way that is helpful.

Sometimes, I need text (typically, although it also applies sometimes to images) magnified by more than 200% and for some people, a default text size around "30px" is well below their starting threshold for "usable".

I generally set a minimum font size, but smaller than I really need, because I currently find that it often breaks layouts in ways that are worse than trying to deal with too-small text. A Web where I could reliably set my minimum font-size to around 20pt and expect stuff to work would be a better Web than the one I know today.

A note on measures:

font-size generally boils down to some "slippery" measure. "em" and "ex" units try to define it based on the size of actual letters but then don't have any underpinning of how big that is "by default" - so it gets supplied by a browser setting, and that can seriously complicate the task of creating a layout. Other units generally depend in part on the font itself. So I find arabic, "cursive" cyrillic, and many characters in asian scripts, and some latin fonts, much harder to read at the same font-size I can read latin text in fonts I typically like. Similarly, I find latin script  in ALL CAPITALS is easer than with normal capitalization at small sizes, although I prefer text at a legible size that uses upper- and lower-case "more normally".

We also have very different-sized screens (or reading surfaces - I still read many things on bits of paper, which brings its own challenges. For the last couple of decades most of those things came through a browser before I printed them).

**The philosophy bit**

On one hand, we need to understand how (and why) content is published today, how users interact with it, and what's the most effective approach to deal with "reality".

On the other hand, we do have a role in providing appropriate guidance on what could and should change. It's important to recognise both the limitations of what that can achieve, and the value of doing it.

"WCAG" (at the beginning in other forms, such as the TRACE guidelines that were a key input document among others) has been around for about 3 decades. In that time it has had an impact on design, and on the technical underpinnings of the specs that enable the Web. I think that has been positive overall. In many cases it has happened despite claims at the time that we were making completely unreasonable requests.

As a community providing accessibility guidance, we (and I personally as an individual member of that community) have also gone down what turned out to be various dead-end paths in our quest to improve the world.

If we don't give guidance on what the overall objectives are - which includes how people with different capabilities actually interact with content, ranging from fairly common approeaches (like "look at it in the default presentation their browser provides") to far less common ("use a screenreader", "zoom everything to 35% or 530%", "convert it to monochrome white-on-black", "step through everything linearly except where links or clear structures enable more efficiently changing where on a page the user is"...), we rely on developers knowing all that. Which is a bad idea, because they don't.

Similarly, if we don't provide practical explanations of what to do, in terms of common approaches to publishing, to support these various needs, we're unlikely to see a broad change in providing better accessibility (except if someone else takes over our role as a fundamental source of that guidance).

To the extent we try to choose and promote particular technical approaches, we run a risk of putting effort into things that get rejected in the long run. I don't think this means we should not make that effort, I think it means we need to be able to accept that we might need to change what we suggest and adopt new approaches easily. I also think it means that we need to be really clear about *why* we choose each particular approach, and explain what is good about it and what problems it can bring.

Hi Charles @chaals — well said. A testable baseline reference and support for user scaling aren't competing goals—both are achievable parts of a proper guideline. The real-world usage descriptions you mention are the kind of grounding this discussion needs. The biggest issue is technology. CSS does not have a stable way to set the actual height of characters on the screen. And the variation between font families can result in a 50%-200% difference for a `font-size` with the same CSS length, regardless of unit. Units like `em` and `rem` just bring more ambiguity into the mix.

**One related note on zoom:** uniform percentage zoom is a blunt tool. A user with ~20/80 acuity may need 12pt/16px body text scaled 400% (48pt/64px), but applying that same 400% to a 48px headline is counterproductive — research by Whittaker & Lovie-Kitchin shows that text above a critical size actually *reduces* reading speed. Proportional scaling based on content hierarchy would better serve low-vision users, but that's a broader discussion.

**A few brief clarifications on `px`:**

The CSS `px` has never been a hardware pixel. Since CSS1 (1996), it's been the canonical unit of the CSS canvas, fully scalable by design. It is the underlying metric all other CSS units reduce to, including `rem`. The `px` is defined as a unit of visual angle. 

All of vision and readability science uses visual angle to specify how big something projects onto the eye's retina. This makes the CSS `px` the ideal unit of measure for guidelines and standards. An `em` or `rem` has no fixed relationship to visual angle, introducing unneeded ambiguity and no reference to the real needs of users.

None of this discourages using `rem`, `em`, or any other CSS unit in practice — that's perfectly fine, but guidelines relating to vision need to be traceable to the science, and that means visual angle. The `px` provides that by design, and no math is required.


Thank you for reading,

*Inclusive Vision Systems, Inc.*

@GreggVan I think your analysis misses a fundamental point.`rem` is relative to "the default text size" - which is dependent on several factors including browser defaults and user modification of those. 30 years after CSS appeared, it's no longer complicated to work out roughly have that translates to "available screen" and make flexible auto-adjusting layouts accordingly.

It's perfectly feasible to provide an accessibility statement based on `rem`. It is reasonable to assume that for people who can't change the browser default (locked-down browser, don't know how, takes too long, whatever makes it impractical) is 16px. It makes sense to assume there are people who have changed that up or down (projecting or using a big screen in a meeting, can't read small text, can only read small text due to specific vision characteristics, could read anything but I work on a very small screen, whatever...).
  
It is not possible to know what scaling people are going to use. It seems sensible to assume the general range of browser options suggests a baseline you should expect to encounter, but the bottom of that range is zero, which is clearly not a useful size. The top of that range in most browsers I use is only about 24px - 150% of the default, a value that I would argue is manifestly insufficient because I keep meeting people who use bigger text, and I do so myself. Firefox has a range up to 72px. Safari allows me to add a stylesheet so I can set the values for myself (as many of us envisaged more people doing back when we worked on WCAG 1 - one example of how we misunderstood the future).

As a wild guess I think we *should* be aiming for a Web where layouts work reasonably with font sizes between about 1.5mm (1 sixteenth of an inch) and about 25mm (1 inch). While these values are unusual, I think they are "within normal tolerances" - and more crucially, I don't believe there are a lot of cases where this imposes a lot of technical complexity.

That would translate in practice to expecting content to work with font sizes as small as 4px, and as large as 72px.

TL;DR: A quick browse around the web suggests that the experience with a large font is awful, but the problems can easily be remedied, and promoting `rem` as a measure instead of `px` would really help.

The longer read:

As an initial research exercise, I set font-size to 64px (in Safari using a stylesheet) and browsed around a bit (~100 pages total across a couple of dozen sites), to see if any common patterns emerged.

News sites were generally unusable, the least awful was probably abc.net.au (Australian public broadcaster - I could read some content).

"Governments" - both whitehouse.gov and un.org worked reasonably well. Various spanish government agencies less so.

Search engines were terrible. Yandex and Baidu were relatively good until they presented an unreadable mash of results, bing/duckduckgo/google didn't even manage to make entering a term look reasonable.

Media sites (video/audio...) were pretty bad. Vimeo was the one that most painlessly let me get to content, but the player was broken, whereas YouTube's player more or less worked but I had a hard time with the rest of the content.

Some standards stuff: W3C homepage was awful, but other content was generally reasonable. Also, BSSC (a place I do work for) turned out to be good - a happy surprise for me.

Shopping sites were terrible with the exception of idealista (a real estate portal in Spain that was more or less usable) - in some supermarkets I could find things (I didn't actually try to buy anything) while larger platforms were worse.

Pretty much every serious problem I encountered was due to layouts set in pixels. Most commonly, line-heights were based on pixel-width of the screen, and were much less than 64px.

Things could be better with slightly more fluid layouts (e.g. https://theguardian.com doesn't use breakpoints to reflow more comfortably even though that's "old hat" in terms of design). The second-most common problem was squeezing large text into too-small boxes, again caused by assumptions that screen size in px correlates far more closely to font-size in px than it did in my testing.

I think it would be useful to do this a bit more systematically. 

I looked at half a dozen pages in each of chinese and russian, nothing in japanese or arabic (I can at recognise stuff in those scripts).
