I am not confident that I can say whether or not many other scripts (a plethora used in India, as well as others like Thai, Coptic, and so on) are legible or have been messed up by layout - but there are many many people in the world who do have the skill to do so at least at a gross level.

It would be good to have a more thorough look at what the problems are, how common they are, and why they arise, including:

- More scripts (or at least script families)
- Variety in screen sizes
- Variety in font-sizes
- broader range of content

My hypothesis is that instead of using screen-width in px as a determinant of layout shape, with line-heights sepcified in px, triggering based on screen size (or widdth, as a reasonable approximation) in terms of actual characters and expressing any measure that's more than half what you expect font-size to be in terms of `rem` would actually resolve a massive proportion of the issues that I found and which I believe are repeated across the Web in general.

I am sure that some more effort in research will provide a more nuanced explanation (I note the same about my **guess** at a range of font-sizes that we can reasonably expect to be workable). 

What I have not found is issues that would be really hard to remediate

> ...I am still waiting for a formal response to the specific questions I raised previously, regarding the "interoperability laboratory" and the "civil responsibility" for the failure of the official validators.

@graphic-designer & all

**From Chair**
Thank you for starting and continuing to engage in this important conversation about absolute and relative units. The conversation occurring here is public and between various individuals interested in the topic. A formal response about the absolute units and relative units may not occur for months as the topic will need detailed consideration.    The informal discussions on GitHub provide input and insight into the group discussions. 

Chairs will consider your question about the interoperability laboratory and will circle back when we have been able to do so (likely next week).

We appreciate everyone's contributions. I ask that everyone continue to focus on the technical conversation about the topic and maintain polite professionalism while doing so. 

Thank you.

Thank you, @rachaelbradley , for the consideration. Please excuse my tone if it has been misinterpreted; my only intention is to cite the technical reality that users face. I appreciate that the "2026 Interoperability Laboratory" will be formally reviewed by the Chairs next week. This technical dialogue is essential for the integrity of WCAG 3.

The field research by Chaals confirms with real-world data what my laboratory already demonstrates: the use of "px" is the root cause of layout collapse.

---

### **Technical clarification to reinforce the REM model**:

As an additional technical detail to verify the "**resilience of the rem-based model**": the laboratory's source code demonstrates that technologies like "**OKLCH (native perceptual contrast)**" only fulfill their purpose within a "**flexible architecture**".

This is not a diversion from the topic, but "**physical proof**": visual precision flows naturally when "**user autonomy**" is respected through "**rem**". Without this resilient environment, any color algorithm, however perfect on paper, becomes a "**rigid barrier**" on the screen. We are dealing with a matter of "**rendering physics**".

I'm not sure that anyone has said that anyone should FIX any font at any CSSpx size (or any size).

 X CSSpx  has only been cited in standards as a **minimum**  level that products should use.    

are we confusing **minimum** with  **only**?

> I'm not sure that anyone has said that anyone should FIX any font at any CSSpx size (or any size).

Is it not common practice to specify a particular size for fonts? 

> X CSSpx has only been cited in standards as a **minimum** level that products should use.

Where is a minimum level cited?

> are we confusing **minimum** with **only**?

I don't think that is the confusion that is causing problems. First, I don't think it is "we" who are confusing things, but I think the guidance we provide on font sizes is insufficient, leading to many people who try to follow our guidance not achieving what I hope they would typically achieve.

Given WCAG 2 doesn't provide a minimum, can you not set defaults to be 4px text, and argue that if the content works at 8px you're conforming?

But I think the world outside is reading "must be able to double the size", and maybe combining that with "18pt is large", and close by that this corresponds to about 1.5em.  From that starting point, 12px seems like a reasonable size according to WCAG  2. 

Browsers typically default to 16px today - presumably because they don't think people are comfortable reading at 12px.

If you were building a browser and knew that people expected to zoom up to 200%, if your baseline for reasonable is 12px you might provide for minimum text size up to 24px and claim you are done, as 2 of the three main browser engine teams seem to do. (If you are building a browser, you would almost certainly notice that if you go much past that, you run into "compatibility with reality" issues on very many websites. Which is a huge pain point for people who do make browsers).

If you look at the WCAG3 draft and try to find a minimum reasonable text size it says "~10pt at typical desktop viewing distances". So it would be reasonable for a browser to assume that if it provides the ability to get to 24pt it's going above and beyond the necessary 10pt x 200% ≈ 20pt

So if web content works at font-size: 24px, what's the problem? If you assume that browser defaults are more authoritative than WCAG (and on accessibility, I would suggest that while that might be true in specific cases, it's a dangerous assumption to build on...) you might come up with "no, you need to handle up to font-size: 32px".

And somewhere around 24px font sizes is indeed where the web seems to fall into a mess.

I think the industry can do better, and I think we can provide clearer guidance on how to do that. At this stage, it seems there is not a giant leap that needs to be made.

> >     I'm not sure that anyone has said that anyone should FIX any font at any CSSpx size (or any size).
> 
> Is it not common practice to specify a particular size for fonts?

I thought we were taking about WCAG and rules that would be made into regulations.  I  didnt know we were talking about common practice. 
If we arent talking about WCAG language then - I  suggest we not do it on the WCAG discussion and not on an Issue called WCAG 3.0 Outcomes
 
> 
> >     X CSSpx has only been cited in standards as a minimum level that products should use.
> 
> Where is a minimum level cited?
> 
EN 301 549  which is what the world uses for anything non-web (and it uses WCAG for web).      and it is WCAGs desire to go beyond Web that gets us into font sizes 

> >     are we confusing minimum with only?
> 
> I don't think that is the confusion that is causing problems. First, I don't think it is "we" who are confusing things, but I think the guidance we provide on font sizes is insufficient, leading to many people who try to follow our guidance not achieving what I hope they would typically achieve.

WCAG Outcomes are not guidance.  They are shalls.    Recommendation may be guideance -- but outcome measures are not.

@chaals 

There is a world of difference between what we do everyday voluntarily - or as we wish-- and out laws and regulations.

Ditto for volunteer standards (you can do it this way if you wish but you don't have to) and standards that will be picked up and used in regulation

WCAG2 is used in regulation
We want WCAG3 to replace it
So we have to write WCAG3 in a way that regulators can use it and industry can live with it being required.  (or else they will just keep using WCAG2)

So of course we look at practice for good ideas.  But when writing a standard that will be used for regulation - we **do not want** to put "everything we use in common practice in one place or another but do not want to be required to do that everywhere" into the standard.   Especially since common practice is not "always practiced" and often is - do it sort of this way -- but no particular measure and lots of variation to fit each different situation and preference. 

At least I don't want to have ill defined and sometimes used - sometimes not practices made mandatory.

A few responses to comments above having gotten back from vacation.

@graphic-designer wrote:
> Browsers are simply following the CSS specifications that prioritize absolute units (px) over global user settings. 

This isn't really true, CSSpx are relative as well, just relative to assumed viewing distance. 

Something I can't tell from your comments is whether you understand that text-size adjustments and zoom-adjustments are both available in the browser, and the zoom adjustments are the default and easier ones to find/use? In fact, the text-size adjustments are intentionally hidden or harder to find in some browsers.

Are you saying that people want to use a default text size rather than a default zoom level?

Later you talk about a "resilient web", but text-sizing (to larger scales) is not a resilient approach. Typically, when text is sized in EMs/REMs and the layout uses a non-font size (e.g. px, %, viewport units etc) the text will then break out of the layout. This isn't good for anyone.

Now, you can size the layout in REMs as well, in which case **it behaves exactly like zooming**... what have you achieved?

Using media queries developers can manage how the layout works when zooming. That is harder to do with text-sizing unless you replicate how zooming works.

The key thing to understand is that zoom increases the effective CSS pixel size, so everything expands. Text-only increases make some parts of the page bigger without affecting others, which is harder to manage.

> I must insist: accessibility is a physical reality of rendering and visual health, not a mathematical abstraction

Sure, but what you haven't outlined is why people would use a hidden setting over the primarily available one. Both make the text bigger, what is the use-case for text-only sizing? (Particularly above 200%)

I don't understand why one method of re-sizing "transfers autonomy to the person's visual health" but not the other?

> While browsers set 1rem to 16px by default, the "px" is a static unit that ignores the User Agent's configuration, whereas "rem" is a dynamic unit that empowers the user.

As @chaals demonstrated, whether the browser increases the text size when specified in PX is up to the browser, not the author. Some do, some don't.

### What's actually in [WCAG 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/) now

It is worth noting that there is **no mention of 16px in WCAG 3**.

* Text sizing asks that users can increase the size to 200% of the platform's default body size.
* Text reflow asks that: "Blocks of text are legible at 320 CSS pixels in the orientation of text, without the need to scroll in the orientation of text.

Those are the only two requirements (so far) which reference CSS pixels.

In neither case would it make sense to define those in REMs.

Thank you for your comments, @alastc . To maintain the focus on "**rendering physics**" and "**interoperability**" as requested by Rachael, I would like to clarify three technical points:

**Persistence vs. Manual Adjustment**: Zoom is an assistive tool that often requires the user to intervene page-by-page or domain-by-domain, and settings can be lost when clearing "cookies" or history. In contrast, "**REM**" respects the global and persistent configuration of the User Agent. The user sets it once for their "**visual health**" and the web adapts natively and automatically. This ensures long-term autonomy.

**Layout Resilience**: You mentioned that text-only scaling breaks the design. The laboratory demonstrates that this occurs when the architecture is rigid (px-based). A "**REM-based architecture**" allows the design to 'breathe' and adapt to the content, preventing the collapse that both @chaals (in Safari/Firefox) and I (in Chrome) have verified.

**Technical Verification**: I invite you to test the "_2026 Interoperability Laboratory_" if you wish to verify how a rigid architecture can inadvertently block user settings, while a resilient one empowers them.

I look forward to the formal review of the laboratory by the Chairs next week.
Sincerily.

Hi @graphic-designer, You said: > Zoom is an assistive tool that often requires the user to intervene page-by-page or domain-by-domain This is not correct, zoom is the **default** user settings in most browsers and works across pages, sites and domains. For example in Chromian browsers (the most used): Also Firefox / MacOS: Also in Safari / MacOS (although slightly harder to find): Also in Safari on iOS: It is not lost with cookies or history. Note the warning from Firefox's settings, have you considered that the people who make the browsers have already thought though this issue and came to the conclusion that zoom was the better option? @chaals, if you still have those sites handy, try a re-run with default zoom set to a similar level instead of text-sizing, I'd predict roughly 90% better results. (My assumption is that roughly 10% of sites work using device detection rather than media queries past a certain size.) > The laboratory demonstrates that this occurs when the architecture is rigid (px-based). A "REM-based architecture" allows the design to 'breathe' and adapt to the content, preventing the collapse that both @chaals (in Safari/Firefox) and I (in Chrome) have verified. I agree that setting large default font sizes does not work on the web at large. However, your proposed solution means getting almost all sites to change how they do layout. That level of education is not possible, I know, I tried in the 2000s (pre-media-queries) when we were trying to meet 200% re-sizing. Particularly when there is a better solution that is _more_ available to users, and works across layout types. I've looked at the [test-page](https://graphic-designer.github.io/2026-interoperability-laboratory/), and it behaves as expected. The only question left is the one I posed above: > Both [text sizing and zoom] make the text bigger, what is the use-case for text-only sizing? (Particularly above 200%)

Draft response to this issue for the AG group to consider:

<hr>

On the primary topic of the issue, WCAG 3 does not use PX or REMs values for text-sizing, so this issue will be closed without change to the provisions.

On the related topic of which units WCAG 3 should use, the main requirements need to use units that can be translated across platforms. CSS px are such a unit when it needs to define how large something appears to a user, as the definition is based on an angle with an assumed viewing distance.

Requirements should also be framed in a way that that can be met with multiple methods. For example, users should be able to re-size text. The mechanisms authors use to achieve that need to be accessibility supported (i.e. available to users in general), but the requirements in WCAG 3 should not restrict authors to a particular mechanism (e.g. text-sizing vs zoom).

> The only question left is the one I posed above:
>
> > Both [text sizing and zoom] make the text bigger, what is the use-case for text-only sizing? (Particularly above 200%)

The use case I have is to avoid images and larger text like headings making the layout unworkable (that's the problem that I still see. At rem=16px a 24px h1 might make sense. At rem=64px a 96px h1 is generally too big. That's harder to deal with than not zooming an image that takes 50% of a narrowed space, but I would claim we do now have the technology and a "workforce" who know how to apply it to solve both problems)

There's another question left (which is really a different issue): Should WCAG describe a reasonable "default size" for fonts (along with the requirement that you can zoom to some level or other)?

By the way, I disagree with your claim that we can't manage a "re-education" and change to the way the Web is built - I believe we do achieve that, but on timescales that are large enough that they are hard to recognise - decades, not years. The conclusion I draw is that we should consider what we ask for and advise in light of those timescales as well as the more immediate ones we generally have in mind.
Yes, zoom works better in most sites than increased text-size. FWIW I don't think the problems that are there are largely due to device-dependence, although once again my survey is anecdotal.

Regarding the draft response:
I formally request that no administrative decision be made until the formal physical review of the laboratory promised by the Chairs for next week takes place (@rachaelbradley). 
Technical consensus cannot be reached by ignoring the browser-rendered evidence shown in the 2026 Interoperability Laboratory. 
We trust the group will prioritize physical browser evidence over administrative drafts.

@chaals - I agree about the large headings getting too big, that's why the text-resize is asking for 200% of default body size, rather than starting size. That's pretty straightforward with media-queries but currently not allowed by WCAG2 text-sizing.

The re-education aspect is a tangent, but we'd need a compelling case for that level of change. With zooming being easier to manage overall, I don't see it.

> Should WCAG describe a reasonable "default size" for fonts (along with the requirement that you can zoom to some level or other)?

If you have a look at the editor's draft, we've got "[Text style readable (minimum)](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#text-style-readable-minimum)", which takes a viewing-angle approach. It is intended to be very base-level readability, but then work with the resizing requirement.

@graphic-designer - I am one of the chairs, I did review the test-case page, and as I said: It works as expected.

The next step of the process is to put the draft response to the whole AG group and see if that gets consensus. No promises on timing for that, just that it should be before the publication of the relevant provision.

Given that the original premise ("don't use 16px") is not the case in the WCAG 3 draft anyway, I suspect the draft response will be approved.

I must point out an inconsistency: @alastc the **WCAG 3.0 Editor's Draft** explicitly uses a **16px** (**1rem**) reference as the baseline for the new readability and contrast calculations (APCA).

Furthermore, international engineering bodies like **IEEE** define 16px as the necessary minimum for body text to alleviate readability issues.Ignoring these technical benchmarks—which are already present in the draft's methodology—undermines the scientific rigor of the process.

---

IEEE Standards. https://brand-experience.ieee.org/are-your-websites-and-communications-accessible
The [editor's draft](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/) does not include 16px, or references to APCA.

@alastc I presume I should raise a new issue.

That said, to get a sense of what we take away from this discussion, other than "WCAG doesn't say `px`":

I think It makes sense to propose that content should enable text-size adjustment (as mentioned above) that covers a significantly wider range than 100%-200% of the default.

With modern capabilities that is well within reach to implement. I recognise that it will likely be a decade before that's the new standard reality, but if we don't ask, we aren't helping to get that change started. 

I think it also makes sense to talk about a reasonable default text size, rather than relying solely on the good sense of browser teams - they have established a de facto standard of "16px", and I think that is OK as a baseline in a world where people can zoom. The reason is to get away from "you can have a tiny default, get to what is a reasonable one, and you're done" - 200% of an unstated baseline is far less than I think we should be recommending.

There's a fair bit of work between these ideas and concrete text in a WCAG3 spec, of course. And more work to make it reality.

Does this seem like a path forward that's worth pursuing? Obviously there are no guarantees of success, but if failure is guaranteed I would prefer not to waste the effort...

@graphic-designer I did not find a mention of 16px anywhere in the WCAG 3 draft (although it is clearly possible I simply missed it in reading). Could you please check whether it is indeed there? 

(As noted above, I am personally of the opinion that some suggestion of a reasonable commonly legible baseline text size *should* be there...)

@graphic-designer I believe that what @alastc said about your test case is that applying browser zoom to it at 200% provides  the same outcome for both boxes. I can confirm, after testing in the same set of browsers, that this is true for values well beyond 200%.

@chaals wrote:
> I presume I should raise a new issue.

I'm not sure on which bit? For context, we have provisions that cover:
- [Minimum text-size](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#text-style-readable-minimum) (currently set at a fairly small equivalent of 10pt).
- [Enhanced text-size](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#text-style-readable-enhanced) (currently set at 12pt, I think 14px?) at a higher level.
- [Text-resizing](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#text-size-adjustable) to 200% of the platform default body size (which would be 16px on web).
- [Text-reflow](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#text-reflow-supported) to work at 320px wide for blocks of text.

So we have a baseline, and I think the sizing approach is more robust/useful than WCAG2's one.

If you think there's something missing, or the values should change (more likely?), that's a good basis for an issue.

@graphic-designer 
- Linking to an organization's brand guidelines is hardly scientific. That is not a standard from IEEE.
- I didn't say I contradicted your results, I said your results were entirely expected. 

There are two mechanisms available to users for making text bigger in a browser, one of them:
- Is more easily available to users. 
- Works better across more sites.

And that mechanism is not text-sizing. It is more complicated on other platforms, but those platforms generally don't have REM at all.

This is the outcome from the "chairs' review", the next step is for the full group to review the response (and your comments) and see if the response gets consensus.

643.title: single pointer and simple pointer are too confusable
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
643.body:
In the [Inputs Subgroup](https://docs.google.com/document/d/18RDQH1piGOCjae1RTymHaP-M_2RXHoXF0WDHqYvw14w/) we keep tripping over the differences between:
> [simple pointer input](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-simple-pointer-input):  input event that involves only a single ‘click’ event or a ‘button down’ and ‘button up’ pair of events with no movement between
> [single pointer input](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-single-pointer-input):  input modality that only targets a single point on the [page](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-page)/[view](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-view) at a time

Some difficulties:
- single _seems_ simpler than simple — so that is counterintuitive
- the notes do provide clarity, but it’s almost the case of defining terms through examples
- one is about input _event_ and the other input _modality_
  * this seems like a difference without a distinction 

Open question:
- Can single-right-click ever be considered as simple or single?

Possible remediation:
- at the minimum, each term should reference the other
- only use one term or the other
- define one term using the other term

The Inputs Subgroup expects to tackle this, and to propose a fix to the wider group, but only after more work on ACT Rules.

[I updated this problem statement after subgroup call 4/21, when we _again_ took >5min to refresh ourselves on the two terms.]

644.title: Prohibiting any action that would disable or alter the native behaviour of right-clicking
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
644.body:
First, my apologies if this is a little out of place or the formatting isn't great. I never really got into git and find it a little confusing.

As a very dyslexic person, when I am separated from text-to-speech and spellchecking it causes significant barriers for me. Nearly all of the assistive tech I used to help minimize barriers involve use of the mouse right-click. When websites disable or repurpose right-clicking it causes me significant trouble.

As an accessibility specialist, the great majority of the time UX that involves repurposing or disabling right-click is going to cause other accessibility issues. When I audit, not being able to use right-click to inspect an element makes things just a little harder than they have to be.

In my opinion, the WCAG should prohibit disabling or repurposing the right-click function.

645.title: [Errors indicated in multiple ways] Add Text treatment (font, style, etc.) also as one of the visual indicators
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
P - Errors indicated in multiple ways
645.body:
Test treatment like using bold etc. should also be used as a visual indicators to make error stand out along with the existing ones.

It will make the requirement like-

**Errors indicated in multiple ways**

Error messages are visually indicated using at least two of the following:

- A symbol that is consistent throughout the [product](https://deploy-preview-414--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#dfn-product)

- Color that differentiates the error message from surrounding[ content](https://deploy-preview-414--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#dfn-content).

- Text treatment (font, style, etc.) that differentiates the error message from surrounding[ content](https://deploy-preview-414--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#dfn-content).

- Text that clearly indicates the error.

646.title: Errors co-located: use “submission status” instead?
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
646.body:
In our subgroup, following disucssion on 'Submission status notified' we wondered if we want to update 'Error messages' to be 'Submission status' or vice versa as they are phrases that refer to the same thing.

And potentially do this across the requirements that concern error messages.

649.title: Proposal: Evolution of Conformance Testing for Modern CSS Interoperability
649.body:
# Issue Proposal: Evolution of Conformance Testing for Modern CSS Interoperability
### Transition from Static Analysis to Computed Accessibility Tree (AOM) Validation.

### 1. Summary
Good morning to the W3C Silver Team:

I observe a critical gap between static validation tools and the real-world rendering capabilities of 2026. A prime example is the use of **Container Style Queries** (`@container style(...)`). Although this API drastically improves the user experience, it currently results in "false negatives" in official validators. **I propose** that WCAG 3 prioritizes the rendered outcome and the **Accessibility Tree (AOM)** over the static syntax of the source code.

### 2. User Needs
* **Real Adaptability:** Users (all genders) with low vision or cognitive disabilities depend on interfaces that react not only to the Viewport but to specific style conditions of the container to maintain legibility and visual comfort.
* **Dynamic Interoperability:** Users (all genders) of assistive technologies need the browser to process modern standards that guarantee elastic behavior without information loss—a task that style queries facilitate natively.

### 3. The Problem
I believe that current auditing tools penalize innovation, creating a **forced technical regression**. By flagging properties like `@container style` as "errors," developers are pushed to avoid more accessible solutions just to obtain a "green pass" from obsolete validators.

This directly contravenes the spirit of the **EN 301 549** standard:
1. **Technological Neutrality:** The standard requires accessible results and protects the evolution of the "State of the Art." Penalizing modern Baseline 2026 standards hinders this evolution.
2. **Observable Results:** Accessibility should be defined by the perception and operability experienced by users (all genders), not by the reading capacity of an outdated syntactic validator.
3. **Robustness:** Forcing the use of legacy techniques reduces the resilience of products in current user agents.

### 4. My Proposed Change
**I suggest** that WCAG 3 Conformance Methods include:
* **Outcome-Based Validation:** If a property like *Container Style Queries* produces a verified accessible result in the Accessibility Tree, it must be considered compliant.
* **Runtime Focus:** Conformance should be measured in the final state perceived by users (all genders).
* **Heuristic Updates:** Reference validation engines must evolve so they do not become a barrier to real-world accessibility.

### 5. Ethical Dilemma
Currently, I face a decision that I find inconsistent:
* If one wishes to display the **standard's logos**, the code is forced to be regressive.
* If one chooses the **ethical path** and uses `container styles` for a real 60fps improvement, the system punishes the project with a "false negative."

From my point of view, it makes no sense for certification to penalize the actual application of modern accessibility.

### 6. Impact
* **For Development:** Eliminates the fear of using clean, modern, and efficient code.
* **For Users (all genders):** Guarantees much more resilient, elastic, and personalized interfaces according to their real viewing preferences.

Best regards,
Ignacio Llorente Fernández de la Reguera
@graphic-designer

653.title: Please adjust 3.1.1 - the definitions of core and supplemental, so WCAG 3 is more equitable.
653.body:
#Please adjust 3.1.1 - the definitions of core and supplemental, so WCAG 3 is more equitable.
## Issue description:
We are concerned that core requirements, as they are currently defined, are inequitable between disability groups. This is both theoretical and in practice. It’s biased theoretically as both the definitions of core and supplemental seem to be biased towards traditional AT users, such as screen readers. And it is biased in practice as we have seen many requirements that are essential to cognitive users, but because  we do not always use traditional AT,  these requirements are downgraded to supplemental. 

WCAG 3 is trying to equitably meet the needs of more user groups, such as cognitive disabilities and low vision, but these definitions work against that goal. 

##Core requirements:
 We propose that core requirements are items that are essential to the user. We define requirements as essential to the user if users can not independently  use the content without this requirement because of their disability.  

If this is included in the fourth bullet about “necessary support,” then please specify that this is part of necessary support. For example:

necessary support is available such as captions, text alternatives, and expanded forms of abbreviations and any requirement that are essential to the user. IE they can't independently  use the content without this requirement because of their disability. 
If making core requirements focus on essential to the user, means that there are too many requirements as core, then we suggest that other bullets in the definition are removed. In any case, really essential support for any group and all groups is included in this one line of essential to the user.  

##Supplemental requirements:
 Items that are important to the user experience, but are not essential due to a disability can be supplemental. This could be a bad user experience but you can still use the content independently.  

The way WCAG 3’s definition of supplemental requirement is currently worded seems very subjective. For example, requirements that are currently more difficult or expensive to implement — more expensive than what? Such as adding audio descriptions to an hour lecture? Audio descriptions are currently a core requirement and are expensive and time-consuming.


The current definition of supplemental could be used to deprioritize some user groups. This would  include downgrading requirements that are essential to these user groups independently  using content. 



##More information 
 For reference, WCAG 3 currently defines three types of provisions in [Section 3.1.1](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#types-of-provision) as follows (so you do not have to find it):

Core Requirements — Requirements that must be met in order to conform. These include requirements that ensure:
content is detectable by user agents and AT,
content is conveyed to multiple senses and can be used by multiple inputs,
content does not cause immediate, physical harm, and
necessary support is available such as captions, text alternatives, and expanded forms of abbreviations.

Supplemental Requirements — Requirements that build on the core set. These include:
quality checks,
stricter or higher levels than those in a comparable core requirement,
requirements that are currently more difficult or expensive to implement, and
requirements that may apply in certain situations.

Assertions — Documented statements you can make about specific accessibility practices your organization follows to improve the accessibility of your content or product.

With thanks

The COGA task force

654.title: Assertions should be core or supplemental
654.body:
#Assertions should be core or supplemental
 ##Issue description:
A lot of assertions are very important. They are processes, but still essential to the user. The way the terms are laid out make them look less important rather than non-process requirements.

We propose that Assertions can be core or supplemental depending on whether they are essential to the user.  If users can not independently use the content without this Assertion because of their disability, then the assertion should be core. 

Supplemental assertions can be accessibility practices that improve the usability for people with disabilities. 

For example, provisions can be labeled as a Core assertion or as a Supplemental Assertion. 

We are glad that AG is thinking of including some assertions at the core level, and we would be happy to discuss this change with you. (See [AG proposal to include some assertions at the core level](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1qWuFM3fFgC_e1Jik05Os11O0Rl86HLDXu9dolwyWWtc/edit?slide=id.g3de2705a4de_0_51#slide=id.g3de2705a4de_0_51).) As a reminder to the working group, the main reason why WCAG 3 decided to include assertions is to help meet user needs that are hard or impossible to cover in testable requirements. If none of the assertions are part of the core level, then many organizations are likely to treat them as optional, a nice-to-have, along the lines of WCAG AAA.

With thanks!

The coga task force

655.title: Assertions are too long and hard to follow. Please replace the  text of how to write an assertion, with a link.
655.body:
#Assertions are too long and hard to follow. Please replace the  text of how to write an assertion, with a link.


## Issue description:
Assertions look very difficult because of all the template information. The template is very wordy and repetitive and makes it hard to find or focus on the few details that are unique to a specific assertion. That The templated information can be in a different section (maybe in conformance) and linked to.

**For example**  the following could replace the text below:


Create an assertion as **_defined in the conformance section_** to show the following:

1.Our organization has:

- a style guide that includes guidance on focus indicators, and 
- a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.


**This would replace the following text (taken from https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#focus-indicator-style-guide) :** 

For each form in the conformance claim, we have reviewed the form designs to reduce the possibility of users making mistakes.
This review includes checking to make sure that we:

1.Our organization has a style guide that includes guidance on focus indicators and a policy and/or processes that the style guide must be followed.

Information that needs to be included publicly:

Title, role or organization making the assertion
Date of assertion (if different from the date of the conformance claim)
Recommended internal documentation (Informative):

Documentation of which forms were reviewed
Documentation of any changes made as a result of the review
Date of usability testing, if applicable


By the way, we also broke out the actionable text into bullet points. We feel that that is also easier to read. 


Thanks!
The coga task force

657.title: Unify the two definitions of "assertion"
657.body:
https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-assertion has:
> assertion: formal claim of fact, attributed to a person or organization, regarding procedures practiced in the development and maintenance of the content or conformance scope to improve accessibility

https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#types-of-provision has:

> Assertions — Documented statements you can make about specific accessibility practices your organization follows to improve the accessibility of your content or product.

These should be the same, probably by having one refer to the other.

658.title: Reference to ISO 639
658.body:
https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#human-language-detectable

> The human language of all content within the view is programmatically determinable, except when a language tag is not available in ISO 639 language codes.

The i18n WG generally recommends referring to BCP 47 and the IANA Language Subtag Registry rather than the ISO list: https://www.w3.org/TR/international-specs/#use_lstr

659.title: Note in Guideline 2.2.3 Clear language
659.body:
A few suggestions regarding the note in https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#clear-language (personal thoughts, not official comments from the i18n WG):

Mandarin is a spoken Sinitic language or variety. For written guidance, layout, and internationalization, the relevant written language is usually Chinese, sometimes with a specified script (or locale) such as Simplified Chinese and Traditional Chinese.

Some other examples are also about scripts or writing systems rather than languages.

For example, vertical layout is associated with writing systems and typographic traditions, not “Mandarin” specifically.

(Also, French and Spanish share the Latin script with English, but they differ from English in morphology, grammar, punctuation conventions, formality, gender, diacritics, collation, line breaking behavior, etc.)

“Right-to-left text layout” should probably say “bidirectional text”.

I think the methodology of starting with UN official languages is not an especially good baseline for accessibility or internationalization, since the UN languages are politically significant, not selected to represent linguistic or script diversity, and omit many major scripts and language families.

editorial: "the Internationalization (i18n) task force" -> "the Internationalization (i18n) Working Group"

664.title: Request for desktop mode
labels: Path: User control and prevent harm
664.body:
Received via email: 

<hr>

I am writing to submit a formal objection to the implementation of Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow) as defined in WCAG 2.2. While the intent is to provide accessibility, the current 400% zoom requirement is creating significant barriers for the elderly and those who rely on desktop computing for essential legal and civil functions.

My specific objections are as follows:

1. Cognitive Load and Disorientation: Forcing a 320px "mobile-style" layout on a desktop display at 400% zoom significantly increases cognitive load for older users. This group often finds the single-column reflow disorienting, as it hides familiar navigation and breaks established mental models of how a desktop interface should function.
2. Barrier to Civil Rights: As government and private sector services move to "digital by default," this specific standard often breaks complex interfaces (such as legal document portals). This effectively prevents citizens from accessing their documents and exercising their rights because the "accessible" view is practically unusable.
3. Monopolization of Design: The current standard appears to prioritize "mobile-first" corporate ecosystems (specifically those controlled by major tech members of the W3C) over the practical, diverse needs of desktop users. This feels less like a "reasonable adjustment" and more like a forced standardization that excludes those who do not wish to use mobile-style interfaces.

I request that the Working Group reviews the "Reflow" requirement for future versions (WCAG 3.0) to allow for a Desktop-Preservation Mode or a reduced requirement (e.g., 200%) that does not trigger a full layout change. We need standards that accommodate disabilities without breaking the web for the aging population.

I look forward to your technical response regarding how these exclusionary effects on the elderly will be addressed in future drafts.

669.title: (Error notifications available) For input errors, "name of the field in error" must be part of the problem description
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
669.body:
Make sure that the following need is covered in the requirement/requirement description.

When there is an input error, **the error message must include the name of the field** where the error occurred.
If error message is too generic and do not specify the field, it can make it harder for people with cognitive disabilities to understand and fix the issue.

Error messages like:

- “This field cannot be empty”
- "Enter value greater than 18"

do not clearly indicate which field has the error.

**Error messages should clearly mention the field name**, for example:

- "Last name cannot be empty"
- "Age can not be less than 18"

672.title: The definition of "minimum bounding box" does not allow vertical writing
672.body:
The definition is:

> the smallest enclosing rectangle aligned to the horizontal axis within which all the points of a shape lie 

This obviously does not work for vertical writing.

677.title: Drop “privacy” and/or “security” as categories for consequences
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
677.body: While the “legal” and “financial” have more clear and widely understood boundaries, consequences in the “privacy” and “security” are harder to distuingish. My suggestion would be to drop both privacy and security.

678.title: [Correct errors] - New Requirement needed- Error description / error message / error suggestion should be easy to understand
labels: Path: Errors⹁ task completion and help
678.body:
Under **Correct Errors**, a new requirement should be added stating that error descriptions, 
error messages, and error suggestions must be written in plain language and be easy for 
users to understand.

## Proposed requirement

Error descriptions / error messages / error suggestions:

- **Must use plain language** — avoid technical jargon, system codes, or abstract phrasing
- **Must be easy to understand** — the user should immediately know what went wrong and 
  what to do next
- **Must not be vague** — messages that leave the user guessing do not meet this requirement

## Failure example (real world)

**Scenario:** A form requires the user to check an "I am not a robot" checkbox before 
submitting.

**What happens:** The user submits without checking the checkbox.

**Error message shown:** *"Only humans are allowed to submit this form."*

**Why this fails:**
- The message does not tell the user what action they missed (checking the checkbox)
- It does not tell the user how to fix the error
- A user unfamiliar with CAPTCHA conventions may not connect this message to any specific 
  field or action on the form
- The phrasing is ambiguous and potentially confusing for users with cognitive disabilities

**A plain language alternative would be:**
*"Please check the 'I am not a robot' checkbox to continue."*

682.title: We need a Page Variations conformance requirement
682.body:
Issue #599, which proposes to remove the “keyboard navigable if responsive” provision, raises an issue that WCAG 3 currently doesn't specify that conformance needs to happen at different variations of a page / view. Note 3 of [WCAG 2.2's Full Pages conformance requirement](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#cc2) says:

> A full page includes each variation of the page that is automatically presented by the page for various screen sizes (e.g. variations in a responsive web page). Each of these variations needs to conform (or needs to have a conforming alternate version) in order for the entire page to conform.

We need something like this for WCAG 3.

683.title: If such a guideline doesn't exist yet, some form of guideline around heartbeat audio?
683.body:
It could go under audio control as a section. I'm not sure, but I do know heartbeat audio can be distressing for some users.
So it could be added.

694.title: Page/view title - Ambiguity when applied to non-HTML documents
labels: Path: User orientation⹁ layout and structure
694.body:
Concerns have been raised regarding ambiguity in how this applies to non-HTML documents (e.g., PDF, Word, plain text) as well as non-document content such as creative works (e.g., films, poems, images). Certain formats may not support programmatically defined titles, and in some cases a meaningful or structured title may not be available. Additional guidance is needed to clarify the scope and applicability across different content types.

Quoting from the doc:
> This is assuming there is an HTML document (web page). What about other types of documents served up on the web? PDFs, Word documents, plain text documents, etc. Should provide examples/tests for those as well, or limit the scope to web pages/web views within web content.  
> 
> Of note is that the WCAG2ICT task force had quite a debate about non-web documents and applicability of this requirement. Some document formats don't support a programmatic title (e.g plain text files), and some documents (like movies, songs, poems, image files) are works of art, so their title may not be meaningful. An example is an untitled poem with an unknown author, or movie titles are often abstract concepts: The Matrix, for example. When you consider documents delivered on the web, a "meaningful" title may not exist.

722.title: Glossary: Edit Video Definition
722.body:
The WCAG definition of “video” (including the note) is potentially ambiguous in that it does not mention text-based images (which are becoming increasingly common and remain depressingly inaccessible).
#video (current)
video
the technology of moving or sequenced pictures or images
Note: Video can be made up of animated or photographic images, or both.
I recommend adding a Note to the existing definition of video:
#video (recommended amendment)
(Additions in **bold**)
video
the technology of moving or sequenced pictures or images **of content, whether graphic, text-based, or a combination thereof**
Note: Video can be made up of animated or photographic images, or both.

723.title: Glossary: Edit Extended Audio Description
723.body:
Recommend changing the current notes under extended audio description.

This definition does not contemplate the impact of intentional text on audio description needs, and it should acknowledge that it will be far more common when a video contains intentional text.

## Current

Note: This technique is only used when the sense of the video would be lost without the additional audio description and the pauses between dialogue or narration are too short.

## Proposed change

(Additions in **bold**)

Note: This technique is used when **information from** the video would be lost without the additional audio description and the pauses between dialogue or narration are too short.
**Note: Videos that contain intentional text are more likely to require extended audio description.**

728.title: 6. Glossary: UPDATE Audio Description Definition
728.body:
## Current as of WCAG 2.2

narration added to the soundtrack to describe important visual details that cannot be understood from the main soundtrack alone

Note 1: Audio description of video provides information about actions, characters, scene changes, on-screen text, and other visual content.

Note 2: In standard audio description, narration is added during existing pauses in dialogue. (See also extended audio description.)

Note 3: Where all of the video information is already provided in existing audio, no additional audio description is necessary.

Note 4: Also called "video description" and "descriptive narration."

## Why this definition should change
This definition is too limited. It focuses on “visual details” and glosses over the importance of text and graphics shared via video. It does not recognize the ever-growing prevalence of text-based content being used, both in live and in prerecorded materials. 

Live presentations often include “screen shares” of text documents, spreadsheets, slideshows, graphs, charts, etc. When this type of content is shared, it is the heart of that portion of the presentation and, as such, is necessarily important enough to be audio described. However, this content is often NOT audio described based on either aesthetics or an ableist assumption that “everyone” can “just read” the content on the screen. This is the environment where WCAG is needed to both provide access AND educate society about the necessity for accessible materials. 
 
Undeniably, some text captured in a video is not “important” enough to be described. For example, in a camera shot of a dozen fast-food restaurants (including their signage), the names of each restaurant might not be important to the video. Instead, a brief description that the shot shows “fast-food restaurants littered down both sides of the road into town” might be sufficient.

However, the existing WCAG definition of “audio description” is insufficient in many cases of text on the screen. (Note: I do not use the term “caption” in this recommendation. WCAG has defined “caption” in another context, and it would add ambiguity that we don’t need.) In many videos, text is used to convey meaning, but the current definition is ambiguous.
In common parlance, many would not include text in the definition of “visual details,” and what is “important” is exceptionally subjective. 

- For example, some might not consider text on the screen that identifies a speaker (by name and/or position) to be “important.” Yet this information provides context and assists the listener in identifying voices. Additionally, the text is obviously somewhat important because the video creator has taken extra steps to add the text to the video (text overlay).
- In other cases, text is the entire subject of the video, such as in the increasingly-popular trend of holding up a series of hand-written signs instead of speaking in the video. In these cases, the text on the handwritten sign is the core of the video. While this type of type would likely be audio described under WCAG (the video is often either silent or playing music in the background), a better, more inclusive definition of audio description would make the need to voice these messages clear and unambiguous.
- Many videos also use documents to convey meaning, but the detail needed to adequately convey the meaning depends on the way the video uses the graphs or graphics for the sighted. Sometimes the graph is conveying a broad theme, and a general description will suffice: “Line graph shows the price of eggs getting higher over time.” In other cases, the graphic is used to convey specific information, and those graphics require audio description in order to make that information accessible (for example, each area of a Venn diagram should be described).
- In some cases, the documents (or graphics with text) used in the video are substantially or wholly text-based. This is a frequent occurrence with informational presentations (including educational content). In these cases, the document should be read aloud in its entirety. If portions of the document are “not important,” then they should not be displayed at all. “Accessibility” demands parity of access to information, so all consumers of the video must have that access. 

A better definition of audio description would differentiate incidental text (such as the multiple restaurant signs) from intentional text (that which is added to the video (text overlay) or constitutes the subject of the video shot).

## Recommended amendment

(additions in **bold**)

audio description
1. narration added to the soundtrack to describe important visual details **or incidental text** that cannot be understood from the main soundtrack alone **and**
2. **verbalization of text overlays added to the video that are not provided by the main soundtrack and**
3. **verbalization of the content of documents and graphics containing text that are not provided by the main soundtrack or provision of an accessible text alternative to the viewer in real-time**

Note 1: Audio description of video provides information about actions, characters, scene changes, on-screen text, and other visual content **as well as verbalization of incidental and intentional text contained in the video content**.

Note 2: In standard audio description, narration is added during existing pauses in dialogue. (See also extended audio description.) **However, standard audio description includes adding pauses in the video and/or the provision of accessible text documents for download whenever pauses in a video's soundtrack do not provide sufficient time to verbalize audio description.**

Note 3: Where all of the video information is already provided in existing audio, no additional audio description is necessary.

Note 4: Also called "video description" and "descriptive narration."

**Note 5: Whenever possible, accessible text alternatives of the content of documents displayed on a video should be available for download and should comply with WCAG 1.3.1.**

733.title: Concerns about the "Avoid Physical Harm" guideline name and description
733.body:
### Issue description
**Guideline name:** The current guideline title “2.6.1 Avoid Physical Harm” (in[ 2.6 Animation and Movement](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#animation-and-movement)) implies that the harm to the user from movement and animation is only physical. But animation and movement can also cause cognitive harm such as preventing users from focusing on tasks and causing fatigue by forcing users to re-orient themselves. 

**Guideline sentence:** The current one-sentence description for this guideline (“Users do not experience physical harm from content”) is worded too broadly. The risk of harm from content is not limited to movement and animation. This guideline description should be more specific to avoid confusion related to other kinds of harm such as child sexual predators, etc.

We suggest the following rewording:

- Change “Avoid physical harm” to “Avoid harm from animation and movement”
- Change one-sentence description to “Users do not experience physical or cognitive harm from content.”

### User needs missing or not adequately addressed  

- **Sensory Processing:** Users may experience sensory processing differences, such as sensory overloads from combinations of movement, flashing, haptics, and audio shifting.
- **Processing:** Complex visual stimulation and movement can lead directly to cognitive overload and fatigue.
- **Cognitive Stress** ([User Story 3.7.4):](https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/#cognitive-stress-user-story) Users with sensitivities need to be able to avoid content that is "busy, confusing, depressing, or has loud noises" or triggers so they can successfully cope with the website and avoid mental fatigue.
- **Distractions** ([User Story 3.5.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/#distractions-user-story)): Users with attention and memory impairments state, "I need tasks to not have distractions," and "I need to turn distractions off easily" because if they lose focus, they forget what they are doing. See [Amy Scenario 2: Changing Color Schemes, Flashing, Blinking, and Automatic Playing Videos or Music](https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/#amy-scenario-2-changing-color-schemes-flashing-blinking-and-automatic-playing-videos-or-music).

With thanks,
The COGA Task Force

734.title: WCAG 3 is currently missing pause, stop, hide all moving and scrolling content
734.body:
### **Issue description**
The current working draft of WCAG 3 is missing essential user controls to manage or dismiss content that moves, scrolls, blinks, auto-updates, or changes without user interaction. This functionality should follow existing WCAG criteria[ 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/pause-stop-hide.html). 

Pause, stop, hide for video/animation appears to be absent in “[Animation and Movement](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#animation-and-movement)” and “[Images and Media](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#images-and-media)” of the WCAG 3 draft.

There is a provision that focuses on [pausing/stopping/adjusting the audio in auto-playing audio](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#page-view-audio-adjustable), but we aren’t seeing anything similar that specifies pausing/stopping/hiding auto-playing video/animation. “User settings supported” has a note that mentions “motion” as one of many examples. Is this the only place where WCAG 3 plans to cover pause, stop, hide for video/animation? 

### **User need missing or not adequately addressed** 
As a user with an attention impairment and impaired memory, I need to avoid distraction. If I lose focus and forget what I am doing, I need reminders of what I was doing, so that I can complete my task. ([MCU 3.5.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/#distractions-user-story), intro)

### **More details**
Users with attention deficits or executive function impairments ([like the Yuki persona](https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/use_cases.html#yuki-a-yoga-teacher-who-has-ad-h-d)) lose focus and cannot concentrate on main content if peripheral content (like carousels or news banners) is moving.

### **Recommendations**

- The user can control all carousels, banners, and animated backgrounds. Possible methods include (1) providing a pause or stop or (2) requiring the user to move the carousel forward or backward (in other words, it doesn't auto-scroll)
- Pausing the movement does not obscure the underlying content or remove the user's ability to manually navigate the carousel/banner.
- Follows [MCU Pattern 4.6.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/#limit-interruptions-pattern) (Limit Interruptions).

### **See also**
Development of the AASPIRE Web Accessibility Guidelines for Autistic Web Users, Dora M. Raymaker, Steven K. Kapp, Katherine E. McDonald, Michael Weiner, Elesia Ashkenazy, and Christina Nicolaidis, Published Online:13 Apr 2019 https://doi.org/10.1089/aut.2018.0020

With thanks,
The COGA Task Force

735.title: Animation section is missing a provision about providing explicit text explanations for implied meaning conveyed via animations
735.body:
### **Issue description**
The [Animation and movement section](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#animation-and-movement) is currently missing and needs to cover implied meaning in animations, including but not limited to the implied meaning in gifs. 

We recommend looking into providing access to explanations for animations.

We recognize that an exception may be needed for instructional animations, which are often part of user interface interactions.

### **Other provisions and resources**
- Text and Wording has [Non-literal language explained](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#non-literal-language-explained), which covers non-literal language in text (but not animations). 
- Images and Media has [Visual information identified](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#visual-information-identified), but it doesn’t mention facial expressions or implied meaning.
- Making Content Usable ([4.1.12 Explain Implied Content](https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/#explain-implied-content-pattern)) requires meaning of text where implied or ambiguous information may cause misunderstandings. 

### **User need missing or not adequately addressed** 

- Users with autism may need explicit explanations where animations may be misleading or confusing from implicit meanings or characteristics of the animation.
- As an autistic user, I need explanations of implied or ambiguous information seen in animations so I do not misunderstand the literal meaning.

### **Recommendations**

- Review all animations used for communication or emotional expression.
- Provide supplementary text or definitions close to the animation (or via supported markup) explaining the implied content (e.g., sarcasm, metaphor, or specific emotion).
- Follows [Making Content Usable Pattern 4.4.12 (Explain Implied Content)](https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/#explain-implied-content-pattern).

With thanks,
The COGA Task Force

736.title: Need to change the name for “Trigger warning available”
736.body:
### **Current draft provision and note**
[Core requirement: Trigger warning available](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#trigger-warning-available) 
A warning is provided before users encounter triggers and a mechanism is available to access the same information without the triggering [content](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-content).

Note: Triggers are flashing, motion lasting more than 5 seconds, and pseudo-motion.

### **Issue description**
“Trigger warnings” is a phrase that usually is about supporting emotional health. So the provision is confusing if that is not included. At a minimum, please change the provision short name. 
 
### **Recommendation**
Call this provision “Motion warnings available.”

With thanks,
The COGA Task Force

737.title: Haptics needs to be added User Settings Supported, and check the overlap with Haptic stimulation adjustable.
737.body:
### **Issue description**
Although the Animation section has a provision “[Haptic stimulation adjustable](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#haptic-stimulation-adjustable),” this focuses on the local level. We recommend adding haptics as an example in the note in the [core requirement for “User Settings Supported”](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#user-settings-supported).

We also found it confusing what the difference in scope was between [Haptic stimulation adjustable](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#haptic-stimulation-adjustable) and [User Settings Supported](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#user-settings-supported). Can [Haptic stimulation adjustable](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#haptic-stimulation-adjustable) be removed if it is included in [User Settings Supported](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#user-settings-supported)? Is it necessary to have haptics in both places?

### **Recommendations**

- Include some form of haptic support in "User settings supported," which currently has a note that says "Accessibility-related user settings include font size, icon size, color scheme, magnification, and motion." Or make clearer in the note that the settings "...include but are not limited to..."
- Evaluate if [Haptic stimulation adjustable](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#haptic-stimulation-adjustable) is still necessary in the Animation section if it is explicitly covered in the "User controls" section. 

With thanks,
The COGA Task Force

738.title: Question regarding photosensitivity and the scope of the "Visual stimulation" provision
738.body:
### **Current draft**
[Requirement: Visual stimulation Exploratory](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#visual-stimulation): Visual stimulation from combinations of density, color, movement, etc. can be reduced or turned off.

### **Issue description**
We know this is still a very early draft of this exploratory provision, but it's not clear if this is strictly related to a user need for photosensitivity, or if additional user needs can be supplied. 

We think this is potentially very useful, and COGA would be happy to discuss this with you.

With thanks,
The COGA Task Force

739.title: Pseudo-motion: Expand to include examples, and consider making this its own provision.
739.body:
### **Issue description**
**Pseudo-motion definition:** The term "pseudo-motion" is used in two Animation and Movement provisions: [No visual motion](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#no-visual-motion) and [No visual motion (no exceptions)](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#no-visual-motion-no-exceptions). WCAG 3 [currently defines “pseudo-motion”](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-pseudo-motion) as “static content on the page that gives the user the perception or feeling of motion” but does not include any examples. 

Please expand the provision or the definition to include examples such as: 

- parallax scrolling
- sharp color changes
- dynamically updating content
- zoom effects
- diagonal lines in a background
- optical illusions 
- stereographic art

**Pseudo-motion provision:** Please also consider making “No pseudo-motion” its own provision rather than bundling it into “No visual motion.” We want WCAG 3 to be really clear that no pseudo-motion should be allowed at all. The current “No visual motion” provisions could be misread as “Content does not include pseudo-motion…lasting longer than 5 seconds.”

### **User need missing or not adequately addressed** 
Users with motion sensitivity can struggle with pseudo motion. These kinds of motions induce sensory mismatch for users with vestibular disorders, can cause migraines, and contribute to cognitive overload.
 
### **Recommendations**

- Redefine pseudo-motion to include examples.
- Consider making “No pseudo-motion” its own provision.

### **See also**
The impact of motion animation on cognitive disability (Edwards, 2022). https://vispero.com/resources/the-impact-of-motion-animation-on-cognitive-disability/

With thanks,
The COGA Task Force

comments.body: Please consider whether the new [decoy font - warning possible pseudomotion on this page ](https://www.mixfont.com/experiments/decoy-font)causes pseudo motion. It may be an excellent example.
These fonts give me a headache - I am not able to look at them.  To me they appear blurry.
One more example of pseudo-motion to consider: Gamma Oscillation images or Sliced Images.

742.title: "Sentences do not include unnecessary words" is not internationally testable
742.body:
Supplemental requirement: [Sentences do not include unnecessary words.](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#no-unnecessary-words)

This appears straightforward in English, but its interpretation is language-dependent.

For example, Japanese has the following pair of sentences:

- 朝は静かだ。
- 朝は静か。


Both are natural Japanese, and the meaning is substantially the same. They mean "The morning is quiet."

Some Japanese grammarians consider "だ" to be a word, while others do not.  (See #547)

If the copula だ is considered a word, does this requirement imply that the second sentence is preferable because it contains one fewer word?  

If not, how should "unnecessary" be determined?

This is not merely a question of style. Different analyses of Japanese do not even agree on the grammatical status of だ. Some analyses treat it as a separate copula, while others analyze 静かだ as a single adjectival form. Consequently, there is no obvious language-independent interpretation of "unnecessary words."

The problem is therefore not simply the definition of "word". Even if the notion of word were defined, the requirement still needs language-specific normative criteria for determining whether a word is unnecessary.

Without such criteria, it is unclear how this requirement can be interpreted or tested consistently across languages.

If "Sentences do not include unnecessary words." were merely editorial guidance, I would have no objection. However, it is presented as a Supplemental requirement rather than guidance. Therefore, it should have objective interpretation and evaluation criteria. At present, such criteria are not provided.

744.title: Update the definition of text
744.body:
The [current definition](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-text) is:
> sequence of characters that can be [programmatically determined](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-programmatically-determinable), where the sequence is expressing something in [human language](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-human-language)

We also have a requirement that visually available text is programmatically:
> **Requirement**: All visible [text](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-text) has a [programmatically determinable](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-programmatically-determinable) equivalent.
> **Applies when**: Content includes contains text that is informative to the user, including text embedded in image formats.
> **Except when**:
> - making visible text programmatically determinable would lead to duplication within the page/view.
> - text is [decorative](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#dfn-decorative), is used only for visual formatting, or is not presented to users.

The definition of text itself doesn't make a requirement, so that is needed, but clashes with the definition.

Also, in WCAG 3 we've had conversations about steering clear of the format aspect, so whether text is added with unicode, images, or something else, it is still text. If an icon is implemented with unicode, i.e. not something in human language, it is not text.

I propose that we simplify the definition to:
> sequence of characters that is expressing something in [human language](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-human-language)

747.title: "Transcripts available" does not account for signed content
747.body:
## Provision content (at time of writing)

> Core requirement: Transcripts available
> Transcripts are available for all audio and video content.
>
> Except when
> * The audio or video content is an alternative for text and clearly labelled as such.
> * It is a background video with no spoken content.

## Issue and feedback

In the "except when" list, "background video" is implied to mean there is "no spoken content". If the definition of "background video" (or if there's a term planned to replace this one) includes language about spoken content, it should also include language about signed content.

We should elaborate further since there are additional ways of communicating meaningful content. For example, maybe a person is holding up a poster board with text written on it. I'm sure there are more we should consider, so should we pose the question to AGWG for broader input?

748.title: "Speakers identified" should apply beyond video content
labels: P - Speakers identified in audio descriptions
748.body:
## Provision content (at time of writing)

> Speakers are identified understandably within all media alternatives.
>
> Applies when
> * There are multiple speakers in the video.
>
> Except when
> * The speaker has a hidden identity as part of narrative structure.
> * Identity is identifiable within the context of use.
>
> EXAMPLE
> Initially using “Maya Angelou” within the context of a story regarding poetry and then using “Angelou”

## Issue and feedback

The provision states it only applies when there are multiple speakers in the video. This language should be updated to broaden the applicability beyond just video.

I propose using a generalized term like "media" because it accounts for:
* Audio without video
* Video without audio
* Video with audio

761.title: 'process' Definition Alignment Needed: WCAG 3 changes are too specific/restrictive, Old definition doesn't quite work either.
761.body:
Raising a concern regarding the changes to the definition of "process." Because process is a cross-provisioning concept that impacts multiple areas, we need to align on this updated language. Our sub-group is finding both the old and new definitions a bit hard to use, particularly with regards to multi-step processes.
Raising a concern regarding the changes to the definition of "process." Because process is a cross-provisioning concept that impacts multiple areas, we need to align on this updated language. Our sub-group is finding both the old and new definitions a bit hard to use, particularly with regards to multi-step processes.

**Current vs. Previous Definitions**

*   **WCAG 2.2 defined ['process'](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-processes) as:**
    > series of user actions where each action is required in order to complete an activity
    > *(Examples: Shopping site checkout, Turing test before registration)*

    *Referenced in: §§ [2.4.5 Multiple Ways](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#ref-for-dfn-processes-1), [3.3.7 Redundant Entry](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#ref-for-dfn-processes-2), [3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#ref-for-dfn-processes-3), [3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#ref-for-dfn-processes-4), [5.2.3 Complete processes](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#ref-for-dfn-processes-5), and in definitions for [mechanism](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#ref-for-dfn-processes-7), [Status Messages](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#ref-for-dfn-processes-8), and an [example under supplemental content](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#ref-for-dfn-processes-9)

*   **WCAG 3 defines ['process'](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#dfn-process) as:**
    > series of [views](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#dfn-view) or [pages](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#dfn-page) associated with user actions, where actions required to complete an activity are performed, often in a certain order, regardless of the technologies used or whether it spans different sites or domains
    *Referenced in: §§ [2.4.1.8 No keyboard traps](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-1), [2.4.2.1 Navigation keys described](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-2), [2.9.1.2 Cognitive test alternatives available](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-3), [2.9.2.2 No time limits](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-4), [2.9.3.1 Preselections visible](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-5), [2.9.4.1 Going back supported](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-6), [2.9.4.2 No redundant entry](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-7), [2.9.4.3 Progress saved](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-8), [2.9.5.2 Information requirements available at start](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-9), [2.9.5.3 Process instructions available](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-10), [3. Conformance](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-11), [3.2.1 Conformance level](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-12), [3.2.3 Defined conformance scope](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-13), and definitions for [mechanism](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-15), and [usability testing](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag3/#ref-for-dfn-process-16)

**Questions for Alignment**
1.  **Why was the original definition changed?** What was the primary driver or use case behind the change? 
2.  **Can we iterate on this?** The new definition feels overly specific and restrictive for our current needs. Calling it a "series of views or pages" sounds strictly like a multi-step process. Outside of the usage of the word "required," in both definition could be applied much more broadly and offered the flexibility needed to accommodate different workflows which might have optional steps or fields.

**Proposed Alternative**
We like the definition of *"Path: one or more elements that support a specific user activity"* and think its structure could be applied well to the definition of process. Our sub-group propose iterating toward something like:
> **Process:** A pre-defined path consisting of interactions intended to achieve a specific outcome.

This gets us away from using the word "series" (which implies sequence to some) and allows the concept to be applied much better to single-page websites and experiences. and "required" since some of these steps are optional.

@giacomo-petri, @hbellis, @Lboniello — please chime in with any additions or corrections or misunderstanding on my part.

771.title: Approach to ACT tests and accessibilty supported
771.body:
Given the updates to accessibility supported (where we will have a default "accessibility support set"), I think there is a change needed to how we frame ACT tests.

This also overlaps with the constant friction between "authors should just follow the standards", and "things need to work for disabled people in real life", mediated by the "accessibility supported" feature in WCAG.

In WCAG 2, the ACT tests have an assumed set of user-agents / AT that are tested against. If something doesn't work, it might be noted in the test.

In WCAG 3, we should have (and will define soon) a default "accessibility support set". Therefore we can carry on including examples which pass, regardless of whether they follow standards.

For example, in the [page-titled tests](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/pull/696/changes#diff-65408a69cf2086445e07f918a6bb2af6bb9110d2b222024de3543b4a5a736871) it includes examples which are not valid HTML, but work in practice.

I'm raising this issue in case people want to argue that we should remove invalid examples.

775.title: Consider unbundling “Pointer contrast sufficient” so pointer size gets its own provision
775.body:
[Pointer contrast sufficient](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#pointer-contrast-sufficient) currently covers two things—contrast and size: “The default pointer meets the @@[non-text-contrast] requirement, and is at least as large as the platform default.”

Consider unbundling these two aspects so each gets its own provision. This would make the [“Pointer Focus Appearance” subsection](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#pointer-focus-appearance) more consistent with the [“Keyboard Focus Appearance” subsection](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#keyboard-focus-appearance), which has separate provisions for contrast and size. 

Or, if there’s a reason for bundling these pointer aspects together, consider renaming the provision so it’s clear from the short name that this provision covers size as well as contrast.

Also, as you build out the tests and methods involving pointer size, please clarify which aspects of size are important, such as:
* Area 
* Thickness of the outline

Thanks for considering!

782.title: “Sensory characteristics not relied on” leaves out haptics/touch
labels: P - Sensory characteristics not relied on
782.body:
**Issue description**
