The requirement should be sufficiently bounded judgment that the result is not arbitrary or based on personal biases. A conformance system in which two competent evaluators can examine substantially the same product, agree on the underlying facts, and nevertheless assign materially different conformance levels because of discretionary scoring is not ready to serve as an international compliance benchmark.

## WCAG 2 compatibility should be transparent, not controlling

[ITIC](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues/284) requests mapping between WCAG 2 and WCAG 3. [Sydney Coleman](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues/506) raises the substantial “compliance debt” organizations may incur when moving from WCAG 2 to WCAG 3. Both concerns deserve serious attention. We strongly support a comprehensive crosswalk. Organizations worldwide have built policies, procurement standards, training, automated tools, design systems, contracts, audit methodologies, and legal requirements around WCAG 2. A migration without an authoritative mapping would impose unnecessary cost and confusion.

However, backward compatibility should not become a normative constraint that prevents WCAG 3 from correcting genuine weaknesses in WCAG 2. Nor should WCAG 3 weaken existing accessibility protections merely because its new architecture makes them inconvenient. The Working Group should eventually publish a requirement-by-requirement mapping identifying whether each WCAG 2.2 A/AA provision is equivalent to, stronger than, weaker than, divided among, subsumed by, or absent from WCAG 3 (similar things were done for WCAG 2 vs. WCAG 1). Where WCAG 3 intentionally reduces an existing requirement, that change should be explicit and justified. Where it strengthens requirements, transition guidance can address implementation burden without compromising the technical definition of accessibility.

## Small organizations need scalable assessment, not reduced accessibility

[Jeanne Spellman](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues/388) asks how WCAG 3 can remain usable by personal websites and small businesses that cannot afford extensive expert assessment.  The underlying concern is legitimate. A standard that can only be credibly evaluated through a large professional audit will have serious adoption problems. The solution, however, should not be to define accessibility differently according to the claimant’s audit budget.

Small organizations benefit from better authoring tools, accessible components, accessible templates, automated testing, clear requirements, inexpensive testing methodologies, targeted sampling, good documentation, education, and straightforward self-assessment. Legal systems may separately recognize proportionality, undue burden, or other exceptions where appropriate. The accessibility need of the user does not change according to the annual revenue of the website owner.

The distinction between technical accessibility and legal burden is again useful. The European Web Accessibility Directive expressly considers organizational size, resources, costs, and benefits when determining disproportionate burden. [[Directive (EU) 2016/2102]](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32016L2102) That is where such considerations belong. A standards body should identify accessibility requirements; a legislature or regulator can determine the circumstances under which a particular actor may be excused from satisfying them.

## A proposed architecture

AFixt recommends that the Working Group reorganize the WCAG 3 conformance architecture around distinct dimensions rather than attempting to encode all accessibility information in Bronze, Silver, and Gold.

* Normative accessibility requirements. These describe the minimum user-facing conditions necessary for accessibility. All applicable minimum requirements within the claimed scope must be satisfied for conformance. Full stop.
* Conformance scope. This identifies precisely what product, service, application, pages/views, processes, states, or other material is covered by the claim.
* Evaluation methodology and confidence. This describes what was actually examined, how representative samples were selected, what automation and manual testing were performed, what technologies were used, known limitations, and the degree of confidence supporting a scope-wide conclusion.
* Accessibility severity and risk. This communicates the consequences of identified nonconformities and assists remediation prioritization without converting known failures into conformity.
* Functional coverage. This identifies the disability-related functional needs addressed by requirements and evaluations and helps prevent systematic omission of groups whose needs are difficult to express through conventional technical tests.
* Accessibility assurance and maturity. This encompasses Assertions concerning governance, policies, training, design practices, procurement, user research, monitoring, testing, and remediation. It describes the organization’s capacity to produce and maintain accessibility but does not compensate for inaccessible product outcomes.
* Enhanced accessibility performance. This is the natural home for Bronze/Silver/Gold or another graduated model. Once the minimum conformance floor is satisfied, higher levels can recognize Supplemental Requirements, enhanced outcomes, and other achievements beyond the minimum.

Such a model would permit substantially richer accessibility reporting than WCAG 2 while preserving the integrity of the conformance decision.

WCAG 3 Conformance: Conforms. Enhanced Accessibility: Silver. Evaluation Confidence: High. Accessibility Assurance Maturity: Level 3.

Another organization might report:

WCAG 3 Conformance: Does Not Conform. Evaluation Confidence: High. One critical nonconformity prevents keyboard-only users from completing authentication. Enhanced accessibility performance is otherwise high.

The second statement contains more useful information than simply awarding the product Bronze because its strengths elsewhere outweigh the failure. It acknowledges the organization’s achievements without declaring an exclusionary experience conforming.

## Conclusion

We support the Working Group’s effort to make WCAG 3 more inclusive, outcome-oriented, scalable, and representative of modern digital products. We support stronger consideration of complete processes rather than isolated pages, functional needs rather than technology alone, representative sampling rather than impractical exhaustive testing, user outcomes rather than source-code formalism, organizational accessibility practices, severity, and accessibility beyond the minimum requirements historically represented by WCAG 2 A and AA.

WCAG 3 is trying to communicate several kinds of information that are all important, but they are not the same information and should not be collapsed into a single designation. A conformance result should answer the conformity question. Other parts of the reporting model can, and should, say much more.

The recurring problems visible throughout the Conformance issue history—sampling, automation, scoring, reproducibility, scope, severity, Assertions, Core versus Supplemental requirements, functional needs, page variations, small-business burden, legal usability, and retro-compatibility—become substantially easier to reason about once conformance is separated from the other dimensions the Working Group is attempting to measure. [[WCAG 3 Conformance Issues]](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3AConformance)

WCAG 3 should be more sophisticated about accessibility than WCAG 2 is. That increased sophistication should not come at the cost of making conformance itself less determinate. A known accessibility barrier affecting one population should not become conforming because an organization accumulated accessibility successes elsewhere. An organization’s good processes should not compensate for an inaccessible product. A low-severity failure should not become a passing requirement merely because its aggregate impact is considered small. An untested portion of a system should not become accessible by inference merely because exhaustive testing is impractical. An accessibility requirement should not become Supplemental because it is expensive to implement. A disability-related need should not receive weaker normative protection because standards developers find it difficult to test.

The last point is especially important. WCAG has historically been strongest where accessibility needs can be translated into deterministic technical requirements. WCAG 3 presents an opportunity to extend equally meaningful protection to needs that do not fit that model. It would be a serious mistake to respond to the difficulty of doing so by making those needs less normative.

Most importantly, difficulty in measuring an accessibility need should be understood as a limitation of the available assessment methodology. It is not a reason to treat the underlying need as less important or to give it weaker normative status.

For that reason, we recommends that the Working Group establish a clear, non-compensatory minimum conformance floor; remove implementation difficulty and expense as criteria for determining whether an accessibility requirement is Supplemental; separate Assertions and organizational maturity from product-level conformity; treat sampling as evidence supporting a conformance conclusion rather than an exception to accessibility requirements; report severity separately from conformity; develop explicit rules governing scope, processes, states, and variations; and use functional performance statements to ensure equitable coverage rather than as containers for compensatory scoring.

Bronze, Silver, and Gold can still have substantial value. Their strongest role, however, is not to redefine what it means for a product to conform. Their strongest role is to recognize organizations that go beyond the minimum. That architecture would preserve the innovations the Working Group is seeking while producing a standard that is clearer for authors, more reproducible for evaluators, more useful for regulators and purchasers, more compatible with established conformity-assessment principles, and, most importantly, more defensible from the perspective of the people with disabilities whose access WCAG exists to protect.

820.title: Input method versus input modality
labels: Path: Input and focus⹁ interactive components
820.body:
The term “[_method_](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-method)” carries a specific meaning in the guidelines:

> detailed information, either technology-specific or technology-agnostic, on ways to satisfy the [requirement](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-requirement)

The current “[Input method flexible](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#input-method-flexible)” provision uses “_method_” more generally. Perhaps “_modality_” would be more accurate and avoid confusion?

Relates back to [a change in PR #812](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/pull/812#discussion_r3817334129).

822.title: Refine "Data entry validated" text
822.body:
Hello, I am shepherding the data entry validated rule.  I imagine this is intended to discourage the practice of having disruptive errors. I listed out a few issues with the current wording, some of these I found some of these were found by others working in the sub-group.

**Current text:**
Data entered is validated after the user enters data, either:
- when the user leaves the field, or
- when the form is submitted.

**issues:**
* **Presentation implied but not stated:** By “data is validated” we seem to mean validation information is presented (that’s what the method says), but that isn’t explicit. In code, the function that does the validation (e.g., figure out if one or more rules applies) and then acts on the results to present some kind of message are usually separated. Should we make it more explicit what we mean?
* **Real-time password verification failure:** While generally considered a cognitively accessible solution, if we were to continue with this requirement as stated, real-time password verification would fail. While getting an interruptive or distracting message while filling out a form/entering a password is likely the real issue, password fields that do real-time password verification are not necessarily the problem; it's the cadence and frequency of the error being read, I would assume.

**Proposed rewrite:**
**Title:** Presentation of data-entry validation

The presentation of data validation is communicated after the user enters data, either when:
- the user leaves the field, or
- the form is submitted.

Applies when:
A data entry field has defined validation rules or constraints (e.g., required fields, specific formatting, or value ranges) that is presented to the user to remediate.

Except when:
- The validation provides real-time, non-disruptive feedback toward meeting complex constraints (e.g., password requirements) and does not mark the field as invalid or interrupt the user's focus with notifications on input.

@hidde for visibility

823.title: Target size guideline removed from the draft in mid-2025: where was this discussed?
823.body:
Hello,

I am a digital accessibility auditor and developer, and I was tracing the history of target size guidance across WCAG versions when I noticed the following.

The [December 2024 Working Draft](https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/WD-wcag-3.0-20241212/#target-size) contained guideline 2.4.3 Target size, "Users are not required to accurately position a pointer in order to view or operate content", with two exploratory requirements:

- Target size minimum: "The combined target size and spacing to adjacent targets is at least 24x24 pixels"
- Target size optimum: "The combined target size and spacing to adjacent targets is at least 48x48 pixels"

The guideline and both requirements were removed in two commits within PR #318: [2905c2d](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/commit/2905c2de5401ad09b7907ddddc40232406c12907) on 24 June 2025, and [16ece1e](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/commit/16ece1ef54949822c1cbc8f07f03a0755aa84e0e) on 16 July 2025.

The PR discussion does not mention target size. The change log entry for the September 2025 Working Draft records "removed exploratory content from draft" but does not mention this guideline.

The guideline does not appear in the September 2025 or March 2026 Working Drafts. It is also absent from the current Editor's Draft under any name, unlike other guidelines from the same section, which were either kept or renamed. And it does not carry the editor's note that points readers to the Editor's Draft for exploratory requirements, because it is no longer there either.

I have not been able to find any record of a decision. Could someone point to where this was discussed, or confirm whether the removal was intentional?

Related: #808, where the COGA Task Force asks for target size and target spacing provisions to be added to Control Information.

Thank you for your time, and for the work the group is doing on WCAG 3.

Yoann Fortin

830.title: Submission status notified - programmatic as well
830.body:
From [Seth Morrow on the comments list](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-agwg-comments/2026Aug/0001.html):

<hr>

I am submitting a focused comment on the current WCAG 3 Working Draft
concerning Guideline 2.5.2, particularly the supplemental requirement
“Submission status notified.”

The current requirement says that data entry interfaces notify users of
submission status when submission succeeds or fails, and its test checks
that the user is notified immediately afterward. However, it does not
explicitly require that the submission outcome be conveyed
programmatically. That differs from nearby requirements such as “Page/view
change notified,” which explicitly require both a visual change and
programmatic notification, and “Change of content notified,” which requires
meaningful visual changes such as status or error messages to be conveyed
programmatically.

I suggest making equivalent programmatic access explicit for submission
state, and distinguishing pending or indeterminate state from confirmed
success and failure when those states exist.

Possible requirement language:

“When a data submission is initiated, its meaningful submission state is
available visually and programmatically. Pending or indeterminate,
confirmed success, and failure are distinguishable when those states exist.
A confirmed-success state is not communicated while the result remains
pending or indeterminate.”

This could remain implementation-neutral. A synchronous operation that
returns a confirmed result immediately would not need an artificial pending
state. For asynchronous or network-dependent submissions, however, a user
should not receive an accessible equivalent of “submitted successfully”
until the application has actually reached that state.

A useful test matrix would include:

- Initiate a submission whose response is intentionally delayed; verify
   that pending/indeterminate state, when presented visually, is also
   programmatically available.
- Complete the submission successfully; verify that the transition to
   confirmed success is conveyed visually and programmatically without
   requiring an unrelated focus movement. 
- Cause a server or network failure; verify that failure is conveyed
   visually and programmatically and that confirmed success is not announced.
- Where the outcome message is temporary, verify that users have
   sufficient opportunity to perceive or revisit the result.

This is especially important for consequential submissions such as
applications, payments, medical or benefits forms, emergency-service
requests, and other transactions where uncertainty about whether the action
completed can itself cause harm. A sighted user may see a spinner, banner,
restored form contents, or visual error state while an assistive-technology
user receives no equivalent state transition—or receives an optimistic
success message that is later contradicted visually.

I also suggest considering whether “Submission status notified” should
remain supplemental. For a data-entry interface, knowing whether a
submitted action succeeded or failed is often necessary to complete the
task at all, and programmatic outcome awareness seems analogous to the core
treatment already given to page/view changes and meaningful content changes

862.title: Content conformance requirements have a contradictory dependency on conformance claims
862.body:
## Problem

The following statement in the [section titled "3.2 Conformance requirements"](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#conformance-requirements) limits the content that is allowed to conform by creating a dependency on a conformance claim:

>For a specified conformance scope to conform to WCAG 3, all core requirements MUST be satisfied.

To see the dependency that creates the limitation, replace "conformance scope" with its definition:

>For a specified product, set of Pages/Views, content, functionality, or components selected to be part of a conformance claim to conform to WCAG 3, all core requirements MUST be satisfied.

Because a product, set of Pages/Views, functionality, or components are all blobs of content, This effectively means:

>For content selected to be part of a conformance claim to conform to WCAG 3, all core requirements MUST be satisfied.

The ramification is that there are no requirements that apply to content that is not selected to be part of a conformance claim.

With this limiting scope, it is not possible to apply the provisions to content unless the content has been designated to be included in a conformance claim, which contradicts the following statement from the [section titled "3.2.2 Defined conformance scope"](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#defined-conformance-scope):

>A conformance claim is not required in order to conform to WCAG 3. 

## Proposed Solution

The definition of the term "Conformance scope" includes the term "content" as an alternative to "product", "set of Pages/Views", "functionality", and "components". In other words, the terms "product", "set of Pages/Views", "functionality", and "components" are not doing any special lifting. The additional terms are all different amounts of content. However, the unqualified term "content" is included, and it is an unspecified amount of content. Thus, the requirements should be applicable to any amount of content.

This makes removing what appears to be an unintentional limitation very simple. We can simplify the conformance requirements to be:

>For content to conform to WCAG 3, all core requirements MUST be satisfied.

However, we could remove the passive voice and make the statement stronger with the following minor revision:

>For content to conform to WCAG 3, the content MUST satisfy all core requirements.

[Preview the proposed solution](https://deploy-preview-861--wcag3.netlify.app/guidelines/#conformance-requirements) that is implemented in PR #861.

863.title: Feedback for the Introduction plain language disclosure
863.body:
I was reviewing the latest draft of WCAG 3.0, and paused when I got to [the first plain language summary in the Introduction section](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#introduction). I'd like to offer some content suggestions to further simplify the language used here, as well as the thinking behind it. The hope is it can be useful as a starting point for helping people understand the standard. ## Use of normative Current: >_This summary is non-normative._ Proposed: >This summary is [not official](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-normative). We call this _non-normative_. It was written to help you understand. Reasoning: - "Normative" is jargon, even to the point where some web accessibility practitioners I know do not know the term or what it means. - Replacing it with "not official" communicates the same underlying intent, but with a less obscure and more widely understood word. - Linking to [the definition of of normative](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag-3.0/#dfn-normative) allows a reader to self-serve in the moment on what official means, using the appropriate, agreed upon terminology. ## First bullet point Current: >- W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0 shows ways to make web content and apps usable by people with disabilities. WCAG 3 is a newer standard than the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2. Proposed: >- This document shows ways to make web content and apps usable by people with disabilities. >- The name of this document is called "W3C Accessibility Guidelines 3.0". It can be shorted to "WCAG". >- This is the third big update to WCAG. This big update is version 3.0. It is newer than [version 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/). >- WCAG version 2.2 is the current official version. >- WCAG version 3.0 is a [draft](https://www.w3.org/standards/types/#WD) and still being worked on. Reasoning: - There are three separate topics in the original sentence: What the document is for, what the document's name and its acronym are, and then that the standard is newer than WCAG 2.0. Breaking them out helps ensure one thought per bullet point. - The use of "big" is a proxy term for the standard's major version bump, using a more commonly-understood term. - Keeping the version numbers consistent as "3.0" and "2.2" and not "3" and 2" reduces ambiguity and avoids potential confusion. - We explicitly state that version 2.2 is normative using the new plain language terminology, and also link to it. - We then also state that version 3.0 is a draft, then link to the normative definition of what that means. ## Second bullet point Current: >- WCAG 3 does not replace WCAG 2. WCAG 2 is used around the world and will still be required by different countries for a long time to come. Proposed: >- WCAG version 3.0 does not replace WCAG version 2.2. >- WCAG version 2.2 is used around the world. >- WCAG version 2.2 will be required by many places for a long time to come. Reasoning: - The original sentence contains multiple topics. We break them apart. - We intentionally avoid using the term "countries" because both public legislature and private organizations consume WCAG. - We preserve the global scope to help reinforce the importance of the standard. ## Third bullet point Current: >- Meeting WCAG 2 at AA level means you will be close to meeting WCAG 3, but there may be differences. Proposed: >- There are [three levels of support](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#cc1) in WCAG version 2.2. They are A, AA, and AAA. >- Supporting level AA means you will be close to also supporting WCAG version 3.0. >- There will be some new things you will need to consider. Reasoning: - We introduce the current version 2.2 levels of support, for people who may not be familiar with them. - Once that is established, we communicate that supporting WCAG 2.2 AA does not mean you also support WCAG 3.0. ## Fourth bullet point Current: >This draft only includes requirements that have reached the developing status. This means that we have a general agreement on the topic but not all the details are worked out. Proposed: >- The people who work on WCAG version 3.0 all agree on the rules listed here. >- The rules are also still being worked on and some things may change. Reasoning: - I am trying to avoid using the term "developing status", as it isn't something we can link to for a definition. - Instead I'm trying to break apart the two thoughts: that there is consensus, but it is also a working draft. ## Fifth bullet point Current: >- We would like feedback on this draft. You can raise a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues) or email [public-agwg-comments@w3.org](mailto:public-agwg-comments@w3.org?subject=WCAG%203.0%20public%20comment). Proposed: >- We would like feedback on this draft. You can [email us](mailto:public-agwg-comments@w3.org?subject=WCAG%203.0%20public%20comment), or [use GitHub](https://github.com/w3c/wcag3/issues). Reasoning: - I am moving email before GitHub as it is more commonplace and less technically complicated to use. - I also intentionally removed the email address as it is a technical term, `mailto:` will automatically handle populating it and the subject. --- ## In context While the proposed version is longer, I feel it helps by breaking things down into one concept per line. ### Current

This summary is non-normative.

  • W3C Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 3.0 shows ways to make web content and apps usable by people with disabilities. WCAG 3 is a newer standard than the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.
  • WCAG 3 does not replace WCAG 2. WCAG 2 is used around the world and will still be required by different countries for a long time to come.
  • Meeting WCAG 2 at AA level means you will be close to meeting WCAG 3, but there may be differences.
  • This draft only includes requirements that have reached the developing status. This means that we have a general agreement on the topic but not all the details are worked out.
  • We would like feedback on this draft. You can raise a GitHub issue or email public-agwg-comments@w3.org.
### Proposed

This summary is not official. We call this non-normative. It was written to help you understand.

  • This document shows ways to make web content and apps usable by people with disabilities.
  • The name of this document is called "W3C Accessibility Guidelines 3.0". It can be shorted to "WCAG".
  • This is the third big update to WCAG. This big update is version 3.0. It is newer than version 2.2.
  • WCAG version 2.2 is the current official version.
  • WCAG version 3.0 is a draft and still being worked on.
  • WCAG version 3.0 does not replace WCAG version 2.2.
  • WCAG version 2.2 is used around the world.
  • WCAG version 2.2 will be required by many places for a long time to come.
  • There are three levels of support in WCAG version 2.2. They are A, AA, and AAA.
  • Supporting level AA means you will be close to also supporting WCAG version 3.0.
  • There will be some new things you will need to consider.
  • The people who work on WCAG version 3.0 all agree on the rules listed here.
  • The rules are also still being worked on and some things may change.
  • We would like feedback on this draft. You can email us, or use GitHub.

865.title: 'No time limits' should be assertion instead of requirement
865.body:
Hello, I've taken ownership as a shepherd for the 'no time limits' supplemental requirement. The current phrasing needs to be improved to create a testable version of this requirement

Current Text:
"The completion of a [process](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#dfn-process) does not include time limits."

Issues:
* The requirement of no-time limit is not testable without inspecting the code. A time limit could be set at 22hrs (for example).
* There is a contradiction between the existence of supplemental criteria for both 
  * no time limits, and
  * time limits conveyed; as you cannot convey a time limit that does (should) not exist.


This requirement probably works better as an assertion. Criteria already exist for the part of this requirement that *could* be testable, namely:
* [Time limits conveyed](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#time-limits-conveyed) 
* [Time-out adjustable](https://w3c.github.io/wcag3/guidelines/#timeout-adjustable) 

Proposed Solution:
Change requirement into assertion

@hidde for visibility.
